stories.Headline: Google reports that cyberattackers use AI frameworks to automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation
stories.Summary:
The Google Threat Intelligence Group reported that state-sponsored and cybercrime groups are increasingly using generative AI to weaponise flaws. These threat actors used multi-agent offensive frameworks to automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without any human intervention. This shift allows intrusions to occur at machine speed, which represents a paradigm shift in how attacks are executed. The reports were published in November 2026, following an analysis of attacks over a specific three-month period. These automated systems can chain complex attack paths to scale operations significantly and increase the velocity of intrusions.

The exploit_agent framework, found on an exposed staging server, compares patched and unpatched web application code to develop exploits. Attackers use Artex, Cairn, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI, while some experiment with HexStrike AI and the open source Agent Zero. Artex is most common among Chinese-speaking groups, while Cairn targeted the US aerospace sector and PentAGI scanned Asia. Between August and October, hackers used a customized PentAGI platform, and some used ZeroHollow for exploit development and routing. These tools allow actors to reverse engineer patches at machine speed to rapidly weaponise n-day vulnerabilities.

The Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant stated that AI adoption leads to reduced human involvement and increased stealth. They noted that the lower barrier to entry has fueled a wave of LLM-generated exploits that often fail. GTIG observed a Chinese group building its own automated attack framework, which is likely intended for espionage operations. They also found that LLMs improve the output quality of influence campaigns and help IPM networks scale political clickbait. The group assesses with high confidence that cybercrime actors will incorporate autonomous tools to increase their campaign reach.

Matt Hartman, the Merlin chief strategy officer, said that US critical infrastructure faces danger from attacks occurring at machine speed. He noted that water utilities, hospitals, and regional electric utilities cannot win this race if they struggle to patch monthly. Hartman stated that AI dramatically lowers the cost and expertise needed, putting powerful capabilities within reach of smaller groups. State-sponsored groups, including Iran-linked APT42 and multiple Chinese APTs, have already adopted these large language models. Phishing-as-a-Service operators, such as the Jieyou phishing service, are using LLMs to configure their chatbots.

The articles explain that attackers still use compromised credentials and target unpatched systems, but the speed of exploitation has increased. Google first noted an increase in LLMJacking in November, where hackers hijack AI systems to resell usage tokens. Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 also found a Chinese-speaking actor using the Cairn framework against over a dozen organizations. Currently, unrestricted autonomous execution generates forensic traffic and leaves behind distinct code-level traces that defenders can potentially identify. However, the reports indicate that the trend toward automation has now reached a critical inflection point for cyberattacks.

Google anticipates that intrusions will become nearly fully agentic as large language models and agentic frameworks continue to advance. Defenders must nail cybersecurity fundamentals today while accelerating the shift toward automated defenses that respond at machine speed. The articles leave open whether attackers will maintain their current noise levels or become stealthier as tools improve. It remains unclear how many more organizations in Asia and the US will be targeted by these specific frameworks. Future reports will likely track if the success rates of autonomous campaigns compensate for any decreases in stealth.

stories.Headline: Clio finds 53% of high AI users in UK and Irish law firms report revenue gains
stories.Summary:
The practice management provider Clio released a new research report on artificial intelligence adoption in November 2026. This study examined how legal professionals in the United Kingdom, Ireland, and Spain use these new tools. The findings link deeper adoption of the technology with stronger revenue gains for various law firms. Legal professionals reported that AI increased their capacity to handle work and lowered their operational costs. The research relied on the personal assessments of the respondents regarding AI adoption and its impact.

The 2027 UK and Ireland Legal Insights Report shows 53 percent of high AI users reported revenue gains. Only 20 percent of those in the two lowest adoption categories reported similar gains in their revenue. In Spain, 93 percent of mid-sized law firms reported that using artificial intelligence boosted their overall revenue growth. The survey included 580 legal professionals, and 80 of those respondents were already existing Clio customers. Almost 60 percent of professionals say their firms increased their use of fixed fees over the past year.

Ferran Sala stated that firms must adapt their pricing structures and workflows to utilize additional AI capacity. He explained that the most successful firms will redesign their models rather than using criteria from the past. The report suggests that AI helps firms manage growing workloads without necessarily expanding their current staffing levels. Some professionals noted that the technology allows them to maintain existing staff despite an increase in total workload. Others reported that their firms opted to recruit more senior or specialized professionals because of these tools.

About 82 percent of consumers prefer fixed fees, while 76 percent favor pricing based on the final outcome. Only 44 percent of consumers would choose hourly billing, and 63 percent prefer payments based on milestones. Some 26 percent of Spanish respondents used AI for legal questions, and 24 percent decided not to pursue matters. Twenty-eight percent used AI to prepare questions for lawyers, while 23 percent were prompted to contact a professional. Many consumers worry about confidentiality, and 55 percent want reassurance that a lawyer will review the AI output.

The report identifies improvements in working conditions, with 90 percent of AI users reporting reduced stress levels. Additionally, 88 percent of legal professionals using the technology reported an improvement in their overall work-life balance. The research indicates that increased efficiency from AI is putting pressure on traditional hourly billing models for firms. Consumers expressed concerns that AI-assisted work might not be properly reviewed, a worry shared by 31 percent. These findings highlight the importance of transparency when explaining how technology is integrated into professional legal work.

Firms must now determine how to integrate these tools while retaining responsibility for reviewing all the final results. The articles leave open how firms will specifically redesign their workflows to maximize the capacity created by AI. It remains unclear how many firms will fully transition away from hourly billing to meet consumer fee preferences. The reports do not state if these revenue gains will persist as more mid-sized firms adopt the technology. Future success depends on whether firms can mitigate risks related to confidentiality and the review of AI output.

stories.Headline: Wolters Kluwer finds 36% of accounting firms have a written AI policy
stories.Summary:
Wolters Kluwer Tax & Accounting released the third edition of its Future Ready Accountant report on November 18, 2026, based on responses from more than 2,600 accounting professionals worldwide. The report found that firms are growing, confident, and widely adopting AI, but few have redesigned how information, workflows, and professional expertise work together. Jason Marx, CEO of Wolters Kluwer Tax & Accounting, said adopting AI is only the first step and the real advantage comes from connecting it to how the whole firm works. The report states that this transformation is what will turn today's growth into lasting value. The report also found that just 1% of firms see AI as a threat to their business model.

Among firms that expected AI to improve client advisory, 70% say AI has delivered better-than-expected results in client advisory services, followed by research and learning and real-time financial insights at 68%, and fraud detection and risk management at 67%. Only 11% of firms globally report that at least 75% of their technology solutions are integrated. Investment plans show 55% plan to implement AI-enabled tools, 52% plan to improve technology integration, and 51% plan to increase workflow automation. Thirty-six percent of firms have a written, firm-wide AI policy, while 44% provide general AI guidance without a formal policy. Among firms with AI policies or guidance, 57% require professional review of all AI-generated technical outputs.

Ninety-five percent of firms with formal AI governance are optimistic about the profession's future, compared with 77% of firms with no governance. Forty percent of owners and directors report a written AI policy, compared with 30% of staff. Globally, 96% of firms now offer advisory and consulting services, up from 93% in 2025, with 62% considering advisory a key service. Among firms where advisory isn't yet a core service, 40% say clients still see them primarily as "tax people," and the same share say compliance workload leaves too little time for advisory work. Marx said there is no single model for becoming future-ready and firms across markets begin from different regulatory, technology, and talent realities.

Marx said what should remain consistent is the standard of trusted information, professional review and accountability, and relevance to the client. He added that future readiness is a leadership choice requiring firms to decide where expertise creates the greatest value and how new capacity will improve client outcomes. Fifty-eight percent of firms are highly interested in partnerships or joint ventures, and 53% in private equity or third-party investment. Among firms that received PE investment or completed M&A, 90% say their technology infrastructure helped attract the deal. Eighty-five percent of firms report increased revenue, and 81% report improved profitability.

Bain's article by Matthew Crupi, Sanjin Bicanic, and John Hazan describes a mining company's capital projects team that spent a Monday afternoon setting up review of its most critical investment projects. By Tuesday morning, agents had reconciled tens of thousands of documents against cost and schedule data, and the first pass was on the table. Bain defines a signal as a fast and trustworthy read on whether work was done correctly, and says competitive advantage accrues to companies that build signals no one else has. Bain's March 2026 cross-industry survey found 91% of respondents said AI helps them be more productive, and 53% reported higher-quality work. Only 27% said AI helps them do new types of work.

Bain reports that Anthropic says human review became the new limit as agent-written code moved through its own organization. Climate Corporation built soil and climate measurement data across US farmland, Monsanto acquired it for about $930 million in 2013, and Bayer inherited it when it bought Monsanto in 2018. Bayer traces its current AI capability to that deal, and its CIO argues the data, not the model, is the part competitors cannot copy. Bain says agentic AI concentrates judgment into four human responsibilities: intent, constraints, validation, and stewardship. Bain says most failures it has seen were not AI model failures but trace back to one of these four responsibilities going unassigned.

stories.Headline: Oakland City Council extends its AI data center moratorium by 10 months to October 2027
stories.Summary:
The Oakland City Council voted unanimously this week to extend the city's moratorium on AI data centers for 10 months, giving the city time to produce a policy protecting residents from public health and safety dangers posed by data center proliferation. The extension passed at Tuesday's council meeting. It keeps the existing 45-day moratorium in place until Oct. 5, 2027. Councilmember Carroll Fife is leading the City Council's efforts to pass the moratorium. Protesters rallied against data centers outside Oakland city hall in September.

The original 45-day moratorium passed on Oct. 6 and was set to expire on Nov. 20. Mayor Barbara Lee backed the original moratorium in her recent State of the City address. Other California cities that already have passed data center moratoriums include San Francisco, Hayward, Oakley, Richmond, Monterey Park, Gilroy, South El Monte, Montebello, and Calexico. Thirty-five public speakers signed up to talk about the moratorium extension, and almost all of them supported it. A speaker for Care for Community Action said her organization surveyed more than 400 residents and found that 73% favor a permanent ban on all data centers being built in Oakland.

Fife said two of the giants in the tech industry have leased space in West Oakland, and another has shown interest in a downtown location. She said she felt it was imperative to take immediate action to protect Oakland residents from what has been seen in other parts of the country. She said the move is not a rejection of technology or economic growth but guardrails against an industry that has steamrolled individuals throughout the entire globe. She said it is important that staff have the ability to do the appropriate study and outreach so the community has a voice in anything that will impact their lives. Lee said residents need to weigh in on any industry that is trying to come to Oakland.

Bill Gilchrist, director of the city's Planning and Building Department, said the city is committed to looking at areas that might be most severely impacted by land use and residential proximity. He said the city will make sure to engage members of the community who may historically have not been able to participate or be invited to participate in this kind of discussion. He said the idea is to do no harm. Laney College professor Peter Brown said not to cast votes based on the illusion of the old economy, where corporate investment in Oakland meant thousands of lasting, good-paying jobs and property, business, and income taxes flowing into city coffers.

Nyah Tisdell, an East Oakland community organizer with Communities for a Better Environment, said community members say no to data centers that will go straight to East Oakland, which already has so much industry and pollution. Rev. Leslie Bowling-Dyer said data centers are part of the necessary infrastructure for the rise of an economically and politically untouchable class. He said people are not being lunatics displaying an irrational fear of technology.

He said technological innovation is not equivalent to social progress. He said technological advance is not the problem in itself, but the people who control it are. Some of the speakers urged the council to consider a permanent ban on data center development in the city. The articles do not state what specific policy the city will produce during the 10 months.

stories.Headline: European Commission proposes MDR 2.0 package to ease AI medical device rules
stories.Summary:
In December 2025 the European Commission published a proposal to amend the Medical Device Regulation, the In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation and the AI Act in a single legislative package, called the MDR 2.0 proposal in the Comment. The Comment, published in npj Digital Medicine on 18 November 2026, reflects the situation of 26 August 2026 and includes the most recent Draft Report of the European Parliament's Committee on Public Health. The authors offer a multidisciplinary expert interpretation drawing on their experience in regulatory science, law, health policy and industry. They ask whether the reforms, if implemented, would materially improve the regulatory environment for AI-enabled medical devices in the EU. A provision-level comparison is provided in Supplementary Table 1.

The proposal aims to eliminate double regulation, reduce documentation requirements and introduce new regulatory tools. It would move the MDR and IVDR from Section A to Section B of Annex I of the AI Act, so that the AI Act's Chapter III obligations would not directly apply to medical devices. The Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, was adopted in July 2026 and permits the Commission to limit AI Act requirements where sectoral legislation provides an equivalent level of protection. It delays the applicability of high-risk requirements to August 2028, and the Commission must adopt the corresponding delegated acts by 2 August 2027. The proposal revises classification rule 11 to make medical device software Class I by default, with up-classification when output informs or drives clinical management in increasingly serious situations, while rule 3.5, which assigns the highest applicable sub-rule, is left unchanged.

It codifies the Helsinki procedure through changes in MDR Article 4 and new Articles 4a, 51a and 51b, and it broadens clinical data to include studies in scientific literature that may not be peer-reviewed, while whether this includes preprints remains unclear. It further broadens the possibility to demonstrate safety and performance solely through non-clinical data, explicitly encouraging New Approach Methodologies such as in-silico testing, and it outlines a new pathway for highly innovative devices with priority and rolling reviews by Notified Bodies after review by a designated expert panel. The European Commission concluded in its evaluation of the current MDR that the challenges limit patient access to innovative medical technologies within the EU and reduce competitiveness. The authors argue that the changes are generally well-targeted but leave specific challenges for innovative AI-enabled medical devices unresolved. In their interpretation, the revision does not remove rule 11's central difficulty but relocates the distinction between informing and driving clinical management to the Class I boundary, where misclassification carries greater risk.

They say the fault lines remain vague, inviting divergent interpretation and inconsistent decisions, and that the rule stays anchored in a comparatively narrow and now dated conception of software risk. They think the current wording and its interaction with rule 3.5 would have the opposite effect to the intended substantial improvement. The authors say relaxing clinical evidence requirements could create space for innovation but raises legitimate questions about whether the resulting evidence base will be robust enough to protect patients, particularly for higher-risk AI-enabled devices. They critique the new pathway as possibly uncoordinated, because scientific advice from the panel and conformity assessment are structured as largely separate steps rather than an integrated dialog among manufacturer, panel and Notified Body. The EP draft report addresses this partially by stating that the notified body shall be able to participate in the expert panel's discussions.

The pathway is confined to conformity assessment and is not linked to health technology assessment or reimbursement, though selected Class IIb and III devices meeting the criteria in Article 7 of Regulation (EU) 2021/2282 may undergo EU joint clinical assessment, while Member States retain responsibility for conclusions on added clinical value, coverage and reimbursement. The authors think success depends on practical implementation of the somewhat vague proposal text, on how broadly or cautiously expert panels interpret the designation criteria, and on whether Notified Bodies can deliver faster reviews. In 2025 the EU's Artificial Intelligence Board and the Medical Device Coordination Group issued non-binding guidance, AIB 2025-1/MDCG 2025-6, on the interplay between the AI Act and the MDR/IVDR, describing how AI Act requirements for high-risk AI-enabled devices can be incorporated into the medical device conformity assessment process. The guidance does not eliminate the existing overlap, since meeting the integrated conformity assessment does not remove the need to fulfill the requirements of both frameworks.

Currently the MDR and IVDR are listed in Section A of Annex I, so for AI-enabled devices classified as high-risk under the AI Act the full set of AI Act requirements, including data governance, transparency, human oversight, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, applies alongside the MDR's general safety and performance requirements. This affects all medical devices that must involve a Notified Body in their conformity assessment, usually Class IIa or higher, where the AI system itself is a medical device or meets the AI Act definition of a safety component. The move of the MDR from Section A to Section B remains an option for targeted revisions. The articles leave open whether the proposal will be adopted, delayed or substantially revised in the ongoing negotiation processes.

They leave open whether preprints count as scientific literature under the broadened clinical data definition. They leave open how broadly or cautiously expert panels will interpret the designation criteria for the new innovative-product pathway. They leave open whether Notified Bodies can deliver faster reviews. The Comment reflects the situation of 26 August 2026 and includes the most recent Draft Report of the European Parliament's Committee on Public Health.

stories.Headline: Lansing residents oppose a data center ban vote as TeraWulf subsidiary sues the town
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday night, Nov. 17, 2026, residents of Lansing, a town in Tompkins County, packed the Lansing Central School District Middle School Auditorium to oppose a proposed data center. They spoke at a special Lansing Town Board meeting held for public comment on a proposed local law. The law would amend the town code to define “cryptocurrency,” “cryptocurrency data mine,” “data center” and “general processing.” The meeting came as officials weigh a possible outright ban on data centers. The company behind the project, TeraWulf, argues in a lawsuit that lawmakers are working behind-the-scenes to stop the potential undertaking.

The law, if approved, would include “cryptocurrency data mine” or “data center” as uses within the Schedule of Land Uses or Activities. That would establish that cryptocurrency data mines and data centers are disallowed uses for the town’s zoning code, according to the local law proposal. This would essentially ban data centers within the town. TeraWulf, a company that started in bitcoin mining and is expanding into data centers, previously proposed a facility at the former Cayuga Generating Station along Cayuga Lake’s eastern shore. The town board is set to vote on the proposed ban during a regular meeting starting at 6:30 p.m.

Wednesday at the middle school auditorium. Pace Ralli, vice president of product development for TeraWulf, took to the podium to defend the proposal. He said it was an opportunity to put an unused industrial property back into productive use, create jobs and rethink what exists on the lakeside waterfront when the coal power plant is taken down. He also asserted the undertaking could bring significant private investment and new tax revenue to the community, helping support schools, public services and local infrastructure. Lake Hawkeye, a limited liability company and subsidiary of TeraWulf, filed a suit against the Town of Lansing, the Lansing Town Clerk’s Office and town supervisor Ruth Groff.

Town supervisor Ruth Groff, who is named in the suit, declined to comment. One member of the public said loons are often heard in the distance because sound really travels over the water, and contrasted that with a data center emitting over 50 decibels of noise 24/7 at the lake’s edge. Another speaker argued that going against the ban “doesn’t mean automatic support of a data center,” and said it means individual projects should be thoughtfully reviewed as they come along. Many attendees showed their support for the ban by wearing red, and a person in red said that with the same supply of electricity and more demand from data centers, everyone’s costs go up.

Lake Hawkeye, which operates at the site of the former Cayuga power plant, is seeking an order directing the Town of Lansing “to conduct a legally sufficient search and produce responsive documents in response” to the LLC’s two state Freedom of Information Law requests. The suit said the Town has not complied with FOIL and appears to have concealed documents responsive to the requests. It said Lake Hawkeye filed the FOIL requests to obtain information about back-channel discussions among Lansing Town officials seeking to thwart the construction of a data center on the site. The document claimed that to avoid detection or produce communications under FOIL, town board members took to a private Google Group managed by Ms. Karen Edelstein, the spouse of Town Board member Joe Wetmore, to discuss strategies to block the Data Center.

It said access to the group was strictly limited by Ms. Karen Edelstein, ensuring that town residents who supported the data center and the jobs it would bring could not join. It said the petitioner sought admission to the private group and was explicitly denied, so it was not able to participate in these discussions of public concern to the Town. The suit contends that the alleged use of a private, exclusionary forum by a quorum of Board members to discuss and formulate official policy on the Data Center Project violates the New York Open Meetings Law, which states all of a public body’s meetings must be open to the general public. The town board is set to vote on the proposed data center ban during a regular meeting, which starts at 6:30 p.m.

Wednesday at the middle school auditorium. People argued for and against the data center ban at the meeting. The articles do not say what the board decided at that Wednesday vote. The articles also do not say how the town will respond to the lawsuit.

stories.Headline: Marcos signs Executive Order 131 adopting a national AI governance framework
stories.Summary:
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed Executive Order 131 on Nov. 12, creating an inter-agency council chaired by Executive Secretary Ralph Recto to oversee the rollout of the country's first national artificial intelligence governance framework. The directive establishes the National Artificial Intelligence Council (NAIC), which reports directly to the president and assumes central authority over coordinating, facilitating and monitoring government AI programs. Under the order, the council will align state initiatives, eliminate overlapping projects across agencies and resolve regulatory or resource bottlenecks. Executive Order No. 131, signed by President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. on November 12, 2026, adopts the Philippines' National AI Governance Framework and establishes the National Artificial Intelligence Council. Palace Press Officer Claire Castro explained that the initiative aims to establish a unified direction for AI development while ensuring that technological progress delivers meaningful benefits to Filipinos.

Recto will lead the 12-member council in his capacity as executive secretary, while the secretary of the Department of Economy, Planning and Development (DEPDev) serves as vice chairperson. DEPDev also acts as the council's secretariat and must form an interim secretariat within 30 days of the order taking effect while submitting a permanent staffing plan to the Department of Budget and Management. Nine other cabinet-level officials sit on the council: the secretaries of information and communications technology, science and technology, trade and industry, finance, education, labor and employment, and budget and management, alongside the chairperson of the Commission on Higher Education and the director general of the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority. The president will also appoint one private-sector representative from nominees submitted by recognized business groups to serve a three-year term, with eligibility for one reappointment. Council members may designate permanent alternates holding a rank no lower than assistant secretary, and the body may invite local government units, state universities, government corporations, academe and civil society groups as resource persons.

Executive Order 131 tasks the council with recommending policy, fiscal, regulatory and legislative measures to accelerate AI adoption while protecting workers and learners affected by automation. The body will also pursue international partnerships and private-sector collaboration to strengthen domestic AI infrastructure and supply chains. To execute its mandate, the council will organize five technical working groups to draft action plans with specific deliverables, timelines and key performance indicators. Section 3 authorizes the council to recommend measures that "safeguard the rights and welfare of workers and learners affected by AI-driven transitions." Section 4 directs the relevant technical working group to "promote AI and digital education and literacy across sectors, and institutionalize scholarship programs supporting AI research, development, and use."

The order directs the Department of Information and Communications Technology to build a digital platform to track agency deliverables and milestones. Concerned agencies must submit quarterly updates through the system, and the council must submit a consolidated progress report to the president within 30 days after each quarter ends. Initial funding for the council will come from existing appropriations of member agencies and sources identified by the budget department, with future allocations integrated into regular agency budget proposals. The council must review the governance framework at least once every two years, or earlier if technological or market shifts require adjustments. Alongside creating the council, Executive Order 131 formally adopts the AI Governance Framework for the Philippines.

The framework rests on four interconnected elements: ethics and principles covering safety, fairness and accountability; technical standards and conformity assessments; a risk-based policy toolkit utilizing regulatory sandboxes, impact assessments and grievance mechanisms while preserving existing sector regulators' mandates; and enabling resources. Section 1 specifically identifies "transparency and explainability, security and safety, accountability and integrity, human centricity, fairness and equity, and sustainable development." Section 1 explains that "AI governance measures shall be proportionate to the nature, context, and level of risk." The framework builds upon the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy for the Philippines, approved in May 2025. Executive Order 131 operationalizes the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy for the Philippines, which the government approved in May 2025, as well as the AI Governance Framework subsequently endorsed by the National Innovation Council.

The issuance also aligns with Chapter 8 of the Philippine Development Plan 2023, 2028 on advancing research, development, technology and innovation. The order takes effect immediately upon publication in the Official Gazette or a newspaper of general circulation. Section 1 describes the framework as the "national strategic guide for policy formulation, regulatory coordination, institutional development, capacity-building, and other governance measures necessary to support and strengthen the country's AI ecosystem." Section 2 states that the council shall "serve as the inter-agency body responsible for coordinating, facilitating, and monitoring the implementation of the AI Governance Framework and related initiatives." The executive order does not immediately introduce mandatory AI subjects or specific classroom regulations.

stories.Headline: OCC chief Gould pledges tailored AI and community bank supervision and more charters
stories.Summary:
Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould pledged on Wednesday to double down on three areas of focus, tailoring supervision to material financial risk, ensuring regulatory burden does not hinder economic growth, and embracing innovation. He made the remarks on Wednesday to the Exchequer Club of Washington, D.C., saying innovation takes many forms, from artificial intelligence and stablecoins to lifting the barrier of entry for new charter applicants. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency has approved 28 charter applications in the past two years, with several dozen more in the pipeline, Gould said. The agency received as many charter applications in 2025 as it did in the previous four years, the OCC chief noted. Gould said a functional chartering process allows the banking system to renew itself and remain dynamic, bringing new capital and new ideas into institutions subject to federal supervision.

Gould said banks are not required to distinguish AI as its own risk category, and the OCC won't treat banks' embrace of AI separately when evaluating risk. He said AI is a component of preexisting business operations and practices, and the OCC intends to maintain a right-size approach to innovation. Gould said supervisory judgment should reflect what new technology does and the potential consequences of its use, and the OCC's workforce and approach will evolve with the technology. He pledged appropriately focused supervision for community banks, saying sound supervision and a healthy banking system cannot be achieved by subjecting all banks to the same standards. Gould cited the OCC's 2025 Community Bank Comeback initiative, which he credited with tailoring bank exams to risk and dedicating a group of examiners to banks with less than $30 billion in assets.

Gould said a lasting Community Bank Comeback also requires new entrants, noting nearly half of community banks have closed since the 2007-08 financial crisis while new entrants have not replaced them. He said this is the ideal formula for the mega banks to grow larger and the system to become less dynamic, and that the OCC is now open for business. Gould emphasized that community banks have an important place in the stablecoin ecosystem, saying the opportunities created by financial innovation should be within reach of Main Street banks. He noted the OCC's analysis last month that found nine banks under its purview held policies or practices between 2020 and 2025 that may have required, encouraged or otherwise influenced debanking based on customers' political or religious leanings. Gould said banks are not a proper vehicle for achieving social or policy objectives outside of the legislative process, and the OCC will help banks resist the temptation to use their privileged positions as financial intermediaries to indulge their inner activists or external interest groups.

Gould noted the OCC during his stint at the helm has put more rules into effect in one-third the time frame than the agency did under its immediate previous leadership. He said he wants to ensure new rules are fit for purpose, and that regulators' short-sighted attempts to eliminate risk from the industry forced a significant amount of lending and investment activity outside the regulated banking system. Gould said the burden of complying with those rules left some community banks out of the loop, and that too big to fail actually created too small to succeed. He cited the agency's work alongside the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. to finalize a uniform definition of unsafe or unsound practices and create clearer standards for the supervisory category of matters requiring attention. Gould said banks should understand the basis for a supervisory criticism and what is required to resolve it, and that transparency via regulation is furthered by bolstering examiner judgment through eliminating checklists and refocusing on material financial risk.

Generative AI consultant Ben Udell said bankers should approach AI-generated work the same way they would review work completed by another employee. Udell said people feel they will not be able to own their work with AI, but if used correctly, with editing, fact checking and review by an experienced banker, it will pass the sniff test. He said when AI is off base, you go back into AI and ask for a better source or a citation, just as you would with a human being working with you. State banking regulators found that approximately 62% of community banks are either using or testing AI technologies. The RFD-TV report was published on November 16, 2026, and the Banking Dive story on November 19, 2026.

The OCC's stablecoin rulebook is final, and the moat fight moves to a second rulemaking, according to a Forkast News headline listed among related stories. Circle, Ripple, Paxos, Fidelity and BitGo received banking charters approved by the OCC, according to a decrypt headline listed among related stories. The OCC invited community banks to seek stablecoin issuer approval before applications open, according to an Unchained headline listed among related stories. The ICBA urged a court to rein in the OCC over trust charters, according to a Banking Dive headline listed among related stories. The OCC finalized GENIUS Act stablecoin rules ahead of a January deadline, according to a decrypt headline listed among related stories.

stories.Headline: HMG Strategy hosts Toronto AI leadership summit on November 24 with CIOs and CISOs
stories.Summary:
HMG Strategy will host its 14th Annual Toronto C-Level Technology Leadership Summit on November 24, 2026, in the Windsor Ballroom at the historic Omni King Edward Hotel at 37 King Street East in downtown Toronto. The event is organized by HMG Strategy, whose Founder and CEO is Hunter Muller, and registration data points to AI, cybersecurity, data modernization and compliance as key priorities. Early registration data shows AI and machine learning as the most frequently selected priority among executives identifying their current technology needs, followed closely by cybersecurity. Data analytics, data modernization and compliance also rank prominently among attendee priorities, and registrants who provided estimated spending levels reported technology investment plans ranging from hundreds of thousands of dollars to more than $10 million. The summit will bring together CIOs, CISOs, CTOs and senior technology executives from major Canadian enterprises and multinational organizations with significant North American operations.

The featured executive panel “Seeing Around the Corner: AI Governance, Ethics, and Accountability” will examine how organizations are developing governance frameworks to address accountability for AI-driven decisions, transparency, sensitive enterprise data, cyber risk and responsible innovation. That panel brings together Vaughn Hazen, CISO, CN; Puroo Maheshwari, Managing Director - Cybersecurity, CPP Investments; Sundeep Sandhu, VP, Technology, Cyber & AI Risk - Global Information Risk Management, Manulife; and Rocco Grillo, Managing Director, Global Cyber Risk & Incident Response Investigations, Alvarez & Marsal. The panel “Security Innovation as a Strategic Differentiator” will feature Maya Beri, SVP & CIO, Sun Life U.S.; Tushar Chandgothia, CISO, goeasy Ltd.; Shilpa Dahiya, Senior Director, Information & Cyber Security, CAAT Pension Plan; and Jeet Jariwala, VP of Information Security, Beem Credit Union. The discussion “Harnessing Data, AI and Strategic Technologies to Drive Long-Term Business Performance” will feature technology leaders from Canada Post Corporation, Heart and Stroke Foundation Canada and SAP. Pam Arpin, SVP & CIO of CPKC, will join Hunter Muller for a fireside conversation titled “Leading Through Transformation: From Merger Integration to AI-Driven Growth.”

Hunter Muller said AI has quickly moved from an emerging technology discussion to an enterprise leadership mandate. He said the challenge for CIOs and CISOs is no longer simply identifying where AI can create value, and that technology leaders must determine how to scale AI responsibly, govern increasingly complex data environments, manage new cyber risks and work with the CEO and Board to deliver measurable business outcomes. He also said technology leadership transcends borders, and that as AI changes the enterprise at unprecedented speed, technology executives are being called upon to lead far beyond traditional IT boundaries. He said CIOs and CISOs are confronting the harder work of enterprise execution: establishing robust AI governance, protecting critical data, reskilling the workforce and converting emerging technologies into measurable business outcomes. He said the 14th Annual Toronto Summit brings this community together to exchange candid insights, strengthen trusted relationships and chart the future of enterprise leadership.

The agenda also includes “Designing the Future Workforce,” with technology leaders from Boeing, Infrastructure Ontario, Daikin Applied Americas and Mattamy Asset Management and Mattamy Homes exploring how AI is redefining roles, skills, operating models and organizational culture. “Scaling Resilience” will have senior technology executives discuss leadership practices that support clarity, performance and resilience amid continuous technological and organizational change, and an Executive Roundtable Exchange will cover AI ethics, lessons from AI implementation, cybersecurity, reskilling and upskilling, leadership resilience and the multigenerational workforce. Speakers and participants represent organizations including CPKC, CN, Canada Post Corporation, CPP Investments, Manulife, Walmart Canada, RBC, Sun Life, Infrastructure Ontario, IGM Financial, Sobeys/Empire, Ontario Health, MDA Space and Subaru Canada. Additional organizations represented within the registered attendee community include BMO, the City of Markham, CPA Canada, Stikeman Elliott and Aon, and other named speakers include Nish Anjaria of Canada Post Corporation, Danny Torchia of Walmart Canada, Sanjiv Purba of Infrastructure Ontario, Michon Williams of Mattamy Asset Management and Mattamy Homes, Naveen Kumar of Boeing, Ashish Srivastava of Daikin Applied Americas and Doug Cannell of Heart and Stroke Foundation Canada. The event is supported by technology partners SAP, Cyera and OpenText, whose capabilities align with the summit’s focus on enterprise AI, trusted data, information management and digital security.

The articles state that Toronto sits at the center of an interconnected economy where financial services, transportation, retail, healthcare, infrastructure and advanced technology converge. They state that Canadian and U.S. enterprises remain connected through shared capabilities, business relationships and innovation that support sustainable growth and enterprise performance at a time of continued economic and technological change. They state that as artificial intelligence moves from pilot programs into day-to-day business operations, technology leaders face the critical mandate of building governed, secure and resilient digital organizations. They state that the Windsor Ballroom provides an intimate setting for executive networking, candid peer discussions and relationship-building, and that the program will feature executive panels, fireside chats, interactive roundtables, peer-driven discussions and HMG Global Leadership Institute Award presentations. They state that HMG Strategy is the trusted source for connecting technology executives to reimagine the enterprise and reshape the business world through a global network of CIOs, CISOs, CTOs and business technology executives.

Qualified CIOs, CISOs, CTOs, CDIOs and senior enterprise technology executives are invited to request a complimentary executive pass for the November 24 summit. To learn more, the articles direct readers to the Toronto Summit home page or the 14th Annual Toronto C-Level Technology Leadership Summit registration page to request a complimentary executive pass. Venue information is available on the Omni King Edward Hotel event page. The media contact is Peggy Pedwano, Chief Operations Officer, HMG Strategy, at 203-221-2702 and [email protected]. A photo accompanying the announcement is available at a GlobeNewswire attachment link, and the articles leave open what the panels and roundtables will conclude.

stories.Headline: AI-driven security updates overwhelm legacy systems and cause widespread outages, officials tell Congress
stories.Summary:
Over the past month, a series of major outages took down a wide range of services, including a nationwide ground halt that stopped all US airfare for hours, days without access to core Microsoft services such as Outlook and Teams, disruptions at Apple's App Store and Apple Pay, major problems at US banks, and delays and cancellations at United Airlines after a system outage. The National Security Agency's in-house communications network for classified information also went down earlier this week. According to the Washington Sun, Wall Street and NSA sources have told Congress that the outages are being triggered by system updates designed to thwart future attacks by AI. Lawmakers have been flummoxed by the outages and a spate of wide-ranging hacks, and early indications suggest that suspicions AI played a role appear to be warranted, though there is nuance in exactly how.

The updates are meant to bolster defenses as AI continues to identify glaring cybersecurity vulnerabilities that could be exploited by bad actors, and load-bearing organizations appear to have inadvertently overwhelmed their systems while pushing them through. A congressional official told the Washington Sun that the models are identifying massive vulnerabilities, which increases the urgency to patch right away, and that organizations are trying to push through a lot of patches all at once, more than the system was designed for. Department of Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters on Tuesday that new technology is being pushed on top of really old computer systems, which overwhelmed them, and he said he could say with 98 percent certainty that this is not a cyberattack. Officials have continued to reassure the public that the outages are not related to any cybersecurity threats.

Experts have warned for years that AI is a dangerous double-edged sword, since it can give cybersecurity researchers a major leg up in identifying possible new attacks, and earlier this year Anthropic claimed in a report that its Claude Mythos model had found more than ten thousand vulnerabilities in existing software. Hackers can use the same tools to exploit these vulnerabilities, setting the stage for an arms race as companies rush to patch the defects. Encode chief strategy officer Nathan Calvin told the Washington Sun that there is some sense in which this is reassuring, in that it means there is not an attack, but that it shows the extent to which safety critical infrastructure we rely on is based on software with large vulnerabilities on legacy systems. To Calvin, it is an arms race that will more than likely drag on as we get more advanced models.

stories.Headline: TaxDome report finds 74% of AI-using clients fact-check or would fact-check their accountant
stories.Summary:
A new report from the practice management platform TaxDome says that 74% of clients who use artificial intelligence have either fact-checked or would consider fact-checking their accountant's work with AI, based on a survey of 1,000 clients who use an accountant or tax professional. The 2026 Accounting Client Satisfaction Report found that AI is now increasingly part of the client relationship, that more clients are willing to pay for faster service, and that clients care more about quick response times than quick work delivery. Sixty-eight percent of clients say they have at least tried AI for their taxes or finances, and 39% have used it, mostly to ask a tax question or understand something. Very few hand it the real work, since only 3% have used AI on an actual return.

One in five clients have already used AI to review work their accountant completed, and among clients who have used or explored AI that rises to 29%, while another 45% have not done it yet but say they would consider it. For some, checking is already routine, since 24% of the clients who have checked their accountant's work with AI do it regularly, and top-paying business owners are checking their accountant's work with AI at 2.4 times the rate of all clients. The clients using AI to check their accountant's work are among the most willing to pay for more, with 78% saying they would pay for structured advisory check-ins compared with 55% of all clients, and 57% wanting a quarterly check-in on their finances compared with 45% of all clients. Across all clients who have tried AI, 61% would pay for structured advisory check-ins, compared with 43% of clients who have never tried it.

Ilya Radzinsky, co-founder and chief product officer of TaxDome, said in a statement on Nov. 18 that in the age of AI the firms that win will be the ones closest to their clients. He said the research shows what that looks like, with quick answers, a heads-up before clients have to ask, and advice they can act on. He said the firms that get it right will earn the trust, and the continued business, that AI cannot. The report says many clients also look closely at what an accountant adds, and it describes clients as not waiting for their accountant to bring AI into the relationship, since most have already started.

stories.Headline: Micron President says China lags behind in high bandwidth memory development
stories.Summary:
Scott J. DeBoer, the President and Chief Technology and Products Officer of Micron, spoke about the global artificial intelligence chip race on November 18, 2026. During an interview with Deirdre Bosa on Yahoo Finance, he addressed the current competitive landscape regarding high bandwidth memory. He stated that China is currently far behind other nations in the development of this specific memory technology. This discussion highlighted the ongoing struggle for technological dominance in the semiconductor industry during a period of rapid growth.

Maintaining a lead in this sector requires a constant focus on outperforming all global competitors through superior core technology. DeBoer emphasized that Micron must partner with key customers to build products that are better than any others available in the world. This strategy involves staying significantly ahead of rivals from China, Korea, and other regions to ensure market leadership. The company believes that the only way to win is to create products that no other entity can build.

DeBoer explained that the memory business has been intensely competitive for the past 30 years without any periods of respite. He noted that there is always someone attempting to beat them, which is why the company takes this competition very seriously. When asked about political restrictions versus innovation, he replied that he can only control the ability to out innovate and compete. He mentioned that political aspects are not in his personal picture because his primary job is to deliver the products.

The context of these remarks reflects a broader international effort to secure the most advanced hardware for artificial intelligence applications. Micron intends to maintain its advantage by focusing on technical excellence rather than relying on external restrictions to hobble competitors. The company will continue to prioritize the development of high bandwidth memory to support the evolving needs of the AI chip market. Future success depends on the ability to sustain this technological gap through continuous research and strategic partnerships.

stories.Headline: Federal Reserve governor Michael Barr urges lenders to give consumers ways to dispute AI credit data
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr used a Monday, Nov. 16 speech in Milan to warn that lenders are gaining access to a growing range of data sources, including rental payments, utility bills and employment patterns, that can serve as evidence of creditworthiness, while consumers often lack a way to review or challenge that information. He called for accessible dispute procedures, ongoing fairness monitoring and detailed records of how artificial intelligence models are validated. Barr also said major banks had encountered AI agents attempting to act inside retail accounts without being able to verify their authenticity or customer consent. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency’s Nov. 12 Semiannual Risk Perspective found that some banks are already testing or deploying customer-facing generative and agentic AI, and its Nov. 4 framework instructed examiners to tailor their reviews to the potential consequences and autonomy of each use.

The rules already on the books set out what a denial requires. Regulation B generally requires creditors to give applicants the principal reasons for adverse action or tell them how to request these reasons, and the explanation must reflect the factors actually considered or scored. When a consumer report contributes to a denial, the lender must identify the company that supplied it, and the lender is responsible for explaining its decision within 60 days of the consumer’s written request. A rent history supplied by a consumer reporting agency comes with a statutory process for disputing errors with that agency, while information a landlord supplies directly and that contributes to a denial generally gives the borrower the right to request a description of it from the lender. A bank that counted irregular deposits as evidence of unstable income must establish whether the AI model saw all the accounts the applicant connected and how it classified the deposits, and a borrower paid weekly should have a way to challenge an income calculation that leaves out one of those paychecks.

Responsibility sits with the lenders and the examiners who oversee them. The OCC is giving federal bank examiners a framework for reviewing AI according to what the system does and how much authority it has, and the report said banks are adapting oversight through measures that include human review, with implementations that should be fit for purpose. For a bank reviewing a credit complaint, that human review depends on being able to retrieve the information and the AI model version used at the time of the decision. In any dispute, the question would be whether the bank can locate the error, correct what it controls and determine whether the corrected information changes the decision.

The context is a push to widen the data used in lending. The May PYMNTS Intelligence report “Who Is the Subprime Consumer? A Behavioral Profile” found that 35% of subprime consumers held neither a credit card nor a store card, compared with 12% of prime consumers, and the article said widening the flow of information used to judge creditworthiness would arguably broaden financial inclusion. The data is already reaching lenders through new channels: in October, Plaid introduced Instant Link, which lets eligible applicants share cash flow information with lenders by connecting accounts to Plaid’s consumer reporting agency. In a survey of 2,304 U.S. adults, PYMNTS Intelligence found in the October report “Giving AI Credit: How Far Consumers Will Let Agents Go” that 63% would let an AI agent compare credit offers, while 49% would let one complete and submit an application with their final approval.

stories.Headline: AI tools drive school book removals as states expand restrictions
stories.Summary:
As a growing number of states pass or propose restrictions on what books children can access in school libraries, authors and advocates are concerned about the role artificial intelligence is increasingly playing in books being removed from shelves. The free speech advocacy group PEN America said in a report published during Banned Books Week in early October that the phenomenon of using AI to guide removals will worsen the snowball effect of book bans that has already gone much too far. Some districts have had AI review their collections to flag certain types of content and make recommendations on what to remove. The first known example of AI being used for such purposes was in 2023, when an Iowa school district used it in response to legislation prohibiting books depicting sex acts in school libraries. Several Texas districts followed in 2025, according to the Houston Chronicle.

The Florida Freedom to Read Project reported in October that a local school district's use of AI to scan library collections led to more than 1,800 titles being removed from shelves to undergo further review. A Utah law requires that if three public school districts, or two school districts and five charter schools, take a title off library shelves, all public and charter schools must follow suit. There are 44 books currently banned statewide under the law, according to PEN America. The organization's October report found that Texas and Florida's bans made up more than 11,400 of the nearly 12,000 total book bans recorded during the 2025-2026 school year. Texas enacted a law in 2025 that prohibits schools from having library materials with indecent or profane content, and Florida has sought to impose similar restrictions for several years.

The Florida Department of Education sent a memo in September to the state's 67 public school districts, as well as charter schools, that directed them to review their library collections and compare them to the department's list of books that have been removed from schools around the state. Florida Education Commissioner Henry Mack wrote that the Department will hold districts, and the superintendents who lead them, accountable for failing to protect students from inappropriate content and material. Maggie Tokuda-Hall, an author and co-creator of Authors Against Book Bans, told USA TODAY that we've crossed the Rubicon and are in a really different place. A spokesperson for Moms for Liberty told USA TODAY the group believes AI recommendations should always be followed by human review. The spokesperson said anyone who blindly trusts AI to make decisions for them is using it in an irresponsible manner.

A Knight Foundation report in 2024 found that more than three-fourths of all adults felt very or somewhat confident that local public schools select appropriate books, including nearly 90% of public school parents, more than 60% of conservatives and 69% of Republicans. Stephana Ferrell, a public school parent who is also the director of research and insight at the Florida Freedom to Read Project, said these are not things public school parents want prioritized right now, and yet it's being amplified at the state level. Moms for Liberty, which describes itself as the nation's largest grassroots organization fighting for parental rights, has chapters that have called for scores of titles to be removed from school library shelves, including Colleen Hoover's "It Ends With Us," "The Kite Runner" by Khaled Hosseini and John Steinbeck's "Of Mice and Men." In October, the group announced a new AI tool to scan school board meeting agendas and identify topics related to parental rights, free speech, the curriculum and diversity, equity and inclusion efforts. A spokesperson for the organization told USA TODAY it may also be used on school library collections.

James Joyce's 1922 work "Ulysses" was deemed legally obscene and faced a nationwide ban until a court reversed it in 1933. J.D. Salinger's 1951 classic, "The Catcher in the Rye," has stirred controversy for decades and was the 10th-most challenged book of the 1990s, according to the American Library Association. A book that was even more widely challenged in that decade was "Heather Has Two Mommies," a 1989 children's book about a young girl raised by lesbian parents. The book's author, Lesléa Newman, told USA TODAY that while there have been longtime battles over her work, as well as other books with LGBTQ+ themes or written by non-White authors, she's noticed a change in recent years.

Newman said things have really escalated in a way that's very disturbing and frightening, and noted that statewide bans now affect dozens of titles. According to the American Library Association, pressure groups, government officials and other decision-makers were behind more than 90% of all book challenges in 2025. Author Lee Wind, whose 2021 book, "No Way, They Were Gay? Hidden Lives and Secret Loves," has faced several bans, criticized what he called very calculated attacks on books and said book bans further marginalize certain groups, such as the LGBTQ+ community.

Wind said he thinks all it's doing is empowering people that want there to be fewer books about diverse people in public spaces to do it more thoroughly. Sarah Lamdan, executive director of the American Library Association's Office for Intellectual Freedom, told USA TODAY she has some optimism that the trend will taper off. Lamdan said one thing that gives her hope is people are becoming fatigued by AI, and the overuse of AI, and the use of AI in contexts where maybe it shouldn't be used. Kris Austin, CEO of Draft2Digital, a self-publishing and distribution platform for independent authors, pointed to the negative feedback loop created by having more state restrictions alongside more advanced AI.

Austin said the next time we see this data, it's going to be worse, and it's going to be shockingly worse. The article carried an editor's note stating the story was updated to add additional information. BrieAnna Frank's role covering First Amendment issues at USA TODAY is made possible by a collaboration among Freedom Forum, Journalism Funding Partners and the USA TODAY Network, and Freedom Forum does not provide editorial input. The article originally appeared on USA TODAY and was reported by BrieAnna J. Frank, USA TODAY, via USA TODAY Network and Reuters Connect.

stories.Headline: South Korea activates emergency response team to stop AI cheating in national exams
stories.Summary:
An anonymous user on the online community DC Inside claimed to have used artificial intelligence to cheat on the 2024 Suneung exam. This individual allegedly used a miniature camera disguised as a shirt button and a smartphone to obtain an average percentile score of 98.6. These claims surfaced shortly after Han Won-seok, the top scorer on this year's tax accountant qualification exam, confessed to using similar AI tools. Han admitted to using a miniature camera and generative AI during both rounds of the national exam in April and July. He scored 397.5 out of 400 points and achieved perfect scores in three of the four subjects.

The current situation requires the Education Ministry to implement strict measures to prevent the use of hidden cameras and smart glasses. YouTuber Kim Min-woo, known as Mimiminu, has urged the government to postpone the upcoming Suneung to ensure proper security. He noted that the exam was previously delayed in 2017 due to the Pohang earthquake and in 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic. To combat these threats, Prime Minister Han Seong-sook vowed on Tuesday to root out AI cheating by activating an interagency emergency response team. The government plans to ban smart devices and deploy additional staff at testing sites to maintain the integrity of the process.

Several education experts have expressed deep concern regarding the ability of authorities to detect modern cheating devices. Kim Min-woo explained that tiny devices hidden in bracelets or buttons can solve complex questions very quickly. Kang Sung-tae, the founder of Gongsin.com, argued that checking for thick-framed glasses is insufficient because many smart glasses from China have discreet designs. He stated that he has warned for years that AI-assisted cheating was inevitable and hoped his warnings would raise awareness. These experts believe that the current screening methods are outdated and cannot stop sophisticated technology.

The South Korean government is now racing to curb these technological breaches before the college entrance exam takes place this Thursday. Authorities are focusing on identifying a wide variety of smart glasses and other wearable electronics that students might smuggle into the rooms. The Education Ministry must now decide if the existing laws allow for a schedule change to better prepare for these threats. If the government cannot guarantee a fair environment, the pressure to delay the exam may increase. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Google ties school search access to its AI tools as districts weigh alternatives
stories.Summary:
Google announced earlier this month that it plans to turn off search engine access as soon as next year for K-12 schools that toggle off its AI tools. The company claimed the decision was necessary based on the technologies' recent fusion. Educators were not satisfied by that. A growing number of schools across the country are looking for search engine alternatives in lieu of Google's AI ultimatum. Some of the country's largest school districts, including in Los Angeles, New York, and Chicago, are considering doing away with Google altogether.

Potential options include DuckDuckGo and Microsoft's Bing, both of which offer users the option to disable AI-generated answers. Google has only offered school districts more ways to interact with AI, such as AI Mode and AI Overview, which provides users with chatbot search functions and summarized results, reported The New York Times. Google disclosed that the company would turn off its Gemini AI program and search engine for schools "until schools decide which services to enable." A January report by the Brookings Institution's Center for Universal Education found that AI can "undermine children's foundational development," and that "the damages it has already caused are daunting." New skill development and problem-solving abilities are among the chief concerns when it comes to early-age AI dependence.

Kamar H. Samuels, the chancellor of New York City schools, said in a statement that if Google doesn't reconsider their position, they will explore other search options. He said they refuse to accept the false binary Google has laid out. Google told the Times in a statement Wednesday that it is actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure its products support students and teachers. Rebecca Winthrop, one of the report's authors, told NPR in January that when kids use generative AI that tells them what the answer is, they are not thinking for themselves. She said they are not learning to parse truth from fiction, not learning to understand what makes a good argument, and not learning about different perspectives in the world because they are actually not engaging in the material.

Children can easily fall into a catch-22 in which they continually offload their work onto the AI, diminishing their self-confidence and self-reliance in the process, according to the Brookings Institution report. After school on October 20, 2025, 16-year-old Taki Allen was waiting with three friends outside Kenwood High School in Baltimore County, Maryland, for a ride home from football practice. Allen was eating a bag of Doritos. At least six Baltimore County Police Department vehicles arrived at the scene, and officers leapt out, guns drawn, forcing the boys to the ground and searching them. Omnilert Gun Detect, an artificial intelligence weapon-detection system that scans security footage for firearms, had used the school cameras to misidentify Allen's bag of chips as a gun.

Allen and his classmates Yui-Osa Ogbeide, Devon Thompson Jr., and Keith Winfield III are all Black. The Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law filed a lawsuit on their behalf Tuesday against the police department, the Baltimore County board of school, school administrators, and several individual officers. The lawsuit says the encounter was terrifying and life-threatening, and that with armed police encircling them for no apparent reason, each student feared for his life and the lives of his friends. After failing to find anything in the search, one police officer reportedly told the students, "AI is not the best," and another said, "Fucking Omnilerts." As the officers were leaving, another said, "Hey, thanks for not running away, that would have been a real problem."

The lawsuit showed that the principal texted school staff and administrators after the police left to laugh about the incident. The lawsuit also points out that the Omnilert Gun Detect system was patented in 2022, "barely a year" before it was implemented in Baltimore County schools. After it identified Allen's doritos as a firearm, it sent a text message to a group of school administrators and police, who reviewed the alert and canceled it. But 10 minutes later, the school principal sent a screenshot of the footage in the security alert to a co-worker, who sent it to the police department, who then responded at the scene. The Omnilert Gun Detect parent company, Omnilert LLC, has claimed that the AI system "distinguishes guns from inert objects such as cell phones, hand tools, common office objects and more" in order to "diminish false positives."

Maryland's Office of the Inspector General for Education found that 99 percent of alerts in Baltimore County schools have been false positives. Damon Hewitt, president and executive director of the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, said these students were failed not only by a technology that is prone to false alerts, but also by the very adults meant to keep them safe when we send them to school. He said that instead of this protection, they were met with guns and traumatized, and that it could have been even worse. Texas Supreme Court Justice James P. Sullivan refused to acknowledge the parameters of the Twenty-Second Amendment during his confirmation hearing in the Senate Judiciary Committee Wednesday, even after Delaware Senator Chris Coons spelled it out for him. Trump has repeatedly said he was "not joking" about pursuing a third term in office, first using that phrasing in March 2025 during a phone call with NBC News's Kristin Welker.

In an April 22 interview with Time magazine, the president said there are some loopholes that have been discussed that are well known for keeping him in power. Senator Ted Cruz got into it with outgoing Republican Senator John Cornyn Tuesday, and the two yelled back and forth about the judicial nomination from the mostly empty Senate floor. Cornyn told Cruz, "I don't find you credible. I'm mad at you!" loud enough that people could hear him up in the press gallery.

Cornyn ultimately said, "Oh, that's bullshit," and stormed away toward the Democratic side of the aisle, according to The Washington Sun. At the time of the fight, Cornyn was refusing to return the "blue slip" for T. Elliot Gaiser, assistant attorney general for the Office of Legal Counsel, who was nominated for a Dallas-area federal judgeship earlier this month. Cornyn said on Wednesday to the Associated Press that Gaiser is not from Texas, has not been vetted, and that this is a lifetime job with better qualified people to hold it. Cruz said on Wednesday that Gaiser was the only option for the seat, lest it be relinquished to the Democrats. Cruz said that if the Senate Judiciary Committee does not move Gaiser forward, the people of Texas will pay the price because it will effectively give the judicial seat to the Democrats, who will keep it vacant in perpetuity.

Cruz said that would be a tragedy. Cruz's political consulting firm, Axiom Strategies, helped Ken Paxton beat Cornyn in the Texas Senate Republican primary earlier this year, and Paxton ultimately lost the seat to Democrat James Talarico. Cornyn said he does not know why a Texas senator would agree to a nomination of somebody from Ohio for one of the most important district benches in the state, in Dallas. After Vice President JD Vance stuck a shiv in Trump's back with a lengthy X post the morning after the Republican Party was decimated from Mississippi to Maine, Trump has suddenly lost interest in his right-hand man. The president said at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, where the secretary of state is playing a prominent role, "How hot is Marco, right?"

and "Is Marco doing a great job? He's been fantastic." Vance, the erstwhile crown prince to the MAGA throne, wasn't mentioned. The president has also been praising Rubio behind closed doors and suggesting that he could be a good presidential candidate, according to sources who spoke with The New York Times. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Zheng Yuanjie uses AI to animate fairy tales as other users steal actors' faces for traffic
stories.Summary:
Zheng Yuanjie announced a career shift on November 17 to revive his fairy tales using AI. He is creating short videos from his past writings for a Douyin account. These animated works are released for all readers to watch for free. Other AI users have misappropriated actors' faces without any authorization agreements. This theft occurred to harvest online traffic through unauthorized short dramas.

The Douyin account Zheng Yuanjie's Fairy Tale World began updating on October 24. It features Good Habit Stories and Chinese Zodiac Fairy Tales with episodes of 4 to 5 minutes. The 1987 A Dream of Red Mansions actors were used in Dreaming Back to the Red Chamber. This drama includes Daiyu's Rebirth and Revenge and features Chen Xiaoxu, Zhang Li, Deng Jie, and Li Ting. The 1987 series cost 6.9 million yuan for 36 episodes across 219 scenic spots.

Zheng Yuanjie, the 71-year-old King of Fairy Tales, says he will keep working hard. He believes imagination is the one thing that AI cannot do for humans. Director Jia Zhangke says AI and live-action films are complementary rather than mutually substitutive. He believes the most touching movie moments come from human judgment and physical sensations. Director Zhang Yimou says AI is a good tool that puts the industry under pressure.

Actor Zhang Li stated she never authorized any institution to use her portrait for AI synthesis. She reserves the right to pursue legal responsibility for the unauthorized use of her image. Some netizens say the style of Zheng's AI animations is rough and not exquisite enough. Ordinary people are affected as AI short dramas compete for attention at zero cost. The entire film industry faces survival anxiety due to these low-cost AI productions.

The 1987 series used 2,700 hand-made costumes and music written by Wang Liping over 21 months. Modern S+ costume dramas now cost between 300 million and 800 million yuan in total. A 41-second AI celebrity video can be customized for a deposit of 40 yuan. Digital human images cost 1,500 to 2,000 yuan, while compliant face authorization is 100 to 500 yuan. Lawyer Li Haiquan notes that performers can claim portrait and performer rights.

AI images may reach a level of authenticity that passes for real in three to five years. This shift could allow ordinary people to replace professional screenwriters and directors. The industry still lacks rules on whether film festivals or theaters should accept AI works. It remains open what standards the evaluation system should use for these new films. The protection of personal portrait and voice rights faces unprecedented and severe challenges.

stories.Headline: Remanence raises $30M seed led by EQT Ventures and FirstMark to help firms train open-weight AI models
stories.Summary:
Paris-based Remanence, a startup that helps companies train and fine-tune open-weight AI models, raised $30 million in seed funding, CEO Pierre-Louis Cedoz told Axios Pro exclusively. The round was led by EQT Ventures and FirstMark, according to the report published by Lucinda Shen on November 17, 2026. The company works with open-weight players so that businesses can train their own AI models rather than relying on outside providers. Axios reported the funding as an exclusive. The report says the funding could wean companies off more costly closed-source models, as open-weight technology catches up with the alternatives.

Remanence's business is built around helping companies train and fine-tune open-weight AI models, which the article describes as its core work. The $30 million seed round is the only figure the article gives for the raise, and EQT Ventures and FirstMark are named as the two leads. The article does not say how the money will be spent or give any other terms of the deal. Cedoz is named as the company's CEO and is the person who confirmed the funding to Axios Pro. The article quotes him only briefly, and the report does not include further comment from him or from either of the lead investors.

No statement from EQT Ventures or FirstMark appears in the article. The report also gives no details on Remanence's other backers, its customers or its plans. The context the article offers is that open-weight technology is catching up, which it says could let companies move away from more costly closed-source models. The report does not say what happens next for Remanence beyond the funding itself. It gives no timeline for new products, hiring or expansion, and it does not say when the round closed.
