stories.Headline: Epic asks court to order Apple to produce 122,000 withheld documents and impose daily fines
stories.Summary:
Epic Games asked a federal judge on Nov. 13, 2026, to order Apple to hand over more than 122,000 internal documents that Epic says Apple is withholding as irrelevant, and to fine Apple for every day it fails to comply after Dec. 2, 2026, according to a motion filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California. Epic says agreed search terms were run on the files of seven Apple custodians, four of them the executives Apple identified as decision makers on the fee (Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Carson Oliver and chief financial officer Kevan Parekh) and three others (Nate Barton, Alex Roman and Phil Schiller). Apple produced 632 documents from those seven custodians, 157 of them from the four decision makers, and is withholding more than 122,000 on claims they are not responsive, which Epic says is roughly 99.14% of the documents directly hit by the search terms. The terms included case words such as "proffer," "contempt," "injunction" and "link-out," and Epic says Apple produced nearly 27,000 documents from the same custodians or their predecessors during the earlier contempt proceeding. According to the filing, Apple's production contains no App Store profit-and-loss statements, no internal analysis of the financial impact of the proposed commissions, and no data supporting Apple's statement that its incremental link-out costs are "essentially zero."

Epic says Apple told it in meet-and-confers that the terms mostly returned press releases, analyst reports and other irrelevant material, and that Apple maintains its relevance review was proper. Epic asks the court to order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents that hit the agreed terms by Dec. 2, 2026, one week after Apple's Nov. 25 deadline to substantially complete production, irrespective of any relevance or responsiveness assessment, so Epic can review them itself, though Apple could still withhold privileged material. Epic also asks for a daily monetary sanction for each day Apple fails to comply after Dec. 2, 2026, without proposing a figure. A hearing on the motion had been set for Nov. 24 before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, but 9to5Mac reported that a new order, not yet public, refers the discovery dispute to a magistrate judge and terminates the related deadlines and hearings. Apple's response was not included in the filing or the 9to5Mac report.

The documents relate to Apple's Aug. 13, 2026 proposal for the commission it may charge on linked-out purchases, which 9to5Mac reported ranges from 5% to 15%, and which the Ninth Circuit sent back to Judge Gonzalez Rogers to decide. Judge Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple's anti-steering rules violated California's Unfair Competition Law and barred it from stopping developers from linking to outside purchase options, and in 2025 she held Apple in civil contempt and barred any commission on linked-out purchases. The Ninth Circuit upheld the contempt finding but sent back the question of what commission, if any, Apple may charge. Epic has separately asked the Supreme Court to uphold the contempt ruling, and its filing cites the earlier proceeding, in which the court found Apple's privilege over-designation intentional and sanctioned it, as evidence that Apple cannot be trusted to fix the problem through its own re-review.

stories.Headline: Paris Hilton and lawmakers press House to pass deepfake victim lawsuit bill
stories.Summary:
Paris Hilton joined Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Republican Rep. Laurel Lee at the U.S. Capitol on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, to press House lawmakers to pass legislation letting people targeted by sexually explicit AI-generated deepfakes sue those responsible. The bill would allow victims to seek up to $250,000 in damages under certain circumstances. The bipartisan DEFIANCE Act passed the Senate unanimously in January but waited 10 months for House action. Hilton and the lawmakers renewed their appeal alongside survivors of digital sexual abuse. Supporters sought a vote before the current congressional term ends.

The legislation would let individuals bring federal lawsuits against people who knowingly distribute sexually explicit digital forgeries without consent, possess them with intent to disclose them, or knowingly solicit and receive them. Certain claims involving creation of a deepfake alone would qualify when the person knew or recklessly disregarded the lack of consent and the resulting harm or likelihood of harm. Successful claims could bring $150,000 in damages, rising to $250,000 when conduct involves actual or attempted sexual assault, stalking or harassment under conditions outlined in the bill. Individuals could alternatively seek compensation for actual losses, including profits earned by those responsible. Courts could order removal or destruction of the material, award attorney fees and permit lawsuits under pseudonyms, and the bill generally provides 10 years to bring a claim from discovery of the violation or the person's 18th birthday, whichever is later.

Ocasio-Cortez and Lee introduced the House version of the bill, which has attracted support from both parties. Republican Rep. Kat Cammack, who chairs the Republican Women's Caucus, helped organize Tuesday's gathering with members of the Democratic Women's Caucus. Hilton said she keeps her promises to survivors and will return to these halls as many times as it takes until the DEFIANCE Act is signed. Lee said in a statement that laws have lagged behind the technology, leaving victims without clear legal tools when their likeness is stolen and weaponized, and that the bill closes that gap. Ocasio-Cortez said every day the bill does not pass and is not signed into law is a day more children, women and people are victimized with no recourse and no accountability for abusers and predators.

Ocasio-Cortez also said thousands of people in this country, if not tens of thousands and eventually millions, could be subject to sexual abuse on our watch due to complacency. Hilton said that ten months ago she stood at the Capitol and told the world what it feels like to have your body exposed without your consent, and asked Congress to do something about it. Hilton said the laws aren't protecting us, and that if this can happen to someone with her resources and platform, imagine how powerless a young girl might feel facing this completely alone. Hilton joined the press conference along with survivors of tech-enabled sexual abuse and advocates Elliston Berry and Elizabeth Cline, and advocate and father Joseph Tucker Daniels, according to RAINN's press release. The bill has attracted 70 cosponsors, including 36 Democrats and 34 Republicans, according to RAINN.

Hilton has publicly discussed the unauthorized release of an intimate video involving her when she was 19 and has since become an advocate for people subjected to sexual exploitation and abuse. She previously helped secure passage of the Stop Institutional Child Abuse Act, signed into law in December 2024, which established new federal oversight and reporting requirements for youth residential programs. Her latest Capitol Hill appearance followed an earlier visit in January, when she joined Ocasio-Cortez and Lee to urge the House to advance the DEFIANCE Act after its Senate approval. President Donald Trump signed the TAKE IT DOWN Act into law in May 2025, making certain nonconsensual publications of intimate images, including AI-generated material, a federal crime, and covered online platforms must remove qualifying content within 48 hours of a valid request. The Federal Trade Commission began enforcing those platform removal requirements in May 2026, and existing federal law also allows civil lawsuits over certain disclosures of intimate images.

The Senate previously approved an earlier version of the DEFIANCE Act in 2024, but the House did not advance it before that congressional term ended, and lawmakers reintroduced the measure in 2025. The Senate approved it again on January 13, 2026, after it had passed the first time in July 2024, and since then the bill has stalled in the House. House leaders have yet to schedule a floor vote despite the legislation attracting 70 cosponsors. Congress has until January 3, 2027, to complete passage of the legislation and send it to the president for approval. If the deadline passes, supporters will have to reintroduce the bill when the next Congress convenes.

stories.Headline: FTC investigates ISS and Glass Lewis over proxy advice competition
stories.Summary:
The articles report that in November 2025 the FTC launched a formal antitrust investigation into ISS and Glass Lewis, focusing on their ESG-related recommendations and questioning whether the duopoly constitutes unfair competition. The following month President Trump signed Executive Order 14366, which directed the SEC to review its regulatory regime as applied to proxy advisors' recommendations. The order also directed the DOL to examine the ERISA fiduciary duty implications of proxy advisors advancing non-financial or political agendas. It further directed the FTC to investigate, in concert with the Department of Justice, potential federal antitrust violations or unfair methods of competition or deceptive practices. On July 1, 2025, the D.C. Circuit unanimously held in ISS v.

SEC that proxy voting advice does not constitute a "solicitation" under Section 14(a) of the Exchange Act. In April 2026 the DOL issued a technical release clarifying that proxy advisory firms whose advice reaches ERISA-covered plans may be ERISA fiduciaries. On August 5, 2026, the DOJ's Antitrust Division withdrew the 1987 Business Review Letter it had issued to ISS, concluding the Letter is not applicable to ISS's current business practices. The Antitrust Division pointed to the concentration of the proxy advisory market, with ISS and Glass Lewis together controlling more than 90% of the market, as a further competition concern. Texas led with Senate Bill 2337, effective September 1, 2025, requiring proxy advisors to disclose their reliance on "nonfinancial factors" and to deliver adverse recommendations to the subject company at the same time they are provided to clients.

Kansas enacted the Proxy Advisor Transparency Act in April 2026 and Indiana enacted HB 1273 in March 2026, and Kentucky and Oklahoma enacted similar statutes later in 2026. The Texas Attorney General investigated ISS in September 2025 under the state's deceptive trade practices and fiduciary duty theories. Florida sued ISS in November 2025, alleging that undisclosed ESG-driven recommendations misled clients and breached duties owed to them. Four states filed coordinated lawsuits in May 2026 advancing similar consumer protection and fiduciary claims alongside alleged violations of the new disclosure statutes. Several state attorneys general and legislators have characterized the proxy advisory duopoly as a "proxy advisory cartel" whose market power distorts governance and imposes politically motivated agendas on American businesses.

On July 24, 2025, both ISS and Glass Lewis filed lawsuits in the Western District of Texas challenging SB 2337 on multiple constitutional grounds. On August 29, 2025, a Western District court granted preliminary injunctions blocking enforcement against both firms. The firms subsequently obtained injunctions against the Kansas and Indiana statutes in June 2026 and against the Oklahoma statute on October 31, 2026. ISS declared that the Texas ruling "safeguard core First Amendment principles."

The proxy advisory firms' arguments rest on three constitutional theories: that proxy voting recommendations are protected speech, that the statutes compel speech and discriminate based on viewpoint, and that the statutes burden interstate commerce in violation of the dormant Commerce Clause. Courts have found these theories persuasive enough to grant preliminary relief, and the viewpoint discrimination challenge has drawn the most attention and signals the statutes may be vulnerable on constitutional grounds. For over three decades, Institutional Shareholder Services Inc. (ISS) and Glass, Lewis and Co., LLC (Glass Lewis) have occupied a singular position in American corporate governance through their advice to institutional investors on how to vote their shares in public companies. Their influence has extended to areas such as board composition, executive compensation, shareholder rights and anti-takeover defenses.

The most viable federal path for regulation now runs through the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, where ISS is already registered and Glass Lewis is reportedly moving toward registration. The SEC's recent proposed rule amending the filer status framework would exempt Non-Accelerated Filers with a public float of less than USD2 billion from say-on-pay, say-on-frequency and say-on-golden-parachute votes. If the USD2bn cut-off is adopted, which the authors expect it will be, 81% of current public companies would be classified as NAFs, with all newly public companies retaining NAF status for at least five years post-IPO regardless of float size. In November 2026 the SEC proposed rules to revise the executive compensation disclosure requirements, which if adopted will significantly reduce executive compensation-related disclosure.

The articles state that AI may pose the greatest threat to the proxy advisors' business model, forcing the question of whether independent proxy advice remains necessary at all. The premise underlying the dominance of ISS and Glass Lewis has always been one of practical necessity, because institutional investors managing thousands of investments cannot independently research and formulate voting decisions. The articles leave open whether, when the dust settles, proxy advisors will remain influential or whether proxy advice will become more regulated, fragmented and technology-driven. The articles note that the injunctions are interim victories and the merits remain to be finally litigated.

stories.Headline: Google backs about $19 billion of Anthropic leases for TeraWulf
stories.Summary:
TeraWulf has obtained Google credit support for approximately $19 billion of Anthropic lease commitments, the company announced on Nov. 4, giving lenders another contractual source of protection as the former Bitcoin-focused operator builds facilities scheduled to begin entering service in late 2027. The Anthropic lease is a 20-year arrangement, and TeraWulf’s Nov. 4 announcement says the arrangements support anticipated project financing at its Justified campus in Kentucky, where Fluor is handling engineering and construction for three buildings. Google’s Nov. 4 agreements cover specified Anthropic obligations, with support beginning after the corresponding building’s last data hall starts operating. TeraWulf’s September-quarter filing, filed Nov. 6, says the relevant backstop takes effect when the last data hall under the corresponding Anthropic lease begins operating. IREN closed $3.65 billion of GPU financing in June, combining borrowing with customer prepayments to fund most of a $5.81 billion equipment bill.

Dividing the approximately $19 billion headline value by the 20-year term produces a simple annual average of $950 million, before considering the actual payment schedule or the stages at which buildings enter service. IREN reported a 6% blended debt cost for that financing, while its lower 3.31% funding calculation included customer advances. A one-percentage-point change in annual interest on a hypothetical $3.5 billion balance changes the yearly bill by $35 million. Using a hypothetical $3.5 billion average debt balance, a reduction from 9% to 8% would save $35 million annually before fees or changes in principal, and over five years a constant $35 million annual saving totals $175 million without discounting. IREN’s original Microsoft agreement, announced Nov. 3, 2025, was valued at $9.7 billion over five years and included a 20% customer prepayment, and 20% of $9.7 billion is $1.94 billion.

TeraWulf Chief Financial Officer Patrick Fleury called the “cost of capital” fundamental to infrastructure development in the company’s announcement, and his argument is that stronger customer credit support can help the company obtain more competitive borrowing terms. The company said the facility, combined with customer prepayments, covered $5.59 billion of a $5.81 billion GPU capital requirement. Subtracting the two published totals leaves approximately $220 million, or 3.8% of that equipment bill, outside the described combination. The rounded 96% coverage figure concerns the stated GPU spending, not every expense across IREN’s development pipeline. Following specified payment defaults or insolvency events, Google can assume a lease or, in certain circumstances, permit termination and pay a fee.

The fee declines over time, has limits linked in part to project financing and can be accompanied by an interest in the landlord subsidiary. The disclosed protection concerns a customer failing to meet covered lease obligations, and it does not promise reimbursement of every cost the developer incurs before completing the buildings. TeraWulf’s planned Kentucky financing package was reported in July as potentially combining leveraged loans and high-yield bonds, and the reporting described a financing proposal, not evidence that the entire package had already been borrowed. Mining firms led declines, with $HUT down over 6%, while $RIOT and $MARA each lost over 3%, $HOOD fell 4%, $MSTR dropped 3.3% and $COIN slipped over 1.5%. The contracts can make construction easier to finance, and their value to shareholders still depends on the cost of borrowing, the equipment the operator must buy and how soon a customer begins paying for an operational facility.

The commercial agreement determines who supplies the computing hardware, and a facility owner leasing equipped space has a different purchasing obligation from a cloud provider that must acquire the GPUs, servers and networking equipment used by its customer. An operator cannot use the full lifetime value to pay today’s contractor unless a customer advances money or a lender agrees to finance against future payments, and borrowing converts part of the expected cash flow into construction funding, with interest and repayment obligations attached. A hypothetical $950 million annual receipt would have to cover whatever expenses the contract assigns to the operator before it became a return on invested capital, and maintenance, employees, insurance and debt service can sit between a customer payment and money available for another project. A loan announcement needs the same distinction, because the maximum amount a bank makes available can exceed the amount drawn, while borrowing may depend on construction milestones, documentation and specified uses of proceeds. Suppose an operator obtains a $1 billion facility but draws $200 million in its first construction stage, and interest on the borrowed balance and fees on unused availability can have different bases, so applying one interest rate to the entire advertised facility may overstate the immediate cost.

Conversely, counting only interest on the first draw can understate the eventual financing burden if the project requires the rest of the facility, and a fair comparison follows the draw schedule through construction and the repayment schedule after operations begin. The date a lease begins earning revenue matters just as much as its length, and a signed agreement can remain economically valuable while producing little current revenue during procurement and construction. Shareholders therefore need the lifetime commitment, the expected service dates and the remaining spending requirement together, and comparing only the contract value with a company’s market capitalization leaves out the capital that must be supplied to earn those payments. A lender examining a hypothetical construction loan would ask which event activates the support, and if a contractor needs payment before the guaranteed rent obligation becomes effective, the financing arrangement must address that intervening period. The distinction has consequences for the price of debt, and protection against a tenant’s eventual failure can improve a lender’s expected recovery without removing concerns about procurement, delays or whether the borrower can complete the asset.

The strongest case for these agreements is therefore concrete, and a credible guarantor can improve financing terms and make an otherwise difficult capital requirement more manageable. The contractual limits remain important even when that case holds, and a guarantor’s option to make a termination payment produces a different outcome from collecting every rent payment over the original lease term. Project lenders may accept that alternative if it covers their exposure, and equity investors have a different concern because their expected return can include profits beyond the repayment of secured debt. IREN’s Microsoft arrangement offers a separate example because the company is purchasing the computing equipment, and the combination answers the construction question in a way a headline contract value cannot. Some cash comes from the customer before service, some from institutions lending against equipment and contracted cash flow, and the residual has to be met through other available resources.

stories.Headline: US restricts advanced AI chip exports to Southeast Asia and Brazil to prevent diversion to China
stories.Summary:
The United States Department of Commerce announced tighter controls on the export of advanced artificial intelligence chips on Monday, November 16, 2026. These new restrictions target Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, and Brazil because Washington believes there is a higher than normal risk of these chips being illegally diverted to China. The move follows a scandal involving the Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed, which was accused of funneling Nvidia chips to China. This regulatory shift comes as President Donald Trump travels to China to meet with President Xi Jinping.

Under these rules, companies must obtain a US license to export, re-export, or transfer advanced semiconductors to the four listed Southeast Asian nations. Overseas data centers providing significant computing power to companies headquartered in China must secure US export licenses by mid-February 2027 to maintain their services. While US-headquartered companies are exempt if they report shipments, non-American regional AI cloud companies and data center operators will need licenses for new advanced chips. Operators serving Chinese customers at scale will face the hardest challenges, as they require separate licenses for those specific clients.

Josh Gilbert, a lead analyst for Asia Pacific at eToro, stated that these restrictions act as a speed bump for the AI ambitions of Singapore. He noted that investors will now seek more clarity because the Nvidia-Megaspeed situation increased political pressure on Washington to limit China's access to computing capacity rented overseas. Matthias Hendrichs, an advisor to AI companies, explained that the rules highlight gaps in current checks since most chips reaching China recently passed through Southeast Asia. He warned that uncertainty regarding chip delivery could cause financing delays of several months for new projects.

Dr. Maria Monica Wihardja from the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute observed that Southeast Asian governments have tried to remain neutral during the rivalry between the US and China. She pointed out that while Singapore and Malaysia have export control laws, Thailand has not fully implemented its framework and Indonesia lacks a dedicated regime. This lack of oversight in some countries may increase the perception that the region is helping enemies of the United States. Experts suggest that these curbs could eventually push the region to toughen its own regulatory oversight to attract more stable AI investments.

Articles.Title: US chip export curbs test Southeast Asia’s AI ambitions, but offer chance to toughen regulatory oversight - CNA

stories.Headline: India's education ministry partners with OpenAI to give ChatGPT to government school teachers
stories.Summary:
In September 2026, New York City announced a one-year moratorium on generative AI for nearly 600,000 public school students up to Class 8, and it banned companion chatbots in every grade. The city took its precedent from Norway, which had announced a similar near-ban for primary school students aged six to 13. Meanwhile, in India, the Ministry of Education has partnered with OpenAI to give ChatGPT to government school teachers from Classes 1 to 12. Andhra Pradesh has also announced an AI tutor pilot with IIT Madras's Bodhan AI in its government schools.

The article says AI is coming into India's schools through procurement deals rather than through public debate. It warns that a school system built on a foreign company's tools can be repriced, changed or switched off by someone else. It adds that children's learning data becomes an asset to be sold, and it calls this the old dependency loop. The article does not give the cost of the OpenAI partnership or the Andhra Pradesh pilot, nor does it name any official who commented on either arrangement.

The article does not name any Indian official responsible for these deals and does not say what any of them said about the partnership or the pilot. It also does not quote anyone from OpenAI, IIT Madras or the Andhra Pradesh government. The only stated positions are those of New York City and Norway, which paused or restricted generative AI in schools. No paraphrase of remarks by those responsible for the Indian arrangements appears in the article.

The context the article gives is that Western school systems are hitting pause on AI while India rushes in without a debate. It frames the procurement route as the opposite of the public discussion happening elsewhere. The article does not say what happens next with the OpenAI partnership or the Andhra Pradesh pilot, and it gives no timeline for either. It ends on the warning about dependency rather than on any announced next step.

stories.Headline: Providence Schools Official: 2 of 58 Student Apps Use Generative AI
stories.Summary:
A Providence Public Schools official told the School Board Policy Committee on Tuesday that the district operates under a self-imposed moratorium on artificial intelligence, and that only 2 of the 58 software programs available to students use generative AI, limited to grades 9 through 12, according to the committee's published meeting recording. The official, who said they serve on the district's AI committee alongside the district's IT director, said students reach the 58 programs through Clever, the district's single sign-on system. The official said Amira, the elementary reading and dyslexia-screening program that drew parent complaints, is not generative and is not a chatbot, and that it was misinterpreted. The remarks came the night before the full School Board's meeting, where committee members said an AI resolution was expected.

The official said the district is moving deliberately and cautiously, and described Providence as a low-use, very little AI district that has been aggressive in protecting student privacy, calling it probably one of the most aggressive districts in New England. The official said the district called every parent who reached out and met with parent groups, and said they have 5 children themselves and want to protect all kids. The official said they had written that evening offering to speak at the next night's board meeting because there is so much misinformation about Amira and AI, and had attached a summary of four major steps the district has taken since July. A speaker noted that RIDE, the Rhode Island Department of Education, has a generic AI policy for students and that the district is drafting its own internally, and said questions about adults using AI are a separate issue.

One committee member said the board is not the expert on AI, calling it very much integrated into curriculum and an operational issue, and said they did not want the board prematurely slinging opinions about things it is not expert on, hoping to propose at the board meeting that the resolution be referred to committee first. Another speaker agreed the resolution could go to the Policy Committee followed by a district presentation at its next meeting, a different speaker said it really should be an administrative call, and another agreed while noting three or four parents had spoken at an earlier public comment period with strong concerns and that there should be a place for their input. A speaker pointed to an online petition launched Nov. 13 that asks the School Board to pause student-facing generative AI in pre-kindergarten through eighth grade and to give parents notice and opt-out rights, describing it as drawing hundreds and hundreds of people. A district staff member said the district needs to know whether the board or the administration owns AI policy so the two sides do not duplicate work, and that the district's AI work had not yet gone through its internal policy process or to the superintendent's cabinet.

No vote on AI was taken at the committee meeting, and members said the district's draft AI policy should come to the Policy Committee so members can really get into the weeds of it. A speaker raised the idea of a full presentation, possibly in December, on which AI tools students use and what protections are in place. Members said their next committee meeting is Tuesday the 15th at 5:30 p.m.

stories.Headline: European Commission sets HR rules for high-risk AI with deadlines from 2026 to 2028
stories.Summary:
The European Commission established the EU AI Act to regulate artificial intelligence, including specific rules for human resources. These regulations target high-risk AI used for recruitment, selection, and employment management, such as tools for filtering applications or monitoring worker performance. Certain transparency provisions under Article 50 became effective on August 2, 2026, while the broader high-risk rules under Annex III will apply starting December 2, 2027. Other deadlines include December 2, 2026, for specific marking obligations and August 2, 2028, for AI embedded in regulated products.

Compliance requires employers to classify their systems based on intended use and influence on decisions rather than administrative labels. Systems that profile natural persons remain high-risk, though an exception under Article 6(3) exists for narrow procedural tasks that pose no significant risk of harm. Under Article 26, employers deploying high-risk AI must ensure human oversight by competent staff and maintain relevant input data. They must also inform affected workers and representatives, keep automatically generated logs for at least six months, and report serious incidents to authorities.

The European Commission is responsible for these mandates and the associated enforcement timeline. The Commission stated that classification depends on how a system fits into a decision and its intended purpose. They clarified that the Article 6(3) exception requires both a qualifying task and a lack of significant harm to be valid. Furthermore, the Commission requires that employers suspend any high-risk system if they believe it creates a risk and notify the provider or market-surveillance authority.

stories.Headline: Sarasota school board adopts AI policy as students warn it lacks clear standards
stories.Summary:
Sarasota schools adopted a seven-page artificial intelligence policy on Tuesday, November 18, 2026, by a 3-1 vote at the first meeting of the newly elected board, after Tom Edwards was named chair and Liz Barker vice chair. The policy said the district will integrate AI into learning while emphasizing critical thinking and creativity. Several high school students voiced concerns about AI in the educational setting during the public comment portion of the meeting. Kennedy Cole, a senior at Booker High and its student body president, said the new AI guidelines do nothing to set adequate standards for AI use. Edwards was absent from Tuesday's meeting.

The policy requires that by July 1 the district must do training on AI, maintain a publicly accessible list of all approved AI instructional tools, report all tools to the Florida Department of Education, and review the effectiveness of the AI tools and student interactions. It also requires vendors to disclose known instructional limitations during the approval process. Superintendent Terry Connor said the policy has been in the works for a year and a half. The new Sarasota school board was sworn in on November 17, 2026, and this year's election saw three new members elected, ousting the former 3-2 conservative majority. The board members sworn in were Heidi Brandt, Liz Barker, Megan Tennimon and Beth Mayberry, alongside superintendent Terry Connor.

Connor urged the board to pass the policy and said he hears what constituents have to say and agrees on a lot of it, adding that the district needs a better grasp of how it expects students to use artificial intelligence. He said the reason it was brought to this particular update is that a Florida state rule requires the district to put some language into the existing policy, as inadequate as it may be at that time. Connor promised to keep revisiting the policy and to include the community in the process of updating it. He said he appreciates suggestions to get more student input, teacher input and community input, and that the district will have that availability moving forward with upcoming town halls and other availability. Beth Mayberry, the only board member who voted against adopting the policy, said that if the district has until July and has already selected the tools it will use to implement the policy and is already taking steps, there is no rush to approve this particular policy as is without getting more input from students, families and the community.

Barker, who voted for the policy, said it gives the district a little bit of structure, some guardrails and a place to start, and that it is absolutely not the end of the discussion but the beginning, and she is not comfortable not having any guardrails at all. Sandra Otis, a student at Sarasota High, said that in addition to her personal opinion that AI usage can stunt educational development, she has noticed that the AI usage policy at discussion is rife with contradictions and includes concerns of student discrimination along with unstandardized and ambiguous enforcement standards. Andrew Light, a senior at Sarasota High, pointed to a clause saying district employees are responsible for the accuracy of AI content, and said that as a student, as the son of a teacher and as a student in classes with very hardworking teachers, he does not really see it as fair to force teachers to take the blame for a model the district approves and regulates. Cole said teachers are not told what tasks AI should be used for, and that today it may be a simple email, but before long study guides, lesson plans and entire units of curriculum are made with AI, which he said is happening in schools right now. Cole added that students do not have firm guidelines either, asking how come in one class they can use AI for citations but in the next they get in trouble for using it for research, and said a campus run by AI quickly gets demotivated, frustrated and apathetic, which he said is happening to his school right now.

Since generative AI went mainstream in late 2022, there have been plenty of important and sometimes difficult discussions about it, especially in education, with questions coming from educators, policymakers and parents. A 2025 Project Tomorrow survey found that 63% of students in grades six through 12 worry about being wrongly accused of cheating with AI. In the last year alone, more than 400 CEOs from various industries, including those from Adobe, IBM and Microsoft, have signed an open letter advocating for mandatory computer science and AI education in schools, seeing AI education as a way to maintain the US competitive edge. In Utah, the Utah State Board of Education's Artificial Intelligence Student Taskforce was formally established just a few weeks ago and now exists under the current Student Advisory Council, meeting roughly four times during the school year to advise the board, alternating between in-person and virtual meetings. The AI Student Taskforce was approved during the October USBE Board Meeting.

Matt Winters, Utah's State Board of Education's former AI Specialist, said the board regularly hears from parents, superintendents and advocacy groups but does not hear from students and teachers as consistently. LeAnn Wood, vice chair of the Utah State Board of Education, said she hopes the task force will give some real boots-on-the-ground perspective of how students feel AI is impacting their education, for better or for worse, because they are the ones who actually have to see it in action. Winters credited students for driving the work forward, saying the story is 100% about the kids, that they figured out how to do this, and that the work is flowing through him, not because of him. Although students have not yet been assigned to the task force, several have helped set the effort in motion, including one student from one of Utah's largest districts who contacted the technology director about a year ago and asked how to get started, a high school senior who recently interned at an AI law office and hopes to continue learning about AI policy, a charter school student who wants to bring his own experience with learning disabilities to the conversation, and another student running projects with the STEM Action Center. Wood said one challenge might be getting more students beyond the 15 who currently serve on the council, and Winters has prompted students on how they can bring in more of their peers, with ideas such as a hackathon or another collaborative, judged experience already taking shape.

stories.Headline: Rio Grande Valley coalition adopts term sheet setting community benefits for AI data center deals
stories.Summary:
In 2026 the Rio Grande Valley Broadband Coalition brought residents, community organizations and local governments together to explore how communities can negotiate with AI data center developers, according to an op-ed by Jordana Barton-Garcia published by the Benton Institute for Broadband & Society on November 18, 2026. The result was the RGV AI Data Center Community Benefit Agreement Term Sheet, which sets out what the region expects in return from developers. Those expectations include protections for water, air and wildlife, local jobs and support for workforce programs, affordable broadband and adoption, and public accountability. The Lower Rio Grande Valley Development Council board, the local Council of Governments, adopted the term sheet on October 28, 2026, for cities and counties in the region to use in negotiations with developers. The coalition translated its priorities into five broad areas, which are environment and resources, workforce and jobs, closing the digital divide, healthcare and telehealth, and governance and accountability.

It also set principles for any agreement, including no NDAs so that all terms are public, and English and Spanish throughout. The principles call for an advisory board with resident-majority representation, and for binding commitments rather than aspirations. Any commitments should be specific, long-term and regional in scope, according to the term sheet. Barton-Garcia is identified in the article as director of the Texas Rio Grande Valley Broadband Coalition. The article says that when an AI data center developer comes to a city or county in the Rio Grande Valley, local leaders are now prepared for the conversation.

The term sheet is described as setting out what the region expects in return from developers. The article does not name any developer, city or county that has used the term sheet in negotiations. The op-ed was published on November 18, 2026, by the Benton Institute for Broadband & Society, which describes the piece as an op-ed. The article does not say what happens next beyond the term sheet being available for cities and counties to use in negotiations with developers. It also does not report any response from developers or from the council board.

stories.Headline: HPE builds Lux AI supercomputer with AMD for Oak Ridge, ranking 14th on TOP500
stories.Summary:
Hewlett Packard Enterprise was scheduled to report its next quarterly results on November 23, with traders watching backlog conversion and cash flow according to a TradingView key facts summary. The company announced its Lux AI cluster, co-built with AMD for Oak Ridge National Laboratory, which ranked No. 14 on the TOP500 list with 220.79 petaflops and supports U.S. scientific AI research. HPE said its networking solutions will be deployed for the first time at a U.S. Department of Energy national lab, powering Lux with 800G switches and data-center management tools. HPE invested $37 million in kind to advance the Genesis Mission and support research, and half of Lux's 3.5 million annual node-hours will go to the mission. Citi kept a Buy rating on HPE but cut its price target to $80 from $92, according to the summary.

Barclays cut Hewlett Packard Enterprise to Equal Weight from Overweight, citing uncertainty about whether AI demand is accelerating hardware adoption and business performance. Elliott Investment Management cut its stake in Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. by 16.3% to 27.0 million shares as of September 30, 2026, compared with June 30, 2026. The summary drew on sources including BusinessWire, Invezz and Reuters, and it carried a disclaimer that it is AI-generated and may contain inaccuracies. The articles do not say what the November 23 results showed, because the summary was published on November 17, 2026, before the scheduled report.

They also do not say how the analysts' rating and target changes affected the share price or what the company said about the cuts. The only stated reason for a downgrade is Barclays' cited uncertainty about whether AI demand is accelerating hardware adoption and business performance. The summary gives no further context on the Genesis Mission beyond HPE's $37 million in-kind investment and the share of Lux node-hours reserved for it. More to follow.

stories.Headline: xAI asks Ninth Circuit to block California AI training data law
stories.Summary:
Elon Musk's company xAI asked a three-judge panel of the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit on Wednesday, November 18, to block a California law. The company argues that AB 2013, which governs AI training data transparency, is unconstitutional and exposes valuable trade secrets. This legal challenge, known as X.AI LLC v. Bonta, No. 26-1591, was heard in Pasadena by Judges Rawlinson, Smith, and Forrest. While a federal judge previously denied a request for an injunction, xAI is now appealing that decision to the higher court.

The law, which Governor Newsom signed in September 2024 and implemented on January 1, requires generative AI developers to post summaries of their training datasets on their websites. California officials maintain that the law only asks for high-level information rather than the actual datasets themselves. xAI claims the mandate forces the company to reveal trade secrets worth billions of dollars and violates the First Amendment by compelling speech. Judge Jesus Bernal previously rejected these claims, stating that xAI failed to prove its data was more sensitive than that of its competitors.

xAI is currently the only major laboratory challenging the law, as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google have not joined the lawsuit. The company argues that the state is dictating what a business must say about its own product, while AI researchers have filed briefs urging the court to uphold the law. The Ninth Circuit has not yet set a date for its ruling, but the law remains in force during the proceedings. This decision will establish an important precedent for whether AI transparency mandates can survive constitutional challenges across the western states.

Articles.Title: xAI tells Ninth Circuit California's AI training data law is unconstitutional - Startup Fortune

stories.Headline: Ukrainian courts dismiss claims and flag abuse as lawyers cite fabricated rulings and AI text
stories.Summary:
Lawyers have submitted documents to courts containing fabricated rulings, non-existent citations and legal conclusions judges never made, and the problem has reached the Supreme Court, the articles reported on 19 November 2026. In case No. 523/9632/24 the cassation court left the complaint without movement and gave the lawyer time to correct the deficiencies, after which the representative filed a motion to restore the deadline for cassation appeal. In case No. 390/2226/24 the defendant's lawyer cited court rulings in the complaint that the Supreme Court established did not actually exist. In case No. 754/17743/25 in the Desniansky District Court of Kyiv a man filed a claim to recognize his right to inheritance to an apartment and to recover 50,000 hryvnias in moral damages, separately claiming 25,000 hryvnias for legal assistance costs, and the claim was signed by a lawyer. In case No. 332/2779/26 in the Zavodskyi District Court of Zaporizhzhia co-owners of an apartment litigated over utility bills, and in case No. 363/1227/26 the Kyiv Court of Appeal considered a claim to compensate 5,000 hryvnias for legal assistance after closure of civil proceedings over debt to a dacha cooperative.

In case No. 754/17743/25 the court found references to rulings of the Supreme Court and the Plenum of the Supreme Court that did not exist, and the lawyer incorrectly stated the content of Civil Code articles, referred to provisions of the Law "On Notariat" regulating different issues and used references to non-existent regulatory legal acts. The court gave the representative time to correct the errors, but the amended claim again contained false references to procedural norms and still included the phrase "this is your main trump card," which the court interpreted as an additional sign of using generative AI without proper verification. The Desniansky District Court of Kyiv recognized the representative's actions as an abuse of procedural rights and dismissed the claim. In case No. 332/2779/26 the Zavodskyi District Court of Zaporizhzhia partially satisfied the claim and recovered 3,223.40 UAH from the defendant, after which the defendant requested 13,000 hryvnias for professional legal assistance costs, and the court denied that claim. In case No. 363/1227/26 verification showed parts of the mentioned rulings did not exist and other decisions concerned criminal proceedings or a corporate dispute rather than compensation for court costs.

The articles state that a law firm cannot shift responsibility for the quality of its work onto artificial intelligence and that the client should not pay for algorithm errors. In the USA a judge of the Delaware Chancery Court fined Richard Rollo, a partner at the law firm Richards, Layton & Finger, $2,500 for submitting a document with erroneous references and incorrect presentation of legal sources. The lawyer informed the court that he used Perplexity Enterprise to edit the document, accepted responsibility and expressed regret for the mistakes made. The articles say the law firm itself avoided sanctions because it had introduced an internal policy on the use of generative AI, limited the use of unauthorized tools and conducted professional ethics training for over 200 employees. The court concluded that the firm took reasonable measures to prevent improper use of AI and that the error resulted from an individual lawyer not following established rules.

The articles state that submitting unreliable references to case law violates the principle of good faith use of procedural rights and that the lawyer's actions in case No. 363/1227/26 showed signs of abuse of procedural rights and improper performance of professional duties. They say case law is gradually outlining the boundary that AI can be used as an auxiliary tool but verification of legal sources cannot be delegated to it, and that these rulings do not mean automatic penalties for every use of AI because the court assesses the specific actions of the participant and their consequences. The articles list ten signs that should alert a lawyer and client, including a reference to a ruling not in the court registry, an incorrect date of a court decision, a case number whose subject is completely different, a quote absent from the original text, a legal position the court did not express, a non-existent article of law, an outdated or incorrect version of a normative act, a lawyer unable to provide the original source, many general theses without explanation of their connection to the dispute, and false references remaining after the court's remarks. They say one such sign does not prove AI use because a person can also make mistakes, but it is a reason for verification. The articles say consequences may include return of the procedural document, dismissal of the claim, case delays, additional costs and risk of missing procedural deadlines, and that the client may primarily suffer negative consequences.

The articles say artificial intelligence was supposed to ease the work of lawyers by analyzing documents faster, finding case law, preparing procedural documents and freeing specialists from routine tasks. They say the algorithm can convincingly write a case number, the date of the ruling and even formulate an alleged position of the Supreme Court, but upon verification it turns out that a ruling with such content does not exist. They say Article 21 of the Law obliges a lawyer to properly perform the legal assistance contract and adhere to the oath and rules of legal ethics, and Article 22 protects attorney-client privilege, which includes information about the client, consultation content, prepared documents and other information obtained during legal practice. They say a lawyer must ensure that uploading case materials to third-party services does not violate protection of personal data and attorney-client privilege, and that the client must know if the lawyer involves AI in preparing the legal position, analyzing case materials or drafting procedural documents. They say the mere use of AI does not mean the law requires separate client consent in every case, and that the greatest risk arises when a lawyer trusts the algorithm without verification.

The articles say law firms should establish clear internal regulations, approve a safe list of permitted services, limit processing of sensitive data, implement mandatory fact-checking of case law and assign personal responsibility to specialists for the quality of prepared materials. They say a lawyer who relies on fabricated case law risks building an incorrect legal position, spending time correcting the document or missing a statutory procedural deadline. The articles leave open what happened in case No. 523/9632/24 after the motion to restore the cassation appeal deadline and what happened in case No. 390/2226/24 after the Supreme Court established the cited rulings did not exist. They leave open whether the lawyer in case No. 754/17743/25 faced any consequence beyond dismissal of the claim and whether the 13,000 hryvnias and 5,000 hryvnias claims were pursued further. They leave open what internal rules, if any, Ukrainian law firms have adopted on AI use and whether courts will treat the listed signs as proof of AI use in future cases.

stories.Headline: AWS adds full fine-tuning to SageMaker AI serverless model customization
stories.Summary:
Amazon Web Services announced that SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization now supports Full Fine-Tuning on November 19, 2026. This new feature allows businesses to train pretrained large language models on their own specific company data. The process helps models adapt to a particular style, task, or domain instead of using general knowledge. Full Fine-Tuning updates all model parameters simultaneously to better absorb complex domain knowledge. This method overcomes the representation power limits found in parameter efficient fine tuning methods.

The service requires no GPU provisioning, cluster setup, or distributed training configuration from the user. Experiments used a Qwen3-4B base model and the Magicoder-Evol-Instruct-110K dataset containing 110,000 coding instruction pairs. The data was split into 99,000 training records, 5,500 validation records, and 5,500 test records. Other supported base models include DeepSeek-R1-1.5B, Nemotron-30B, and Gemma-4-26B. Users can set hyperparameters like a learning rate of 2e-5 and a global batch size of 8.

AWS stated that this serverless approach lets engineers focus on tuning without managing infrastructure. They explained that Full Fine-Tuning modifies the weight matrix uniformly to use the full representational capacity. The company noted that this results in stronger model convergence and better activation alignment across layers. They claimed that the quality advantage of this method grows as the dataset scale increases. AWS mentioned that the service handles compute allocation and checkpoint management automatically.

The articles state that LoRA methods can hit an accuracy plateau on complex tasks. This limitation affects businesses that need to capture complex patterns for diverse and scaling datasets. Using a frontier model called Amazon Nova Pro, the LLM-as-Judge metric showed FFT reached 90.0 percent correctness. The PRIMECODE scorer measured code fidelity using BLEU, F1, and ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L metrics. MMLU was used as a guardrail to detect if the model forgot general knowledge.

Fine tuning is used to increase accuracy on domain work while reducing per token inference costs. LoRA reduces trainable parameters by freezing weights and injecting small low rank replacement matrices. However, the low rank nature of these updates can limit the power of the model. Full Fine-Tuning is more effective for complex domains where large, high quality datasets are available. This method avoids the localized distortions that are characteristic of low rank fine tuning methods.

Users can now launch jobs using the SageMaker Python SDK by setting the training type to full. The articles leave open how effective values for hyperparameters will vary across different specific tasks. They note that Full Fine-Tuning is not universally superior to LoRA in every single scenario. The effectiveness of the process is described as being extremely sensitive to the chosen hyperparameter settings. The text ends before completing the final comparison between the two different tuning methods.

stories.Headline: Exa raises embedding throughput about 50% on AWS Inferentia2 chips to index billions of documents
stories.Summary:
Exa boosted embedding throughput by about 50% to index billions of documents on AWS AI chips, the company said in a post published on the AWS blog on November 18, 2026. Exa said it is building one of the few true web indexes by aggregating and serving knowledge from across the web, along with private and synthetic sources. Exa said it optimizes the index for semantic search, grounding agents and humans in true, high-quality data. Exa said it uses multi-tower semantic machine learning models to embed web data and query data into the same vector space. Exa said the keystone technology behind this is an in-house vector database.

Exa said the database must ingest as much high-quality web data as possible and embed all of it. Exa said the unit economics of embedding therefore underlie everything it does. Exa said that at the scale of tens or hundreds of billions of documents, finding hardware that delivers the best performance per dollar is not a tuning detail. Exa said any per-document cost improvement compounds into a significant number. Exa said inference runs on an asynchronous pipeline that must be high-volume and fast to serve recent data quickly and shrink the time between discovery and serving.

Exa said every structured web document it ranks as high enough quality must be embedded before it can be served. Exa said raw web data moves from crawlers into an asynchronous pipeline of parse, moderate and filter, then embed, with the result served from a vector database. Exa said its experience with the Neuron hardware family began with a backfill. Exa said moving to a superior document model meant re-embedding its existing corpus, and it selected 30 billion high-priority documents for re-embedding. Exa said a migration like this temporarily doubles the embedding load, which made it exactly the right moment to re-evaluate its hardware choices.

Exa said the doubling was a clear trigger to reconsider its hardware and optimization choices. Exa said AWS Inferentia2 figures refer to performance on the smallest instance type, an Inferentia2 xlarge instance (inf2.xlarge), with one chip and two NeuronCores. Exa said its workload runs on a single NeuronCore, so it runs Kubernetes pods that pack onto larger instances without leaving any cores idle, giving container homogeneity across the embedding fleet. Exa said the same process runs on a Trainium2 NeuronCore and scales the same way through data parallelism. Exa said its initial Inferentia2 implementation was a straightforward data-parallel, FP16 representation of the model.

Exa said that from that baseline it became a march to push throughput as high as possible, using the Neuron SDK and support from the AWS Trainium team. Exa said a progressive series of optimizations ultimately delivered roughly a 1.5× throughput improvement from the naive compile. Exa said the first was weight layout optimization, which eliminates unnecessary transposes by aligning the weight layout with the scheduling and layout of the broader model. Exa said it also enabled autocast, letting the compiler downcast matrix multiplications to lower precision while preserving dynamic range. Exa said the downcast outputs met its correctness gate of 0.999 cosine similarity against the reference, so the accuracy impact was within its acceptance threshold.

Exa said the Neuron Kernel Interface library provides optimized kernels for common model layers and operations. Exa said these pre-built kernels deliver immediate gains on common features, and it used them to quickly remove the most straightforward sources of inefficiency. Exa said a drop-in attention kernel gave it the next bump in performance. Exa said profiles from the Neuron Explorer consistently showed large amounts of spill and reload from high-bandwidth memory, which kept the Tensor Engine from being fully utilized through the forward pass. Exa said it wrote a custom weight-stationary fused SwiGLU MLP kernel that eliminated the HBM stalls, using the higher-level NKI language for layout operations, loops and memory operations and dropping into the lower-level NKI ISA only for specific tensor operations.

Exa said keeping most of the kernel in the higher-level language makes it more understandable for engineers and easier to debug. Exa said per-accelerator throughput measured with the other on-chip core idle was significantly higher than what it saw with both cores running simultaneously. Exa said that gap meant its theoretical data-parallel throughput should have been well above its realized aggregate performance, which pointed to contention between the cores. Exa said profiling and experimentation showed its workload was not yet saturating the Tensor Engine, and the remaining headroom was its to claim by making the computation leaner. Exa said it rewrote the attention kernel around the exact shapes in its model to cut FLOPS spent on padding.

Exa said generic kernels are built to handle any shape, so they cannot take advantage of the specific shapes in a given architecture. Exa said it also folded attention operations into single matmuls where the generic kernel used multiple instruction steps. Exa said that cut the inner-loop operations needed to compute the same values, which reduced HBM round trips and produced the final significant speedup. Exa said its final version was a 47% improvement in performance and cost per 1 million documents embedded, against its initial baseline. Exa said agents developed all of these optimizations inside a simple three part harness that lets them verify correctness, measure performance and profile the workload to find the next direction.

Exa said that using Flyte, an ML ops workflow platform, each agent runs its own workflow. Exa said the workflow compiles a NEFF Neuron executable and checks a forward pass against a baseline dataset, which must reach 0.999 cosine similarity to the canonical model. Exa said it then profiles one forward pass and runs a 30 minute saturation benchmark on real hardware. Exa said the harness supports agents at different costs, with lightweight models handling tedious work like grid searching compiler parameters and correctness checks preventing drift. Exa said reasoning agents test complex hypotheses and find bottlenecks, while the strongest code generators write custom kernels to fix them.

Exa said matching each agent to its task keeps costs in check, and validation keeps capable agents from drifting. Exa said that because many agents do not know the latest features and syntax, neuron agentic development skills also helped. Exa said it has so far optimized Inferentia2 for the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2), but tuning one hardware family in one Region has hard limits. Exa said spot and on demand availability vary by Region, and organizations with many consumers compete with themselves. Exa said locking into one Region or instance type almost guarantees a compute shortage, and possibly degraded service.

Exa said it schedules compute across multiple Regions from one Kubernetes control plane. Exa said its scheduler compares performance per dollar across instance types and packs pods onto the cheapest nodes, rescheduling as embedding demand shifts. Exa said each hardware type it optimizes for brings it closer to the global optimum, which is why its Inferentia2 work carried over directly to Trainium2. Exa said shifting hardware profiles lets it free up nodes other teams need or absorb their unused reserved compute. Exa said that for a long lived model, optimizing across hardware pays off enormously.

Exa said that at the scale it operates, extracting maximum cost-performance from a flexible pool of hardware is what matters. Exa said adding Neuron hardware to that pool and optimizing it with NKI has proven to be a major source of long-term cost savings. Exa said the post was published on the AWS blog on November 18, 2026. Exa said the post details how it optimized its embedding infrastructure for cheaper, more flexible inference workloads on AWS Neuron hardware, AWS Inferentia2 and AWS Trainium2. Exa said an agentic development workflow drove the optimization.

Articles.Title: Exa boosts embedding throughput by 50% to index billions of documents on AWS AI chips

stories.Headline: Anthropic floats on the US stock exchange, making its seven founders multi-billionaires
stories.Summary:
Seven founders of the AI firm Anthropic will become multi-billionaires on paper very soon. These individuals left the rival company OpenAI in 2021 to start their own venture. The company announced on Wednesday that it is floating the business on the US stock exchange. This move follows five years of growth from an unknown start-up to a tech giant. The firm is now worth more than a trillion dollars.

Anthropic will sell its shares at $83 each on the US stock exchange. This price makes the founders' shareholdings worth at least $19.3bn each. Dario Amodei will have $19.7bn, while Daniela Amodei and Jack Clark will have $19.8bn. Jared Kaplan also has $19.8bn, while Chris Olah and Sam McCandlish will each have $19.9bn. Tom Brown will hold the highest amount at $20bn.

Chief executive Dario Amodei left OpenAI because he worried some people put profit before safety. President Daniela Amodei says her brother is the person who makes the company ambitious. Chief compute officer Tom Brown argued that datacentres are an enormous source of prosperity. Jack Clark serves as head of public benefit and leads the Anthropic Institute think tank. Chief science officer Jared Kaplan heads technical research and teaches at Johns Hopkins University.

Chris Olah is the interpretability research lead and is reportedly exploring morality and AI. The New York Times describes Olah as boyish with the zeal of an evangelist. Sam McCandlish is the chief architect who helps implement policy to mitigate AI risks. These seven founders will each own around 1.6 percent of the company. Their stakes will crystallise into hugely valuable assets after the shares go on sale.

Dario Amodei studied physics at Princeton and Stanford before switching to biology and biomedical sciences. Daniela Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz and worked for Matt Cartwright. Tom Brown led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI and previously worked on the Google DeepMind project. Jack Clark is a former technology journalist from Brighton who studied at the University of East Anglia. Chris Olah received a $100,000 Thiel Fellowship after leaving the University of Toronto early.

The company will now move from being a private start-up to a public entity. The founders will transition from being tech entrepreneurs to some of the world's wealthiest people. The articles do not state when the shares will officially begin trading. They do not mention the specific reactions of rival firms to this valuation. The text leaves open how the founders will use their new wealth.

stories.Headline: Israeli study finds 78% use AI for health questions but only 38% verify answers
stories.Summary:
A new Israeli study found that 78% of respondents have used artificial intelligence for health-related questions, while only 38% verify its answers against additional sources, raising questions about public trust in the technology. The study was published Thursday by the Samuel Neaman Institute for National Policy Research at the Technion-Israel Institute of Technology, Shenkar, Wikimedia Israel, and the Israel Internet Association. It found that 85% of Israelis have used AI to satisfy their curiosity, and 78% used AI to get answers to health-related questions. Only 38% of respondents said they verify AI-generated answers against additional sources, even as 53% acknowledged that the technology can produce incorrect information. The study, which examined information consumption habits and public trust in Israel in 2026, also found that 73% of respondents described AI's impact on their search and learning habits as positive.

Beyond health-related questions, 71% reported using AI to understand concepts, 70% sought tips and advice, 55% used the technology for news and current affairs, and 25% used it to write computer code. According to the data presented, 63% use algorithmic information sources at least four days a week, compared with 29% who use traditional information sources such as television, radio, print newspapers, and other internet sites including Wikipedia. The gap is largest between the 25-34 year-old demographic, where it reaches 50 percentage points, gradually narrowing with age. When comparing information appearing on Wikipedia and information provided by AI, 28% of Israelis said they tended to prefer Wikipedia, while 29% said they tended to prefer AI tools. Among daily users, the research showed that trust levels are close, with 53% of users trusting Wikipedia and 49% trusting AI tools.

The study found that about half of Israelis believe AI responses are based on up-to-date information, and 41% believe the information AI provides is generally accurate and factual. On the other hand, 53% were aware that AI models may generate incorrect information, with 61% of the 18-34 year-old demographic being aware of this compared to 41% for those aged 55 and older. A notable gap was also found between Jews and Arab Israelis surveyed, with 59% of Jews being aware of this issue as compared to 29% of Arab Israelis. Researchers found that 55% of Israelis regularly read AI-generated summaries and then consult additional sources, while 28% rely solely on the summaries and do not do further research. Among those who read Wikipedia daily, 55% said they verify AI responses against additional sources, compared with 33% of those who do not read Wikipedia at all.

As part of the study, researchers asked 1,226 respondents open-ended questions examining how the use of AI had changed search and learning habits. Of these, 73% said they had experienced a positive change, while 2% said they had experienced a negative change. Exploring the changes, 28% of respondents mentioned the speed of finding information, 26% cited ease and convenience, and 20% cited new learning opportunities, while 14% explicitly stated that AI had replaced search engines for them. iPanel conducted the survey using an online panel and quota sampling of Israel's adult population, aged 18 and older, in Hebrew and Arabic. The full findings of the study will be presented on Thursday at a conference at Shenkar, with the participation of Prof. Sheizaf Rafaeli, president of Shenkar, Michal Wander Schwartz, CEO of Wikimedia Israel, and Dr. Eran Leck, senior research fellow at the Samuel Neaman Institute for National Policy Research at the Technion.

stories.Headline: Democrats prepare to take Congress and press Trump on AI rules and data center costs
stories.Summary:
Democrats are preparing to take control of Congress in January, setting up a possible confrontation with President Donald Trump over artificial intelligence, data centers and how much responsibility technology companies should bear when AI causes harm, according to azfamily.com. Polling showed AI was a significant issue for many voters in the midterms. An NBC News exit poll found that 56% of voters considered AI and data centers a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote, while 76% of respondents opposed construction of a new data center in their community. In both cases, those respondents favored Democrats by about 30 percentage points. Caroline Lynch, a former congressional committee counsel and founder of the lobbying firm Copper Hill Strategies, said the election could mark a turning point.

Lynch said one of the most promising areas for compromise is who should pay for the enormous electricity demands of AI data centers. She pointed to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a Senate proposal that would require data centers to pay for the additional electricity infrastructure needed to serve them rather than passing those costs to other customers. That proposal goes further than the Ratepayer Protection Act, which passed the Republican-controlled House 417-3 in September and required states to consider adopting protections for electricity customers but did not require them to implement those protections. Lynch said there is currently no comprehensive federal requirement governing how much of those costs data center operators must absorb. Democrats are also exploring ways to hold AI developers responsible when their technology causes harm, including situations in which autonomous AI systems commit fraud, breach computer networks or expose sensitive information.

Lynch, a former prosecutor, said existing criminal laws generally require prosecutors to identify a responsible person or corporation, and applying those laws when an AI system acts beyond its instructions presents unresolved legal questions. She said Congress may eventually have to address whether AI developers should receive protections similar to Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which shields online platforms for content created by third parties. Rep. Yassamin Ansari has called for a pause on advanced AI development and a ban on superintelligence, while Sen. Mark Kelly has proposed taxing certain AI-related windfall profits to help fund worker retraining. Lynch believes narrower regulations have a better chance of attracting support than sweeping restrictions on advanced AI.

Lynch predicted Democrats may advance AI bills in a bid to call the president's bluff, forcing Trump to decide whether to block measures addressing concerns about the technology. Lawmakers could also try attaching AI provisions to larger spending bills, making a veto politically more complicated, she said. Democrats will gain control of congressional committees and the ability to summon technology executives for oversight hearings, and Texas Rep. Greg Casar has discussed calling AI executives to testify under oath. Lynch cautioned that such hearings can produce more political theater than substantive results, but she noted that several leading AI companies have publicly supported some form of federal regulation, which could make the hearings less confrontational than previous congressional investigations of social media companies.

Articles.Title: What’s next for AI regulation once Democrats control Congress?

stories.Headline: House lawmakers introduce bipartisan bill to create federal cyber and AI review board
stories.Summary:
House lawmakers introduced a bipartisan bill on Wednesday to create a federal board. This board would investigate major cyberattacks, artificial intelligence incidents, and technology failures. Rep. Morgan Luttrell of Texas introduced the ROOT CAUSE Act with Rep. Ritchie Torres. The proposal follows outages that disrupted air travel, workplace software, and National Security Agency operations. These disruptive events occurred over the last week before the bill was introduced.

The ROOT CAUSE Act creates a National Cyber and AI Investigations Board in CISA. This board would examine serious disruptions from faulty updates, configuration errors, or AI failures. The AI INSIGHT Act by Rep. Matt Van Epps addresses AI agents on civilian networks. Rep. Andy Ogles of Tennessee introduced the SECURE IT Act on Wednesday for IT security. These measures exclude national security systems, defense systems, and intelligence community systems from their authority.

Rep. Luttrell stated that action is critical because adversaries are becoming increasingly sophisticated in this space. Rep. Van Epps said every agent on a federal network is a potential target for adversaries. Rep. Ogles noted that recent outages exposed American dependence on shared IT infrastructure. He stated that stronger coordination between government and industry is needed as cyber threats grow. The bills aim to prevent the executive branch from abolishing the board without Congressional acts.

Sens. Maria Cantwell and Mike Rounds urged Jay Clayton to coordinate a national response to AI threats. They wrote that the digital economy cannot rely on individual companies to solve these problems. The senators cited AI's role in uncovering flaws in PHP software used to run websites.

They noted that banks cannot always distinguish authorized AI agents from rogue actors accessing customer accounts. The proposed SECURE IT Act would keep company participation in its coordination efforts entirely voluntary. The board proposal comes nearly two years after the Trump administration emptied the Cyber Safety Review Board. That previous board had faulted Microsoft for security failures that allowed Chinese hackers to access emails.

Recent disruptions include a Friday FAA ground stop that delayed more than 10,000 flights. A Microsoft outage disrupted workplace tools, and maintenance caused a Tuesday outage of the classified NSANet. The Trump administration emptied the previous board during an investigation of China's Salt Typhoon telecom intrusions. Democrats will take control of Congress in January with Rep. Bennie Thompson chairing the homeland panel.

CISA would establish supporting capabilities for AI agent tracking within one year of the act's enactment. The legislation would prevent outside officials from altering or suppressing the findings of the new board. The articles leave open whether the proposed bills will pass under the new Congressional leadership. They do not state if the current administration supports these three specific legislative proposals.

stories.Headline: Law firms face pressure to modernize for AI as Perry AI and Alecto raise seed funding
stories.Summary:
The legal industry is currently facing significant pressure to modernize its operations or risk being left behind during the artificial intelligence era. This shift was highlighted during the TLTF Summit 2026, where experts discussed whether private equity funding could accelerate the adoption of new technologies. Many firms previously believed their unique economic position protected them from the kind of disruption seen in other sectors. However, the current environment suggests that law firms must now adapt to the same technological pressures affecting the broader economy.

The transition toward AI requires substantial capital and a willingness to change traditional business models to ensure growth and innovation. While some firms seek outside investment to turbocharge these efforts, more capital does not always guarantee a seamless transition to AI. Recent financial activity in the sector includes a 2.2 million dollar seed round for the startup Perry AI, which intends to hire talent in India, Singapore, and the United States. Additionally, the AI-powered conveyancing provider Alecto raised 20 million dollars in a seed round with investment from Mishcon de Reya.

Rhys Dipshan reported that the legal industry is experiencing a rude awakening regarding its ability to operate at its own pace. The reporting suggests that while outside funding is a potential catalyst, the process of AI adoption remains complex and challenging. Other industry observations indicate that legal professionals in the United Kingdom and Ireland who use AI extensively are more likely to see stronger revenue effects. Experts also suggest that firms should consider the nationality of their AI tools to mitigate risks and gain commercial benefits.

The broader context shows a surge in high-profile marketing and investment, such as the partnership between Harvey and Wimbledon. Some new AI providers, like Alecto, explicitly claim that their ultimate goal is to replace traditional law firms entirely. As these technologies evolve, firms must balance the need for rapid modernization with the risks associated with AI transformation. The industry continues to monitor whether private equity will successfully bridge the gap between traditional practice and modern efficiency.
