stories.Headline: Governor Gavin Newsom proposes tougher AI regulations and urges federal oversight for 2028 presidential candidates
stories.Summary:
California Governor Gavin Newsom visited Washington, D.C., on November 18, 2026, to unveil new proposals for tougher artificial intelligence regulations. The governor spent several days meeting with bipartisan lawmakers, including House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, to request disaster recovery funding for wildfires. During a roundtable and a subsequent press exchange, Newsom argued that supporting government oversight of AI should be a basic requirement for any serious 2028 presidential candidate. He framed these efforts as a national necessity, contrasting his approach with the current administration's policies.

The new California report suggests mandatory safety standards and independent oversight for advanced AI models to ensure public safety. It proposes the implementation of emergency shutdown procedures, often called kill switches, and limits on the ability of AI to autonomously create more powerful versions of itself. These recommendations follow an executive order Newsom signed in September to accelerate the implementation of safety legislation. The governor has already discussed continuing this regulatory work with Governor-elect Xavier Becerra, who will take office in January.

Newsom criticized President Trump for allowing AI companies to self-regulate, suggesting this approach primarily benefits the president's political allies. He compared the lack of oversight to an airline that operates without independent analysis, calling the current situation a national crisis of confidence. In response, White House spokeswoman Luz Huston stated that American leadership in super intelligence is essential for national security and economic prosperity. She asserted that President Trump remains committed to protecting consumers while ensuring the United States leads the world in this technology.

The governor's visit occurred while President Trump was in China for meetings with President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Newsom traveled to the capital directly from Ukraine, noting that neither the president nor Vice President JD Vance had visited that country. Although he has not yet decided if he will run for president in 2028, Newsom indicated he would make a determination after leaving office in January. He presented the California regulatory framework as a potential national model that the federal government should adopt.

stories.Headline: Better Markets urges human accountability and audits to keep AI risks off households
stories.Summary:
Better Markets released a report on November 18, 2026, titled AI and the Real Economy: What’s at Stake for Main Street, written by Evan LeFlore, the organization’s Director of AI, Innovation, and Economic Opportunity. The Washington, D.C. group said the report examines artificial intelligence’s role in household and small-business finances by asking who captures the value AI creates, who carries the risk, and who pays the bill. LeFlore said the potential impacts on Americans’ financial lives are widespread, and that loan decisions, 401(k) risks, and everyday affordability are only part of the picture. He said workers, savers, borrowers, and taxpayers will inevitably feel the impact. LeFlore said oversight is being pulled back just as the risks grow, noting that the SEC withdrew its proposed rule on AI conflicts of interest and that the CFPB has been hollowed out and pulled back its guidance on AI-driven credit denials.

He also said banking regulators’ updated model-risk-management guidance exempts the generative and agentic AI that poses the newest risks, while the AI industry spends heavily to shape the rules meant to govern it. The report recommends keeping a human or firm legally accountable for actions an AI agent takes, so that a company deploying an autonomous system owns what that system does. It says every adverse decision needs a real reason, because “the model told us to” is not an explanation, and that fair-lending laws, including the disparate-impact doctrine, should be enforced as written. The report also calls for independent audits over vendor promises, so claims that a model is fair or expands access are checked by someone who is not selling it. It recommends closing the AI carve-outs in banking regulators’ model-risk guidance and supervising the handful of AI model and cloud providers the financial system now depends on as systemic chokepoints.

It further recommends giving savers a clear, accessible description of their AI exposure on investment statements and target-date fund labels, and requiring transparency on the debt and off-balance-sheet financing behind the data-center and broader AI buildout. LeFlore said change is certain but progress is not, so whether AI’s gains are broadly shared depends on the policy choices made today. Better Markets describes itself as a nonprofit, nonpartisan economic advocacy organization dedicated to making the economy work for all Americans and protecting the public interest in Washington policymaking. The group said it works to support policies that create sustainable, durable, and broad-based economic growth and rising living standards while protecting jobs, savings, and retirements. The full report is available through the organization.

stories.Headline: LinkedIn's Sundara Raman Ramachandran details scaling a distilled LLM ranking system to 1.3 billion members
stories.Summary:
LinkedIn has implemented a scalable large language model based ranking system for its search and recommendation workloads, serving 1.3 billion members globally, TechGig reported on November 18, 2026. Sundara Raman Ramachandran, a tech lead at LinkedIn, detailed the challenges and solutions in an InfoQ presentation. The company reduced a 7 billion parameter model to 400 million parameters through multi-teacher distillation and pruning. Context compression cut job description prompt lengths from 2,000 tokens to 150 through summarisation, or to a single embedding.

These offline optimisations produced an 8x to 10x throughput improvement with less than 2 per cent quality loss. LinkedIn introduced a dedicated scoring API in the open-source SGLang engine to bypass unnecessary decode phases in ranking workloads. Inference optimisations addressed CPU bottlenecks with batch tokenisation and batch integrity across inter-process communication. GPU underutilisation was tackled by replacing synchronous blocking copies with asynchronous non-blocking copies for probabilities. A custom Item-Aware Attention Mask concatenates multiple item prompts into a single LLM input, reusing query key-value pairs.

Python-specific issues included latency spikes from garbage collection, mitigated using gc.freeze after model warm-up. The Global Interpreter Lock bottleneck in gRPC servicer and SGLang worker processes was resolved by using multiple processes. Learnings include benchmarking production traffic with Poisson distribution and ensuring absolute parity between offline and online systems. LinkedIn reported a 5 per cent to 10 per cent increase in auction metrics, such as relevance and engagement, due to LLM-based re-ranking.

stories.Headline: Siemens India showcases industrial AI and digital twins to cut engineering timelines and costs
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is being integrated into India's manufacturing, infrastructure and transportation sectors in a push aimed at boosting productivity and encouraging sustainable practices, according to TechGig. The report says the move could reduce engineering timelines and costs, and it describes the integration of AI with engineering knowledge, real-time operational data, automation and digital twins as central to Siemens India Innovation Day 2026. That event, held under the theme "AI for the Real World," highlights AI deployed in industrial environments where reliability, safety, cybersecurity and measurable outcomes are critical, the article says. Applications named in the report include AI-assisted engineering, predictive maintenance, automated quality inspection and process optimisation, all of which rely on a connected foundation linking information technology and operational technology.

The article explains that digital twins are virtual representations of products, machines or infrastructure assets used to design, simulate, validate and optimise their physical counterparts, which helps find problems digitally so corrections are faster and cheaper before physical construction. Physical AI extends artificial intelligence into machines and physical systems so they can interpret objectives and respond to changing conditions autonomously, a progression from rule-based to intent-based automation. For India, the report says, this offers a chance to leapfrog older stages of industrial automation and compress technological progress that previously took many years, while companies that do not adopt Physical AI risk falling behind global competitors. Every AI model depends on physical infrastructure including computing capacity, electricity, cooling, connectivity, automation and resilient operations, and the challenge for customers is to design and operate that capacity efficiently and reliably at scale, according to the article.

Autonomous buildings use connected data and domain-specific AI to sense conditions, predict requirements and take governed action, with potential applications in energy optimisation, predictive maintenance and improved occupant comfort, the report says. Sunil Mathur, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Siemens Limited, noted that energy accounts for a significant portion of operating costs in industries like hotels and cement plants, making efficiency improvements impactful. On railways, the article says India's transformation can leverage digitalisation, automation and data to enhance infrastructure intelligence, with technologies such as Signaling X, Communications-Based Train Control and predictive maintenance applications supporting safer, more connected operations and better asset availability. The stated objective is to gain greater value from every train, signal, power system and physical asset throughout its operating life.

stories.Headline: Agent builders weigh browser infrastructure tools for authenticated access, stealth and scale
stories.Summary:
AI agents require specialised browser infrastructure to interact with web systems that lack clean APIs, according to TechGig. These tools provide hosted or self-hosted browsers that agents can drive programmatically, managing sessions, authentication, stealth and isolation for developers. Running browsers reliably at scale, with logins, sessions, stealth and isolation, poses a significant infrastructure challenge that these tools are designed to address. The article was published on November 18, 2026, and describes a range of tools rather than a single product launch. Agent builders weigh several needs when choosing among these tools, including authenticated access, session persistence, stealth and anti-bot capabilities, scale and isolation, and framework compatibility.

Anchor Browser focuses on authenticated enterprise access for SSO, MFA and VPN-protected applications, offering persistent session state and integration with existing agent frameworks via an SDK. Browserbase provides a general-purpose platform for hosted headless Chromium sessions and works with Playwright, Puppeteer or Selenium. Browserless offers hosted or self-hosted browser endpoints supporting Chrome, Firefox and WebKit, while Steel is an open-source, self-hostable remote browser infrastructure with built-in stealth, CAPTCHA handling and proxy options. Browser Use combines an open-source automation library with a low-cost, pay-per-minute hosted cloud, featuring built-in stealth and CAPTCHA handling. Bright Data Browser API integrates hosted Chromium with its large proxy network and excels at proxy-heavy scraping at scale, handling fingerprinting and CAPTCHA solving for tough sites.

Kernel isolates each Chromium instance in its own virtual machine, providing strong separation between browser workloads and billing by memory time for isolation-sensitive use cases. Lightpanda is an open-source headless browser built for speed and low memory use, optimising for fast page reading at scale, though it does not render graphics. The article states that the optimal tool depends on the agent's specific workload, and that prioritising authenticated access, public web data collection, control or fast content reading guides the selection process. It does not name any company or individual as responsible for these tools beyond the products described, and it does not include statements from the vendors themselves. No further steps, timelines or announcements are given beyond the guidance that selection should follow the workload.

stories.Headline: Dharma-AI researchers predict fine-tuning job duration from pre-dispatch configuration with a CatBoost model
stories.Summary:
The articles report a preview of an upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models, by Bruno Duarte, Gabriel Pimenta de Freitas Cardoso, Isis F Carvalho, Breno de Almeida Beleza and Felipe Lima of Dharma-AI, posted on Hugging Face on November 18, 2026. The authors took 272 real supervised fine-tuning jobs from their production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors. The usual FLOP-based estimate explained little of what they observed, with R² = 0.31 and MAE 12.41 h. A CatBoost regressor seeing only information available before dispatch reached R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The full version of the paper will be on arXiv soon.

The FLOP baseline counts scheduled evaluation tokens as well as training tokens, and the authors swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65, with the best setting, 30%, still leaving a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features, with the FLOP estimate itself, MFU fixed at 0.45, included as a feature called baseline_time. The 272 SFT runs covered several model families up to 15 billion parameters, both LoRA and full fine-tuning, and jobs ran on 1, 2 or 4 GPUs drawn from a pool of 8 to 32 H200s across 1 to 4 nodes. Durations ranged from 1.6 to 172.4 hours, with a mean of 23.43 h and a median of 15.29 h. The stack was Hugging Face Transformers and Unsloth, modelled as a categorical feature with no assumption of a fixed speedup between the two.

The authors say the gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do: the regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs. They note that real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance. They say a job is more than its optimization loop, since before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization, during training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads, and at the end the final model goes to object storage. They write that on a multi-tenant cluster all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O, and that two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart. They state that everything is known before dispatch, with every input coming from the submitted configuration, and that this is what makes the prediction usable for scheduling.

As a second baseline the authors took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work, and extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still corresponded to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time, which the authors say says nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. Ridge brought MAE down to 7.23 h, and CatBoost and XGBoost landed within one standard deviation of each other on every metric, with CatBoost carried forward because it had the lowest mean error across the board. In CatBoost's feature importance, num_eval_data ranked first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind, and SHAP values told the same story. The authors caution that feature importance is not a causal claim, and that larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time because in their data bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale.

The authors compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost, with feature selection combining correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. They treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem, predicting the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done, with queue time excluded. On top of the raw configuration they derive quantities such as num_eval_data, num_saves and num_params_saved, and per-GPU token volumes. Across all 272 out-of-fold predictions, 80% are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h, and up to 60 hours the median error stays at about one hour or less, with the long tail where the model struggles read as a data limitation given only 13 runs above 60 hours. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE dropped from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

The authors list limitations: SFT only, with other training and alignment strategies such as RLHF, DPO or RLVR not included; one GPU type, since every run used H200s and the fitted model is calibrated to that infrastructure and should not be expected to transfer numerically to other GPU generations without retraining; and few very long runs, with errors widening above 60 hours. They say a predictor for mixed pools would also need hardware descriptors such as compute throughput, memory capacity and bandwidth, and interconnect topology. They say what does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. They add that the full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure. They note that in practice the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can plan around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

Next on the authors' list are hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs. They invite readers to follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when the full paper is out and to leave questions in the comments. They say they would like to hear how readers estimate job duration on their own clusters. The articles leave open the contents of the full paper, including the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters, which they say will be reported there. They also leave open how the method performs on other GPU types and on configurations with few observations.

stories.Headline: Kasey Chappelle and Adam Grimshaw explain how compliance teams layer AI rules and standards
stories.Summary:
There is no single rulebook for AI governance yet, and instead compliance teams must work with layers that include regulation such as the EU AI Act, sector-specific guidance from financial regulators, and standards such as NIST and ISO 42001. In the second episode of the From principle to practice series from the Elliptic Institute, David Carlisle asks Kasey Chappelle and Adam Grimshaw where those layers stand today and what compliance teams can do while they develop. The episode explores how the EU AI Act, financial regulators such as MAS and a patchwork of US rules fit together for organizations building their own approach. The series examines what AI governance and risk management mean for compliance teams, with the people building Elliptic's own AI governance framework answering one key question in each episode.

The discussion covers why the real value of ISO 42001 is the risk-based management system behind it, even though standards lag the technology. It also addresses why technical controls for AI are still fragmented and what that fragmentation means for organizations building their own controls. The episode considers what the move to cloud teaches about shared responsibility for AI models and hosting, and why organizations cannot wait for perfect clarity before acting. These points turn the principles in the Elliptic Standard into practical steps for compliance teams.

Kasey Chappelle and Adam Grimshaw answered questions from David Carlisle about where the layers of AI governance are today. The episode frames the EU AI Act, guidance from financial regulators such as MAS and a patchwork of US rules as layers that compliance teams must fit together. It presents the value of ISO 42001 as lying in the risk-based management system behind the standard rather than in the standard alone. It also explains why technical controls for AI remain fragmented and what that means for organizations building their own.

stories.Headline: US senators urge White House to launch national effort against AI enabled cyber threats
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, November 18, 2026, Senators Maria Cantwell of Washington and Mike Rounds of South Dakota urged the White House to launch a national effort against AI-enabled cyber threats. The lawmakers sent a letter to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warning that artificial intelligence is rapidly increasing the ability of attackers to discover and exploit software weaknesses. They noted that current defenses are not keeping pace with these threats, which have already powered cyber intrusions in Japan. The senators also highlighted concerns from banks regarding AI agents and the widespread use of Chinese-developed AI models for nefarious purposes.

The proposal requires the White House task force on AI, chaired by Clayton, to accelerate the deployment of defensive AI tools and establish security standards for autonomous agents. This effort would involve a meeting between AI developers, cybersecurity firms, critical infrastructure operators, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. The lawmakers want CISA to lead the adoption of tools that can continuously identify vulnerabilities and block attacks across hospitals, utilities, banks, and government agencies. Additionally, they requested a national cyber defense grand challenge to demonstrate how AI can reduce the time between discovering a vulnerability and implementing protection.

Senator Rounds, who chairs the Senate Armed Services subcommittee on cybersecurity, has repeatedly called for more action to confront the risks posed by AI. The senators stated that while the United States possesses the necessary technological expertise, it currently lacks a coordinated national strategy to implement effective defenses. Director Clayton has not officially commented on the letter, but he recently told Fox Business that AI scanners are helping defenders identify and patch vulnerabilities faster than ever before. He explained that recent technology outages at airlines, tech companies, and banks resulted from these large-scale system upgrades and patching efforts.

This request follows an urgent FBI warning about a Chinese tool that automates cyber intrusions in the United States, South Korea, and Japan. Furthermore, a Government Accountability Office investigation from the spring found that Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT, and Grok all provided terrorist attack plans during safety tests. The senators believe that without a coordinated strategy, the time required to test and install patches across interconnected systems could disrupt essential services for weeks or months. They argue that a unified approach is the only way to ensure that national security and critical infrastructure remain resilient against evolving AI threats.

stories.Headline: Tokenomics Foundation launches as Linux Foundation project to set open AI cost standards
stories.Summary:
The Tokenomics Foundation launched in August 2026 as a project of the Linux Foundation, working alongside the FinOps Foundation, which did the same job for cloud spending, according to a November 18, 2026 opinion piece by Raul Leite in InfoWorld. Its members include large AI buyers such as banks and retailers, plus cloud and model providers, and it does not sell a product or ship a cost-tracking tool. Instead it acts as a standards body whose working groups publish open, vendor-neutral definitions, so everyone means the same thing by input, output, reasoning and cached tokens, and standards for cost data that mainly extend FOCUS, the FinOps billing format, so AI providers report usage in the same way. The actual measuring is done by tools on the market, like AI gateways and observability platforms, and the Foundation's job is to make sure they all speak the same language.

The piece defines AI tokenomics as the practice of managing that economy and connecting the cost structure to business outcomes, noting that one token is roughly 4 characters, or 0.75 words, in English, and that the term has nothing to do with crypto, where it means the supply and incentives of a coin. Leite describes a stack mapping everything that shapes the cost of an AI answer, from energy and hardware at the bottom through infrastructure management, inference, model selection, and access and control, to demand at the top, and says its value is showing where to look before you start cutting. He also presents Big-T, an idea like Big-O notation in programming, describing how fast token use grows as more people use an app, including agent-multiplied growth where agents spawn other agents and calls pile up fast, and unbounded growth where a loop with no exit runs until someone pulls the plug. The key insight, he writes, is that the multiplier is usually invisible, since a user asks one question and the app makes five or 10 calls behind the scenes.

Leite, a principal solution architect at Red Hat who says the views are his own, writes that token prices keep falling but AI bills keep rising, because cheaper tokens lead teams to build bigger systems with longer conversations, more documents per question and agents calling agents. He says the big savings usually come from the middle and the top of the stack, using a smaller model for simple tasks, caching repeated work and sending less context, and he advises asking of every workflow how many model calls one user request really triggers. He sums up the Foundation's mission as moving AI from experimental spending to accountable operations, since most organizations cannot connect their AI spend to an outcome their CFO would accept, and says it wants to fix that by building open standards, benchmarks and a shared language. The goal, he writes, is not just about making AI cheaper but about making it worth it.

stories.Headline: Commonwealth Bank releases CodeCheck, an open-source AI tool for finding software vulnerabilities
stories.Summary:
Commonwealth Bank of Australia released CodeCheck, an open-source AI cybersecurity tool, on November 19, 2026, according to TechGig. The tool is designed to help businesses identify potential software vulnerabilities earlier in their development processes. Security engineers at the bank developed CodeCheck based on an internal AI capability already used in the bank's own software development. The public version lets other businesses apply a similar approach when reviewing their code. The tool works with OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic's Claude Code to analyse software, investigate potential security weaknesses, and provide evidence for engineers to review.

CodeCheck uses an AI harness that guides coding agents through a structured security review of individual code changes, files, or entire codebases. Businesses can supply extra context about what their applications are meant to do, which helps the AI judge vulnerabilities based on the software's design. According to the bank's GitHub documentation, the tool reviews security in four stages, examining entry points, data flows, and potential weaknesses before assigning agents to investigate using the Common Weakness Enumeration framework. It then combines duplicate findings and assigns independent AI agents to challenge the initial results before generating a report. Findings include how untrusted input reaches affected code, an independent reviewer's assessment, and a severity score based on the Common Vulnerability Scoring System 4.0, and they follow the Security Analysis Results Interchange Format data standard.

The tool supports diff-aware reviews of commits, branches, and pull requests, and organisations can customise it with CWE-based security playbooks. CommBank Chief Security Officer Nicola Nicol said the bank built the capability to strengthen its internal defences before making it publicly available. CodeCheck is a free download from GitHub for businesses using Codex or Claude Code, though organisations remain responsible for costs tied to their AI coding agents and underlying models. The bank recommends running the tool in an isolated environment, mounting reviewed code with read-only permissions, restricting network access, and preventing AI agents from accessing credentials, warning that prompt-based restrictions are not deterministic.

CBA also notes that CodeCheck sends reviewed code to the selected model provider, making that provider's data-handling and security policies relevant, and that token consumption and processing costs rise as the codebase grows, so it recommends spending limits or timeouts for unattended reviews. Some providers restrict cybersecurity-related requests, which can interrupt authorised reviews or end responses early, and the final report might not always show when part of an assessment was interrupted. CBA has released CodeCheck as a one-time open-source project and does not plan to actively maintain, update, or provide ongoing support for the public repository. Organisations that adopt the tool will be responsible for maintaining their own versions and evaluating any modifications they make.

stories.Headline: AI finds software flaws and firms rush patches, raising outage risk, experts say
stories.Summary:
Recent tech outages at Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab disrupted businesses and consumers, and a temporary ground stop at US airports also caused chaos, though Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy cited aging air traffic control infrastructure for that one. Politicians and tech executives, including Armadin CEO Kevin Mandia, suggest organisations are using AI to discover software vulnerabilities in their systems. That has led to a mad rush to apply patches quickly, according to Senator Mark Warner, vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee. Mandia stated that updating at speed may prevent testing all potential outcomes of an update.

Nicole Perlroth, a former cybersecurity reporter, noted that pressure to patch faster increases the likelihood of breaking things in unexpected, cascading ways, in a post on X. The article, published by TechGig on November 19, 2026, says organisations are rolling out a higher volume of fixes, potentially overwhelming systems. Fast updates may hinder full testing, leading to system disruptions, experts say, and more tech outages are expected as firms accelerate patching in the AI era. Last month, AI discovered significant flaws in a programming language used by up to 70 per cent of websites, contributing to the increased patching activity.

The report ties the recent outages at the banks, Microsoft and the FAA to the rush to fix cybersecurity flaws discovered by AI. Mandia added that while nobody wants an outage, organisations will become operationally better at updating in the AI age, and he anticipates near-term cybersecurity pain will lead to long-term gains. Warner, the senator who described the mad rush to patch, and Mandia are among those pointing to AI vulnerability discovery as the driver of the faster patching. Perlroth's warning focused on the risk that speed creates, with pressure to patch faster raising the chance of unexpected, cascading breakage.

The article does not say what the organisations themselves said about the outages. The context given is that organisations use AI to find software vulnerabilities, which prompts quick fixes, and that the fast updates may skip full testing. The report says more tech outages are expected as firms accelerate patching in the AI era, and it notes the near-term pain may give way to long-term gains as organisations get better at updating. stories.Headline: Hong Kong Monetary Authority explores agentic AI to detect crypto financial crime
stories.Summary:
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority began exploring the use of agentic AI to monitor crypto asset transactions on Tuesday, November 18, 2026. Executive Director Raymond Chan announced this initiative during a speech at a workshop hosted by the central bank to combat money laundering. This new technology aims to analyze both onchain transfers and offchain customer transactions to identify anomalies. The system would specifically flag rapid fund layering that occurs when users switch between cryptocurrency and fiat money.

This approach requires integrating blockchain analytics, scam intelligence, and customer due diligence into a single on-chain AI agent. Such a system would allow for the monitoring of suspicious wallets and the rapid freezing of illicit funds. Raymond Chan noted that illicit addresses received over 150 billion dollars in 2025, with stablecoins making up 84 percent of those transactions. He also highlighted the Virtual Asset Intelligence Taskforce, which was established in November 2025 to strengthen these efforts.

Raymond Chan stated that the central bank wants to make financial crime monitoring more effective and efficient through AI. He explained that criminal networks use digital assets for human trafficking and fraud because of their global reach and pseudonymity. Chan admitted that no single tool provides complete protection, so the city must rely on multi-layered safeguards. He noted that the primary challenge is quickly linking digital wallet activities to real-world identities to stop funds from disappearing.

The Virtual Asset Intelligence Taskforce treats crypto crime as an ecosystem issue involving regulators, law enforcement, and trading platforms. This public-private group includes the Hong Kong police, the Customs and Excise Department, and the Securities and Futures Commission. By collaborating with licensed crypto trading platforms, the task force has already improved the quality of intelligence. These agencies continue to work together to strengthen the prevention and detection of crimes across the entire digital asset landscape.

stories.Headline: Chinese bottle-cap manufacturer challenges AI automation hype at Shanghai conference
stories.Summary:
Zhu Shihui, a manufacturer of bottle caps, presented a critical perspective on artificial intelligence during an AI Engineer conference in Shanghai in early November. The speaker challenged the prevailing hype by arguing that the final stage of implementation represents half of the total journey. Zhu criticized consultants who believe every industrial process can be easily automated regardless of the existing infrastructure. This presentation highlighted the practical difficulties of integrating advanced technology into traditional manufacturing environments. The speaker explained that many factories rely on pre-digital equipment and employ workers, averaging in their late 40s, who lack deep digital skills.

Furthermore, these companies often operate on margins so thin that they cannot afford a complete digital transformation. Instead of using an aggressive approach, Zhu suggested that the best method is to exercise humility. This requires seeking out the tacit knowledge of an organization to serve as the foundation for any technological change. Zhu argued that the current trend of ignoring human expertise in favor of automation is a mistake. The presentation served as a reminder that technical capabilities must be balanced with the reality of the workplace.

Other attendees, such as Ryo Lu, also questioned how self-worth is measured when code can be written by machines. Lu expressed a desire to build tools that increase human involvement rather than proving that people are needed less. The conference showcased a relaxed attitude toward artificial intelligence in China, where practitioners view it as a marketing tool rather than a global threat. Demos included a 35 billion-parameter model from AutoArk running on an iPhone 16 Pro and robot hardware from DYNA. The event also featured a significant number of women engineers, contrasting with the gender dynamics often seen at similar events in America or Australia.

stories.Headline: Solicitor-General Ruth Higgins warns faulty automated systems risk eroding public trust in the law
stories.Summary:
Commonwealth Solicitor-General Ruth Higgins SC used one of her first public appearances since starting in June to question how artificial intelligence affects what she called the humanity of the law. She spoke at the Australian Securities and Investments Commission annual forum, where ASIC chair Sarah Court had been due to hold a fireside chat with her before Court withdrew late because her voice gave out. Journalist Amelia Brace, the forum's co-MC, took Court's place for the conversation with Higgins. The event had been expected to touch on ASIC's case against Star Entertainment, in which Higgins was the lead barrister.

Higgins said human judgement sits at the centre of the legitimacy of the law, and she warned that faulty automated systems risk eroding public trust. The Star case did not end as ASIC had hoped, despite large fines and bans for former chief executive Matt Bekier and lawyer Paula Martin, who are now appealing. Justice Michael Lee also criticised the way the case was pleaded when he dismissed the claims against the non-executive directors. The forum was held on 19 November 2026, and Capital Brief reported her remarks that afternoon.

Higgins is the government's top lawyer, and her warning places responsibility for the use of automated systems on those who design and rely on them, though the article does not set out any specific proposal or rule. ASIC has separately put consumer harm arising from AI on notice, according to a related item listed by Capital Brief dated 18 November 2026. The same outlet listed a government move on mandatory AI rules and a response to an OpenAI hack, dated 10 November 2026, and an APRA warning on market volatility and AI risks to financial stability, dated 12 November 2026. The articles do not say what, if anything, follows from Higgins's remarks.

The wider context is a run of regulatory attention to AI across Australia's financial watchdogs, including ASIC's notice on consumer harm and APRA's flagging of risks to financial stability. Capital Brief also reported that the High Court has finally embraced livestreaming, and that the Australian Institute of Company Directors has updated its guidance. The articles do not say whether Higgins will repeat her warning in a formal setting or whether any review of automated systems in government legal work is planned. No next step is stated beyond the remarks at the forum.

stories.Headline: Ackman says Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta can better handle data center constraints than neoclouds
stories.Summary:
Bill Ackman said in his third-quarter letter to Pershing Square shareholders that Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta are better positioned than smaller AI infrastructure providers to handle data center constraints. The letter followed Democratic victories in several key gubernatorial elections, including Gina Hinojosa’s defeat of Republican incumbent Greg Abbott in Texas on November 3. Hinojosa, the governor-elect, has pledged to suspend approvals for new data centers until lawmakers introduce stronger protections for communities, electricity consumers and water supplies. The US midterm elections brought renewed attention to political opposition against AI data center construction, with voters supporting candidates who called for tighter regulation and restrictions on new developments. Local ballot measures aimed at limiting or blocking data center projects added to the uncertainty surrounding the industry’s expansion plans.

Ackman identified capital availability, regulatory approvals, electricity supply, semiconductor access and political considerations as major constraints on data center development. He wrote that standing up new data center capacity requires permitting, power, chip supply and the navigation of political considerations in addition to capital. He said the neoclouds and other secondary participants face meaningful challenges with each of these requirements. Amazon trades as NASDAQ: AMZN, Microsoft as NASDAQ: MSFT, Alphabet as NASDAQ: GOOGL and Meta Platforms as NASDAQ: META. McKinsey estimates that global investment in the data center sector could reach $6.7 tn by 2030, with approximately $5.2 tn allocated to infrastructure supporting AI workloads.

Ackman argued that smaller infrastructure providers face greater difficulties meeting these requirements than the largest technology companies. He said the neoclouds and other secondary participants face meaningful challenges with each of these requirements. He identified capital availability, regulatory approvals, electricity supply, semiconductor access and political considerations as the major constraints. He wrote that standing up new data center capacity requires permitting, power, chip supply and the navigation of political considerations in addition to capital.

Neocloud companies, which specialize in supplying cloud computing infrastructure for AI workloads, have benefited from shortages of available computing capacity. Major hyperscalers are among their customers, outsourcing certain workloads to third-party providers while reserving internal resources for operations requiring their own infrastructure. This demand supports the neocloud business model, but continued revenue expansion depends heavily on bringing additional capacity online. Unlike established hyperscalers, smaller providers generally have fewer financial resources to absorb construction delays, secure electricity supplies or manage prolonged permitting processes. Their growth depends more on increasing available computing capacity than on raising prices for existing services.

Texas, the country’s largest market for planned data center development, is expected to adopt a tougher approach under Hinojosa. Projects already under construction or holding the necessary permits are generally better positioned to proceed than developments still seeking regulatory approvals. Some developers could shift planned investments to states with more favorable conditions, including Louisiana and Oklahoma. Others may delay projects while awaiting clarity on electricity pricing, water requirements and tax treatment. The decisions taken by incoming governors and state legislatures in 2027 will determine how much planned infrastructure proceeds on schedule and whether developers must revise their investment strategies.

For the AI industry, the central risk is a slowdown in the deployment of computing capacity rather than an immediate halt to all construction. Potential moratoriums on construction and permitting could delay infrastructure investments, particularly for companies dependent on rapidly increasing computing capacity. The consequences of the November elections will depend on the scope and duration of new restrictions. The articles do not say what Ackman’s letter concluded about the neoclouds’ prospects beyond the challenges he named. The articles do not give the date of Ackman’s third-quarter letter or the size of Pershing Square’s holdings.

stories.Headline: Jassy says Amazon is talking to outside AI agent companies about shopping access
stories.Summary:
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on Tuesday at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World conference that Amazon has not permanently closed the door on outside AI shopping agents making purchases on its platform. He said the company has not said it will never open things up, but that any arrangement has to offer a good customer experience and a fair exchange of value. In September, Amazon publicly blocked Meta's Muse agent from making purchases on its platform, saying the block helps ensure a safe, secure, and reliable customer experience. Amazon has said it applies its policies evenly, and users have also reported that Instinct AI and OpenAI's Dots struggled to buy items on their behalf on Amazon.

Jassy said Amazon is talking to every one of those companies, and he added that every retailer should have the right to decide how it interacts with agents. He said he believes the primary way people will use agentic shopping is in concert with the retailer they like to use, telling an app to buy the deodorant they normally buy using past orders, shipping information, and payment information. Amazon is also betting heavily on its own AI shopping tools, including Alexa for Shopping and Buy for Me, which are guided by Amazon's About You customer dossiers. The outside agents, which include Meta's Muse, Instinct AI, and OpenAI's Dots, are advertised as capable of taking action on a customer's behalf, including making online purchases.

That capability could cut retailers out of the browsing experience they have long controlled, and it raises thorny questions about ad sales, account security, identity verification, and who is on the hook when an order goes wrong. Other companies have taken a different tack, with Shopify openly embracing outside AI shopping agents. Home Depot's chief information officer recently told Business Insider that the home improvement store's online marketplace wants agents to identify themselves first. The article does not say what happens next beyond Jassy's comments that Amazon is talking to the agent companies.

stories.Headline: Jason Wei leaves Meta to become chief scientist at AI startup Mercor
stories.Summary:
Jason Wei, known as the father of Chain-of-Thought, left Meta to join the AI startup Mercor on November 18, 2026. Brendan Foody, the CEO and co-founder of Mercor, announced the hire on the X platform. Wei has officially taken the role of Chief Scientist at the company. This move follows his time at Meta's Superintelligence Lab. He previously worked at Google Brain and OpenAI.

Mercor is an AI unicorn valued at 200 billion US dollars that recently completed a 750 million dollar Series D financing. The funding involved NVIDIA, Salesforce, Benchmark, and General Catalyst. The company was founded in 2023 by Brendan Foody, Surya Midha, and Adarsh Hiremath. It provides expert data services and talent recruitment using a network of over 5 million people. The new funds will support post-training infrastructure, model evaluation, and AI agent workflows.

Brendan Foody stated that Jason Wei will help build a research team focused on data and evaluation. He noted that Wei had been a customer and a communication partner for the company for several years. Jason Wei expressed happiness about joining Mercor after spending over a year at Meta TBD Lab. He believes that data will shape the next frontier of AI development as more companies train models. His work will intersect with his previous experience in creating evaluation benchmarks.

The transition affects AI labs and enterprise customers who need specialized data for financial, legal, or software engineering tasks. Mercor's research team already includes Edward J. Hu, the first author of the LoRA paper. Other team members include Victor Barres and Minyang Tian, with researchers from Ai2 and Anthropic. The company uses the APEX benchmarks to test if AI can complete actual work requirements. They recently improved a Qwen3.5-397B model score from 16 percent to 27 percent on APEX-Agents.

Wei became famous for a 2022 paper on Chain-of-Thought Prompting that improved multi-step reasoning in large language models. While at OpenAI in 2023, he worked on Deep Research and OpenAI o1. He developed SimpleQA in 2024 to measure factual accuracy using 4326 questions. In 2025, he released BrowseComp for web search and HealthBench for medical conversations. He then joined Meta's Superintelligence Lab in July 2025.

Wei will now focus on promoting research in data and evaluation for real work scenarios. Mercor is expanding its services from providing expert data to helping customers adapt AI models. The company aims to discover tasks models cannot complete and use experts to build training data. The articles do not state the specific projects Wei will lead first. They leave open the long-term impact of his move to a data-focused startup.

stories.Headline: Calif uses OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber AI model to uncover Java4Shell flaw in Java
stories.Summary:
Security researchers have identified a critical vulnerability in Java, the widely used open-source programming language, which is listed as CVE-2026-114938 and known as Java4Shell. The flaw allows hackers to gain remote access to sensitive internal systems and affects Java 17.0.6 on systems running x86-64 Intel and AMD chips with AVX-512 VBMI support. The cybersecurity startup Calif brought Java4Shell to light using OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber AI model. Oracle, the owner of the Java trademark, and the OpenJDK project have released software patches, while Amazon has issued fixes for its Corretto Java builds and Red Hat is rolling out patches for its Java distributions. Other at-risk Java distributions include Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, and SAP SapMachine.

The flaw resides in a performance shortcut Java uses to decode Base64 data faster, and when this shortcut receives a specially crafted Base64 string, it writes data beyond its allocated memory and corrupts other information. Attackers could exploit this to access application memory containing credentials or to run malicious code on the server. Calif researchers demonstrated this by exploiting Java4Shell to breach Keycloak, an authentication system. Other applications potentially compromised include Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, PingFederate, Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has urged organisations to immediately patch the Oracle Java vulnerability, and the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team issued an advisory warning that Java4Shell could allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code.

CERT-In advised users of affected Oracle Java SE and Oracle GraalVM products to implement available patches immediately. Google has rolled out mitigations and patches across its services and developed detection to ensure no exploitation, according to The New York Times. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security also issued an alert advising organisations to identify affected systems and apply vendor updates as they become available, and it stated that no active exploitation of Java4Shell has been observed yet. The use of AI tools to uncover critical security vulnerabilities, as seen with Java4Shell, highlights underlying infrastructure flaws. Fouad Matin, who leads cyber preparedness and safety at OpenAI, noted that this research shows how AI can assist expert security researchers in finding serious software flaws.

stories.Headline: AI code generation erodes developer comprehension of software systems, researchers warn
stories.Summary:
The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence for code generation is quietly weakening a crucial architectural characteristic, which is human comprehension of software systems, according to a TechGig report updated on August 11, 2026. The article says this erosion of understanding is termed cognitive debt and intent debt, and it poses significant risks to a system's ability to evolve safely. It cites Margaret-Anne Storey's expansion of Peter Naur's idea of programming as theory building, which holds that a system includes not just the code but also the mental model held by its developers. A system that is not understood cannot evolve safely, the article states.

The article names three forces that accelerate this decay. Decentralised architectural decision-making can fragment global understanding of a system's why, and team churn compounds this as departing engineers take their mental models with them. The most recent and rapid force is generative AI, which commoditises code generation and removes the comprehension naturally formed during design, implementation and verification. Architects can watch for large pull request sizes, reliance on agentic code reviewers as sole approvers, superficial human review feedback and missing design reviews for critical changes. Further signals include knowledge concentration around a few individuals, shown by a high Degree of Authorship or a low truck factor, and growing onboarding friction measured by the time new hires take to contribute to design and architecture.

The article says a lack of documentation for design decisions, particularly the why behind them, contributes to intent debt, and monitoring pull requests that touch core modules without adding Architecture Decision Records can help. Domain leakage, where changes degrade architectural boundaries and cause unintended side effects, signals a breakdown in local reasoning and shared understanding. In an AI-assisted workflow, human code reviews must shift from mere quality gates to comprehension checkpoints that validate and spread the understanding reached before code generation. The article adds that shared mental models across teams are vital, especially at bounded context seams, and this requires deliberate team topologies and rotating engineers across modules to prevent knowledge silos.

Treating comprehension as an inherent architectural characteristic demands leading indicators, fitness functions and continuous practices, the article states. If comprehension gaps are discovered only after AI-generated code is in production, the opportunity for cheap intervention is lost. The article says deliberate and continuous engineering of comprehension, particularly at core domains and system seams, is essential for building truly evolvable software systems. It does not say what specific actions organisations have taken or what happens next beyond these recommendations.

stories.Headline: Ashwini Vaishnaw says India will issue an AI regulation consultation paper within a month
stories.Summary:
India’s government is drafting an AI law, and on 8 October Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said a consultation paper on AI regulation would come within a month and would probably form the basis of future regulation. In July, media reports said MeitY was examining the autonomy of AI agents as part of a possible new law. The article, by Manoj Chugh, was updated on 18 November 2026 and published on ETGovernment. It argues that the AI that should worry policymakers most is not the one that fakes a video but the one that approves a loan, files a return or moves money with no human pressing the final button. That is agentic AI.

The article says the government’s signals so far point to safety, a human-first approach, skilling, deepfakes and psychological harms. It says an agent is given a goal, access to systems and the authority to act, and it reads an invoice, checks it against a contract, raises a payment and emails the vendor. It proposes five principles: shared, graded accountability with a named deployer and a named executive for every agent acting with real authority; autonomy tiered by consequence, so any action that moves money above a set threshold, signs or changes a contract, or touches sensitive personal data needs human approval; tamper-evident action logs; agent incidents in the six-hour regime; and precise definitions of agents by their authority to act. It cites the 2026 amendments to the IT Rules requiring platforms to label AI-generated audio and video, CERT-In’s 2022 directions requiring cyber incidents to be reported within six hours, the RBI’s FREE-AI framework recommending board-approved AI policies for banks and other regulated entities, and the DPDP Act, whose consent manager framework comes into force this week, with penalties of up to ₹250 crore.

Dr. Pavan Duggal, a Supreme Court advocate of over 30 years, Global Chair of the AI Accountability Forum and author of more than 200 books on cyber law and AI, said on the Corridors & Boardrooms podcast that the old instinct to blame whoever built it no longer works because the builder cannot predict how an agent will behave. He proposes graded liability, looking at what each party contributed, whether model creator, integrator, deployer or user, and assigning liability accordingly. He pointed to a deeper gap: the Contract Act recognizes agency but not AI as an agent, so when an agent takes a decision on someone’s behalf, the law is silent on whether that decision is binding. Experts suggest a presumptive burden of proof, so once harm is claimed those who built, integrated and deployed the agent must show they took due care. The article says the defense that the algorithm did it is not good enough.

Dr. Gulshan Rai, whose team drafted the IT Act in 2000, said on the same podcast that the hardest problem was converting the virtual into something the law could recognize, and that at that time there was not even a digital signature in the country. His team wrote the Act in plain English because the common man would have to live with it. Section 66A, added in 2008, was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015 because its language could reach ordinary online speech, and Dr. Rai believes 66A would not have been enough for generative or agentic AI anyway, adding that drafters should be very, very careful. In July 2016, hackers sent about $171 million out of Union Bank of India’s accounts through SWIFT, and working with the RBI and the government the bank recovered all of it within days; Dr. Rai, who coordinated the national response, says the lesson was that you need a single authority who can talk to regulators, banks and foreign governments at once. The article says enterprises should not mistake the absence of an AI law for the absence of law.

The article says the AI debate for two years has been about what models say, misinformation, bias and deepfakes, and that agents change the question to what AI systems do. It says content harms are about what people believe while agent harms are about what happens to their money, their data and their contracts, and that the second category needs its own chapter. It says a person harmed by an agent usually cannot prove what it did, so the courts can offer no remedy. It says the 2025 governance guidelines relied on existing laws and voluntary compliance, and that MeitY Secretary S. Krishnan has since signaled that the time for more may have come. It says the cyber security policy Dr. Rai wrote in 2013 still awaits a successor because, as he put it, somebody has to be made accountable and sit down and do it.

The article says the consultation paper is where the intent to examine AI agents must become concrete, and that the consultation paper should state plainly that the enterprise deploying an agent is the data fiduciary for what that agent does. It says boards do not need to wait for MeitY and can start by having the executive team take an inventory of every agent in production or pilot, including those inside vendor platforms, mapping each agent’s authority, what it can approve, spend, send, change or delete, and building and testing a kill switch. It says boards need to plan for resilience, and that experience shows the process fixes about half of security problems and configuration about 30%, while the role of technology is only about 15%, yet that is where most of the money goes. It says the question to ask every quarter is what the agents did that no human approved and whether it could be explained to a regulator. It says that if agents are left out of this paper, the next chance may be years away.

stories.Headline: Indonesia's House of Representatives proposes adding an AI bill to the national legislative program
stories.Summary:
Commission I of the House of Representatives proposed adding a Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence to the National Legislative Program. This proposal occurred during a coordination meeting held on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, at the Senayan Parliament Complex in Jakarta. The meeting focused on preparing the priority legislative program for the year 2027. This move aims to address the rapid development of the digital world through formal legal frameworks. The proposed legislation would enter the medium term plan if the necessary academic text is completed.

Commission I is currently managing other priorities, including the Draft Law on Broadcasting and the Draft Law on Cybersecurity and Resilience. They are also finalizing a single article amendment to Law Number 23 of 2019 regarding the Management of National Resources for State Defense. This specific amendment is required to align the law with a decision made by the Constitutional Court. Dave Laksono, the Deputy Chairman of Commission I, stated that the draft law is a necessity due to digital growth.

He noted that several other regions have already established significant regulations for this technology. He specifically mentioned that Malaysia, Singapore, China, Europe, and the United States have advanced their legal frameworks. Laksono believes that the opportunity for the artificial intelligence bill to be prioritized remains open. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Mark Ruffalo urges followers to oppose S.5653 over AI data centers and ICE camps
stories.Summary:
Marvel star Mark Ruffalo criticized Senate Democrats on November 18, 2026, for supporting a new legislative package. The actor used his Instagram account to post a video and text attacking the political leadership. He claimed that Democrats are bending to Republicans and giving President Trump more power over specific issues. Ruffalo expressed anger that this is happening while many Democrats celebrate their recent midterm election wins. He urged his followers to contact their legislators to stop the progress of the bill.

The 494 page Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, known as S.5653, fast tracks AI data centers and ICE camps. It would allow President Trump to build more pipelines, mines, and power plants faster than ever before. The bill guts Tribal sovereignty, Native American rights, the Endangered Species Act, and the Clean Water Act. A manager amendment was released on November 7, 2026, and an explainer was updated on November 8, 2026. The Senate took a cloture vote on the motion to proceed on Monday, November 9, 2026.

Mark Ruffalo stated that the bill is a horrific legislative win for the fossil fuel industry and Republicans. He asked why Senate Democrats are ignoring their election mandate to topple the agenda of President Trump. Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York voted in favor of the legislation despite the actor's public protests. Ruffalo called the title of the bill cynical and warned of a devastating rollback of environmental laws. He believes the bill gives the president more power than he already possesses under current law.

Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon told the New York Times that he cannot support the current bill. He argued that the administration has spent two years waging a war on new clean energy projects. The Bipartisan Policy Center stated that federal reviews of business applications now take years or even decades. They noted that delays on polluting projects also block conservation projects and clean energy technologies. The bill affects public lands, endangered species, and the permitting process for various national business applications.

The Bipartisan Policy Center noted that previous reform attempts were introduced in both the House and the Senate. Senators worked for over a year to negotiate a compromise that addresses the nation's permitting process. The bill earned a 65 to 31 vote in the Senate on November 18, 2026. Twenty one members of the Democrat caucus voted for it, including John Fetterman, Jon Ossoff, and Raphael Warnock. Other supporters included Martin Heinrich, Sheldon Whitehouse, Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, and Mike Lee of Utah.

The legislation now moves forward after receiving wide bipartisan support from members of both political parties in the Senate. The Bipartisan Policy Center intends to continue updating its explainer as the legislation advances through the Congress. The articles do not state if the bill has been signed into law by the president. It remains unclear how the administration will handle the handshake promises mentioned by Senator Ron Wyden. The text does not specify the exact date for the final vote or the next step.

stories.Headline: Researchers in Mexico use a five-stage human-AI workflow to make shifts in violence representation visible
stories.Summary:
Researchers across institutions in Mexico, including the Metropolitan Autonomous University, Universidad de las Americas, and Tecnologico de Estudios Superiores de Ecatepec, published an exploratory study in Frontiers in Computer Science on how recursive human-AI interaction can make changes in the representation of violence visible. The authors developed a five-stage exploratory workflow grounded in mixed-initiative design, in which computational tools handle structured comparison and generative variation while human contributors supply critical judgment. The first stage involved an exploratory computational evaluation of a non-probability corpus containing 105 news items addressing violence in Mexico, applying techniques to identify recurring terms, prominent actors, geographic locations, and underlying semantic relationships. The team then organized and visualized these computational findings to prepare structured materials for subsequent participatory evaluation.

The second and third phases brought these computational visualizations into an interactive participatory workshop conducted with 15 participants. In the fourth stage of the workflow, the authors analyzed changes across textual and visual iterations. The fifth stage integrated the project findings through expert-supported synthesis, producing both an infographic and a video that summarized the workshop results. The results suggest that recursive human-AI interaction can make changes in the representation of violence visible by combining semantic analysis, participant interpretation, and visual synthesis.

The authors noted significant methodological boundaries, stating clearly that the study employs an exploratory design that does not attempt to estimate population parameters or establish causal relationships. They explained that the reported findings and observed narrative shifts remain specific to the non-probability corpus of 105 news articles and the 15 workshop participants. Despite these constraints, the study authors concluded that the collaborative, mixed-initiative framework effectively demonstrates how computational methods can support generative exploration and comparison while keeping human interpretation central to the analysis of complex media narratives. The article was published in Frontiers in Computer Science, volume 8, as Article 1877314, with a DOI of 10.3389/fcomp.2026.1877314, and was reported by Denise Maddox for Scienmag on November 18, 2026.

Articles.Title: Recursive Human-AI Interaction Can Make Changes in Violence Representation Visible

stories.headline_source: Recursive Human-AI Interaction Can Make Changes in Violence Representation Visible

stories.Headline: Judge Ehsan Amirkhani proposes a reverse-traceability test for judges to verify AI drafts against the original record
stories.Summary:
On 9 October 2026 the judiciary of England and Wales published a position statement on judicial use of AI, JURIST reported on 19 November 2026. The statement says judicial decisions remain with judges and AI cannot displace evaluation of evidence or judicial reasoning. It says every AI output used in judicial work must be reviewed, verified and approved by the responsible judicial office holder. It describes cautious testing of lower-risk applications including summarisation, chronologies and document analysis. It does not give blanket approval for AI to draft judgments.

The article poses a design question: what should a judge verify when the danger is a missing argument rather than a false quotation. It sets out a hypothetical civil claim where service of a prescribed notice is a prerequisite to possession. The claimant establishes title, the defendant puts service in issue and identifies evidence suggesting the notice never arrived. A draft correctly sets out the law of ownership, cites genuine decisions and grants possession. If service is a necessary condition of relief and remains disputed, the reasoning has bypassed a question on which the outcome may turn.

The author is Dr Ehsan Amirkhani, presiding judge of Branch 2 of the General Civil Court of Kermanshah, Iran, and an independent legal researcher writing in a personal academic capacity. He says no confidential case materials are used and all case examples are hypothetical. He proposes a short, judge-led reverse-traceability test beginning with the authorised record: the pleaded issues, material written submissions, relevant hearing record and evidence properly before the court. The judge identifies objections that, if well founded, would defeat an indispensable factual or legal step in the proposed disposition. The test then asks where the final reasons answer each such objection.

The article cites Ruiz Torija v Spain and Hiro Balani v Spain, both decided on 9 December 1994, in which the European Court of Human Rights examined failures to address arguments of potential significance. It cites the Court's Guide on Article 6, civil limb, on reasoned decisions enabling parties to understand they have been heard and to exercise a right of appeal. It says the Convention doctrine is not directly applicable to Iranian courts or a universal mandate to answer every pleading point. It says the transferable insight is that a court must make intelligible the path from the legally material disputes to its decision. It says repetitive submissions need not be restated, some objections become immaterial once a case is resolved on an independent ground, and other points can be answered by the reasoning as a whole.

The article says the judiciary's October 2025 AI guidance warns against hallucinations and disclosure of confidential material and emphasises the personal responsibility of judicial office holders for work produced in their names. It says a procurement or deployment policy should preserve traceable access to sources and that a polished interface concealing the record can make meaningful verification more difficult. It says controlled evaluations of authorised tools could assess whether reviewers identify omitted outcome-sensitive objections, whether final reasons treat them accurately, and how much time the procedure adds. It says such testing should distinguish errors caused by document extraction, summarisation and drafting and should examine false alarms. It says nothing justifies feeding parties' pleadings or non-public evidence into public AI services and that the judiciary of England and Wales confines judicial use to approved systems under its own arrangements.

The article says the same reverse-traceability check can be performed manually where no approved tool exists and that the legal safeguard should not depend on purchasing technology. It says the judge should check the losing party's strongest legally relevant case, not merely arguments fitting an early draft, and that institutional audits should ask whether the procedure consistently represents both sides. It says the proposed working aid creates no new general right of public access to judicial notes or draft deliberations. It says the next task is to make the October 2026 commitment to human oversight operational. It says that if the path from the original objection through the governing law and relevant evidence to the reason actually adopted is broken, the drafting process is not finished.

Articles.Title: The Objection an AI Draft Leaves Out: Why Judges Must Check Rulings Against the Original Record

stories.headline_source: The Objection an AI Draft Leaves Out: Why Judges Must Check Rulings Against the Original Record

stories.Headline: SimonMed's Sean Raj presents studies showing AI cuts fracture reporting time and improves chest X-ray reports
stories.Summary:
Sean Raj, MD, MBA, chief medical officer and chief innovation officer at SimonMed, will present two scientific studies at the Radiological Society of North America 2026 meeting in Chicago, the company announced on November 16, 2026. Both studies draw on data from SimonMed's nationwide outpatient network. One examines how AI-driven worklist prioritization shortens the time it takes to report fractures on musculoskeletal X-rays. The other evaluates how fine-tuning a vision-language foundation model on outpatient data affects the quality of automatically generated chest X-ray reports.

The fracture research analyzed more than 510,000 musculoskeletal radiographs from over 200 centers, tracking turnaround from before the AI system was introduced in 2022 through its full integration in 2025. Mean turnaround time fell 83.8% for exams showing a fracture, from about two days to under eight hours. Turnaround for fracture-negative studies improved as well, and the company said the gains came without penalizing routine workflow. Raj will present that paper, titled "AI Worklist Reprioritization: Measuring Fracture Detection Turnaround Time for MSK X-Rays in Nationwide Outpatient Imaging," on December 2.

Earlier that day, Raj will present a poster on the vision-language model for automated chest X-ray report generation, before and after institution-specific fine-tuning. The investigational model was trained on more than 5 million chest X-ray image-report pairs, fine-tuned on more than 150,000 SimonMed adult outpatient exams, and tested on a consecutive cohort from 143 outpatient centers. Fine-tuning improved sensitivity with a modest reduction in specificity, and the largest gain came in pulmonary nodules, where sensitivity rose from 62.6% to 80.8%. Raj said the research shows AI can reduce fracture reporting times from days to hours, and that autonomous chest X-ray report generation represents a step toward helping radiologists work more efficiently.

The findings support improved generalizability through local model adaptation, and suggest fine-tuned report generation models may reduce radiologist workload while maintaining clinically acceptable performance. SimonMed said the work highlights its efforts to advance AI technology designed to interpret medical images and generate clinically relevant reports, with the potential to improve both diagnostic performance and radiologist workflows. For referring physicians, the company said, actionable results arrive within hours instead of days.

stories.Headline: Imagen Technologies raises $100M to expand radiologist recruitment and train AI models
stories.Summary:
Imagen Technologies, a New York-based radiology practice that describes itself as artificial intelligence-enabled, has raised $100 million in growth capital as it seeks to boost physician recruitment, the company announced on November 19, 2026. The funds come from both new and existing investors, though the company did not name the specific contributors behind the raise. Founded in 2015, Imagen currently provides radiology services across 28 states and handles more than 2 million imaging studies every year. Imagen estimated that its physician head count has grown 100% year over year, with the company now employing a team of more than 230 radiologists and cardiologists. Leaders said they will use the funds to further build out what they believe is the best place for radiologists to practice their craft.

As part of the capital raise, Imagen also secured the rights to up to 150 million additional imaging studies, which it will use to train its AI models. Those scans include X-rays, CTs, MRIs and ultrasounds, and the company plans to build and validate models against the diverse, real-world caseloads that its radiologists handle every day. Imagen's AI strategy centers on improving the experience of practicing radiologists while boosting clinical quality and efficiency, and as its technologies advance it plans to reinvest the resulting benefits into its radiologists and the resources that support them. Laurence Eckel, an associate chief medical officer who joined the company in April after spending 26 years with the Mayo Clinic, said in a November 18 statement that Imagen is building the entire practice around the radiologist, from the technology they use to the clinical teams supporting them. He said the goal is to create a place where physicians can do the best work of their careers and feel proud of the practice they are helping build.

Serge Sicular, the chief medical information officer who also leads emergency imaging at the Mount Sinai Health System, said the greatest opportunity for AI in radiology is not simply to make physicians faster but to give them better tools to deliver exceptional patient care. Imagen said the growth capital will also help further accelerate radiologist recruitment and retention, and it plans to invest in other clinical resources, operational infrastructure and technology to support physicians. Previous contributors have included venture capitalists, hospitals and health systems, and technology entrepreneurs, with institutional investors including Google Ventures and DFJ. The company also previously touted new leadership appointments in August amid rapid growth and recently published new research in Population Health Management.

Articles.Title: ‘AI-enabled’ radiology practice raises $100M in growth capital
