stories.Headline: New Zealand Commerce Commission issues AI guidance for businesses
stories.Summary:
The Commerce Commission of New Zealand released new guidance for businesses on November 18, 2026, regarding the use of artificial intelligence. This regulatory framework helps companies understand how existing consumer protection and competition laws apply to their modern technological tools. The commission issued these instructions because businesses are increasingly using AI to conduct transactions, engage with consumers, and support commercial decision-making. These guidelines aim to clarify the legal landscape as AI continues to change the way various businesses operate. The new guidance specifically explains how the Commerce Act 1986 and the Fair Trading Act 1986 apply to AI systems.

It highlights potential legal risks and provides practical steps that companies can take to manage those risks effectively. The framework requires that businesses remain fully accountable for all outcomes, regardless of whether decisions are made by people or algorithms. Companies must ensure that the information they provide is accurate and that all consumers are treated fairly. Deputy Chair Anne Callinan stated that using artificial intelligence does not shift the legal accountability or responsibility of a business.

She explained that the commission is not focusing on regulating the technology itself, but rather its impact on markets and competition. Callinan urged boards and senior leaders to treat AI as a governance issue that requires constant monitoring. She emphasized that leaders must ensure sufficient safeguards are in place to oversee how the technology influences corporate decisions. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Nvidia spends $58.1 billion on AI stocks as interim CEO Colette Kress keeps Huang’s strategy
stories.Summary:
Nvidia spent $58.1 billion buying other companies' stock in the nine months ending Oct. 25, nearly 12 times the $4.95 billion it spent in the same period last year, according to quarterly results the company posted late Tuesday. That figure almost matches the $61.2 billion Nvidia spent on its own stock buybacks, which was up from $36.3 billion a year earlier. It was Nvidia's first earnings report without Jensen Huang as chief executive. The company reported $115.8 billion in revenue for the three months ending Oct. 25, more than double the $57 billion of the prior year and above analysts' expectations of $109 billion.

The near-even split between outside stakes and buybacks shows Nvidia's growing dual role as both chip supplier and investor in the AI industry, with its equity investments focused on frontier labs, infrastructure financiers and other private companies, according to its Q3 2026 CFO commentary. Nvidia has invested in OpenAI and Anthropic. This raises the question of circular financing, meaning whether Nvidia is funding the demand that drives its chip sales. James Kisner, managing director of technology at equity research firm Water Tower Research, said that if AI spending falters, Nvidia could suffer from both lower chip sales and falling valuations for the companies it has invested in. He told Fortune that the pain is magnified because the company is double exposed.

Kisner said Nvidia's billions in free cash flow mean it can afford to pour $58.1 billion into other companies' stock, but that can be seen as fueling its own demand. Equity securities generated only $1.8 billion in net gains for Nvidia in the quarter, which included a $1 billion loss from non-marketable equity securities. Kisner said Nvidia has incentives to keep investing given how much its growth has benefited shareholders, and he said the markets really reward the company for pouring out this money. He said the strategy reflects Huang's approach of spreading money around to keep the ecosystem going, and he sees interim CEO Colette Kress continuing it with a little more conservatism at the margins.

Kress told analysts on the Nov. 17 earnings call that giving returns to shareholders is a top priority, with Nvidia having $227.3 billion left under its buyback authorization program that she said it intends to use by the end of fiscal 2028. She said another priority is supporting Nvidia's suppliers, who are working feverishly to build more and might need assistance in terms of capital. Kress said Nvidia is also willing to help finance select customers' data centers, but she told analysts it is a lot of work to understand whether those are the right types of investments. She said Nvidia's future commitments to neoclouds, the small firms that buy Nvidia chips and rent out computing capacity, totaled $32 billion in the quarter, and she said total credit guarantees reached $118 billion, including $105 billion in credit support for the PORTS-Pike data center project in Ohio, which will host Nvidia infrastructure under a 20-year lease with OpenAI. Kress also said some guarantees only take effect once customers get financing for their data centers and may no longer apply if construction runs into trouble.

Articles.Title: Nvidia poured $58.1 billion into AI companies’ stock in 9 months—and an analyst warns it’s now “double exposed” if the boom slows

stories.Headline: Lawmakers move to preserve 2026 CSAT exam papers as police investigate Lee Jin-woo for AI cheating
stories.Summary:
Lawmakers sought to preserve exam papers on November 19, 2026, to investigate AI cheating. Lee Jin-woo, 32, faces allegations of using artificial intelligence on several high stakes tests. He scored a perfect mark on the Legal Education Eligibility Test. He also took the College Scholastic Ability Test for the 2026 academic year. Police are now investigating him for fraud and obstruction of official duties.

The request covers original question booklets, OMR answer sheets, and scoring records from the 2026 CSAT. Rep. Jung Sung-kook sent letters to the Ministry of Education and provincial education offices. Rep. Park Jung-hun noted Lee's papers were kept at Younghoon High School in Seoul. The 2026 CSAT was administered on November 13 of the previous year. These materials include handover documents for each test district and site.

Rep. Jung Sung-kook said authorities should check for AI cheating on past exams. He argued that a lack of handwritten calculations might suggest AI use. He proposed reviewing score distributions and work traces for medical and dental admissions. Jung stated that these traces are circumstantial evidence to be weighed with other material. He suggested expanding the review if multiple suspicious cases are confirmed.

Lee Jin-woo is affected by these allegations and a police investigation. Some people allege he cheated on the 2024 and 2026 CSAT exams. Reporters and instructors waited for him at the IDA Admissions Research Institute. About 2,000 people joined a YouTube live stream to watch his verification. Lee failed to appear for the session and could not be reached.

Lee previously scored in the sixth to eighth grade bands on earlier CSAT exams. He entered Korea University in 2024 and Seoul National University dental school in 2026. Doubts arose after a top certified tax accountant was caught cheating with AI. The Korea Institute for Curriculum and Evaluation usually destroys booklets after one year. The retention period for the 2026 CSAT papers has already lapsed.

Police are searching for Lee after he disappeared from his Gwanak District home. He was last seen leaving lodgings in Gwangjin District on the morning of November 19. He had agreed to metal detectors and endoscopic checks for the verification session. The police investigation will now determine the facts behind the cheating allegations. It remains open whether Lee actually used AI to improve his scores.

stories.Headline: Portland council president Jamie Dunphy introduces a proposed city AI moratorium for a December hearing
stories.Summary:
Portland City Council President Jamie Dunphy introduced Ordinance 2026-423 this week, a proposed moratorium on new artificial intelligence in city government, and the full council will hear it on December 3, 2026. The measure would add a new Chapter 34.20 to the Portland City Code, establishing a temporary moratorium on the City's procurement and implementation of artificial intelligence. Nothing has passed yet, and the Portland AI moratorium is a proposal, not a law. The draft carries a $250,000 ceiling on exempted pilots, a ban on no-cost deals, and an expiry date of December 31, 2027. The city's own announcement of Ordinance 2026-423 states the details.

Under the draft, the City could not sign new AI contracts or roll out AI, including upgrades that add or expand AI functionality in software the City already owns. Pilots, trials, trades, giveaways, purchase orders and no-cost agreements are covered. Existing contracts and pilots could continue through their current terms but could not be renewed, extended or amended to add AI functionality unless the council grants an exemption by ordinance. A pilot can proceed if the council approves it with a cost of no more than $250,000, a duration of no longer than 12 months, and a ban on using City data to train vendor models. Basic AI in existing software such as spell-check and spam filtering, and cybersecurity uses, are exempt, and a citywide AI inventory is due within 60 days of adoption, updated on an ongoing basis.

Dunphy said the aim is to protect public privacy, security and civil rights while the administration gets the Data and Privacy Office running and writes legislative guidelines. He said, "Emergent AI technology carries substantial risks to both the public and the City, meaning we cannot simply go full steam ahead without establishing proper policy guardrails in City Code." He told reporters, "I'm not saying we shouldn't have AI." He said, "We have to have thoughtful, smart AI, and we shouldn't run full speed into whatever the latest technology is just because it's there." At a Tuesday press conference he said of the police pilot, "That pilot is already up and going and, as of now, they have a set scope."

OregonLive reported that the proposal could affect a Portland Police Bureau program using AI to screen suspects' data files, such as those on mobile phones or in online profiles, for child sexual-abuse material, as described by reporter Isabel Funk. Dunphy said that if the bureau wanted to connect it to the internet, expand its uses beyond internet sex crimes, or use it for retail theft, "that would not be allowed." Chief Bob Day said in a statement that the bureau is always looking for smarter, more efficient ways to work, particularly given staffing challenges, and wants to balance innovation with accountability, transparency and public trust. OpenAI has been offering a free CSAM classifier to vetted groups. Chicago has been eyeing an AI gun-detection pilot that would run six months across six districts.

KOIN reported that the Data and Privacy Office was established in March and is not yet operational. According to the ordinance summary on Portland.gov, the moratorium could end ahead of schedule if the Data and Privacy Office is certified as operational and the council adopts AI legislation. KOIN reported that Dunphy cited the growing volume of software and services with embedded AI being sold to the City as a reason for concern about how fast governments are being pushed to adopt it. The FBI has warned about the ARTEX AI hacking tool, which reportedly breaches networks in under three hours. A $250,000 budget over 12 months works out to roughly $20,800 a month.

The moratorium would expire on December 31, 2027, unless the council extends it by ordinance. If the council adopted the ordinance on December 3, which is not guaranteed, 60 days would land on February 1, 2027. The articles lay out five predictions for the December hearing without stating them here. The record is silent on whether the ordinance will pass.

stories.Headline: California analyst Gabe Petek warns governor-elect Xavier Becerra of a $2 billion deficit driven by an AI stock slowdown
stories.Summary:
California is collecting billions in unexpected tax revenue from a stock market driven by enthusiasm over artificial intelligence, but the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office warned in its annual economic forecast on Wednesday that the state should not count on that money to solve its deeper budget problems. If the market slows next year, the state would face a small deficit of $2 billion by the end of fiscal year 2027-28, the office estimated. That gap could grow to $15 billion a year by fiscal year 2028-29, according to Legislative Analyst Gabe Petek. An abrupt crash could produce an annual $35 billion shortfall by fiscal year 2028-29, and the state would not have enough money in reserve to cover it. The forecast marks the fifth consecutive year the state has projected a deficit despite revenue growth.

Closing a hole that large would require state leaders to essentially scrap all service expansions since fiscal year 2019-20, including the extension of Medi-Cal to undocumented immigrant adults, Petek said. Alternatively, he said, it would take a new tax larger than the current 10% to 12% income tax on top earners, which voters just made permanent through Proposition 3. The report offers a first look at the financial challenges facing Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, who will unveil his first budget in January along with an updated outlook from the state finance department that could differ sharply from the analyst’s analysis. In June, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a budget he said would balance the state’s finances for two consecutive years and cut future deficits in half, but that plan largely depended on AI boom revenue to delay major cuts to healthcare services, especially for undocumented immigrants. Those cuts will take effect next year unless Becerra finds new funding to sustain the services.

Becerra has said little about his budget priorities, though he signaled openness to new taxes such as a “fair share” tax on the wealthy and a charge on drivers by the miles they drive to fund road repairs. He also said he would seek to reverse cuts to healthcare access for undocumented immigrants but has not shared specifics. In a Wednesday statement, Becerra’s spokesperson Jonathan Underland said the governor-elect is “hard at work” preparing his January budget proposal and “remains committed to delivering a responsible, balanced budget that protects the services Californians depend on and focuses on bringing down costs.” The analyst’s office said the risk of a downturn requires the incoming administration to “rebuild budget resilience” by saving aggressively, repaying outstanding debts and implementing long-term cuts or revenue increases. Assembly Democratic leaders responded to the forecast by praising voters’ passage of Proposition 2 earlier this month as a directive for the Legislature to be prudent with tax dollars.

Articles.Title: Becerra faces a $2 billion budget deficit as potential AI bust looms

stories.Headline: KB Securities invests 2 billion won in UNIST Holdings regional tourism AI fund
stories.Summary:
KB Securities announced on November 19 that it invested 2 billion won into a specialized venture investment association. This specific fund focuses on deep tech and artificial intelligence for regional tourism and is managed by UNIST Holdings. The investment was made through Npay Startup, which is a venture capital platform that connects various investors with emerging companies. This transaction represents the first time a financial firm has committed capital using this particular digital investment platform.

The total value of the fund is 15.4 billion won, which includes 10 billion won from the Korea Venture Investment Corp. fund of funds. UNIST Holdings will use these resources to identify regional startups that utilize AI technology in the tourism sector to provide them with growth capital. The Npay Startup platform was launched in July with official support from the Ministry of SMEs and Startups and the Financial Supervisory Service. This initiative aims to shift the flow of venture capital away from the greater Seoul area toward promising local companies.

A representative from KB Securities stated that this move is meaningful because it expands the supply of venture capital to regional areas. The official added that the firm intends to continue contributing to balanced growth and the revitalization of regional economies through productive finance. This action follows a meeting on the 12th of this month where the Financial Supervisory Service urged financial firms to diversify their channels for supplying capital. The regulator specifically cited the review of this funding proposal as a positive example for other comprehensive financial investment business operators.

stories.Headline: Boston Dynamics and GlobalFoundries plan Atlas humanoid robot testing at chip plants from early 2027
stories.Summary:
Boston Dynamics, a subsidiary of Hyundai Motor Group, announced on November 17, 2026, that it is expanding its strategic collaboration with GlobalFoundries. This partnership will involve on-site testing of the Atlas humanoid robot at advanced semiconductor manufacturing facilities starting in early 2027. GlobalFoundries will be the first semiconductor maker and the first customer outside the automotive industry to test this specific robot. The companies intend to identify suitable tasks for humanoid robots in precision manufacturing and conduct AI training to explore physical AI applications.

The initiative requires the deployment of additional Spot quadruped robots across major sites in Singapore, Dresden, Germany, Burlington, Vermont, and Malta, New York. GlobalFoundries has already operated Spot in Burlington for over four years and used two units in Singapore since April. Those Singapore robots traveled about 900 kilometers through sub-fab areas and completed over 90,000 inspections with a 99 percent success rate. The company now plans to use these visual inspection capabilities to more than double the number of routine checks performed.

Pradip Singh, the chief manufacturing officer at GlobalFoundries, stated that Spot improved facility efficiency and helped the company move toward predictive maintenance. He described the upcoming Atlas testing as a necessary step toward achieving AI-enabled manufacturing. Zack Jackowski, the chief product and technology officer at Boston Dynamics, noted that innovative companies are already gaining tangible operational value from robotics. He added that the data being collected will be extremely useful for future innovations in the manufacturing sector.

Boston Dynamics is currently validating Atlas for automotive tasks at the Robotics Metaplant Application Center in Georgia. This center began pilot operations in June 2026 and officially opened in September 2026 to teach the robot tasks like parts sequencing. Hyundai Motor Group intends to begin deploying the Atlas robot at the HMGMA vehicle manufacturing plant in 2028. This broader strategy aims to bring automotive production expertise into the precision semiconductor industry to test the robot's versatility.

stories.Headline: South Korean authorities tighten exam security after student uses AI and miniature cameras to cheat
stories.Summary:
Authorities in South Korea are scrambling to prevent students from using AI and miniature cameras to cheat on college exams. A top scorer on a national tax accountant certification exam, surnamed Han, confessed on Sunday to using these tools. Han used a miniature camera to photograph questions and send them to an AI system before checking answers on a smartphone. This cheating scandal has occurred just before the upcoming College Scholastic Ability Test. Women's rights activists say this crisis reflects years of ignored warnings about hidden cameras.

Proposed laws from 2015, 2017, 2018, 2021, and 2022 sought to regulate cameras disguised as pens, glasses, neckties, water bottles, clocks, and belts. Rep. Chang Byoung-wan and Rep. Jin Sun-mee of the Democratic Party introduced bills requiring permits or registration for manufacturing, importing, exporting, selling, and possessing these devices. These bills also called for a system to track the distribution history of disguised cameras within Korea. In 2018, over 200,000 people signed a presidential petition for a ban, and another 230,000 signed a similar petition in 2021. All these legislative efforts were scrapped when the respective National Assembly terms expired.

Park Ji-hyun, a former interim leader of the Democratic Party, criticized the government on social media this Monday. She stated that delaying regulations under the pretext of technological advancement is now undermining fairness in society. Professor Lim So-yeon of Dong-A University warned that people should not assume technology is inherently neutral. Lim argued that laws and regulations should be used to protect society rather than claiming nothing can be done about AI. Heo Min-sook of the National Assembly Research Service questioned if violations of women's rights are regarded as matters of fairness.

Online commenters expressed frustration, calling the controversy a disaster of lawmakers' own making and a paradise for cheaters. Women's rights advocates say the cheating uproar could have been prevented if officials heeded repeated warnings about illegal filming. These advocates note that the issue only attracted attention after exam fairness was threatened. The victims of illegal filming, known as molka, are mostly women. The public feels there is nothing left to rely on because exams are believed to level the playing field.

Legislative efforts to regulate miniature cameras began in 2015 to prevent crimes targeting women. A senior legislative specialist in 2021 argued that a balance must be struck between regulation, technological advancement, and industrial growth. The Blue House pledged to participate in legislative discussions in August 2021, but the proposed laws still expired. Miniature cameras are currently sold on Chinese online shopping websites and in Seoul retail stores. Some devices were even tested during a CPA exam before the tax exam cheating occurred.

The government will inspect students' glasses, clothing, and personal belongings for concealed devices during the College Scholastic Ability Test. Additional exam supervisors will be deployed to prevent the use of AI-powered smart glasses. Over 551,864 students sat for the 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test under these heightened security measures. The articles do not state if new legislation will be introduced to permanently ban disguised cameras. It remains open whether the government will successfully stop all AI-enabled cheating in future national exams.

Articles.Title: Oh, now you care: Women's rights activists say AI cheating crisis reflects years of ignored warnings about hidden cameras

stories.Headline: Students at Transylvania University petition to cancel campus chatbot licenses and fund human-centered education
stories.Summary:
Last March a handful of students at Transylvania University in Lexington, Kentucky, created a petition that tried to slow the advance of artificial intelligence on their campus, and about a third of the college's students signed it. The petition asked the administration to cancel its chatbot licenses with A.I. giants and to put the money into what it called human-centered education instead. Transylvania is tiny, with under 1,000 students, but the New York Times reported on November 19, 2026, that campus resistance to A.I. has swelled across the country and around the globe. That resistance includes a growing group of conscientious objectors who refuse to use A.I. at all, from California to Sydney to Paris. The pushback carries specific demands, which students and faculty are increasingly publishing in manifestoes.

They want colleges not to partner with A.I. companies, and they want professors not to be required to use generative A.I. in lessons or grading. They also want students to be allowed to refuse assignments that require chatbots without any impact on their grades. Polls show the vast majority of American students use chatbots for school work, and college leaders have generally embraced A.I. as key to preparing students for the work force. Much of the opposition comes from the political left and focuses on how A.I. could harm the environment, diminish the power of workers or be used in warfare. Some of the loudest voices are studying the arts, where human creativity is paramount, or the law, as tech companies face lawsuits over potential copyright and privacy violations.

There are also deep concerns that A.I. degrades the experience of college itself by removing the productive struggle of learning. As A.I. use grows, more students and faculty are sounding alarms and trying to slow it down. The articles do not say what the colleges have answered or what happens next beyond the growing petitions and manifestoes. What is clear is that the objectors are organizing across campuses and publishing their demands, while college leaders continue to embrace the technology. More to follow.

Articles.Title: College students are increasingly pushing back against campus AI mandates, demanding opt-outs from AI-required assignments and an end to enterprise licenses (Dana Goldstein/New York Times)

stories.Headline: SoftBank's Son admits missing Anthropic investment was a mistake and keeps backing OpenAI
stories.Summary:
Masayoshi Son, the founder and chief executive officer of SoftBank Group, admitted on Wednesday that he made a mistake by missing an earlier chance to invest in Anthropic. He shared these reflections during the Nikkei Dialogues on the Future conference held in Tokyo on November 18, 2026. The executive discussed the inherent difficulties of selecting a winner among several rival developers of artificial intelligence. While he regretted the missed opportunity with Anthropic, he confirmed that he continues to focus his current investments on OpenAI. This admission comes as the broader landscape for artificial intelligence shifts toward a period that Son describes as the real show beginning now.

The strategic focus of SoftBank Group involves navigating a competitive market where various AI firms are vying for dominance. Son emphasized that his primary objective is not simply to generate profit through these financial ventures. Instead, he believes that the true purpose of his investment strategy is to actively create the future through these technologies. The chairman and chief executive officer is responsible for the investment direction of SoftBank Group and its various AI initiatives.

He explained to the forum that his goals extend beyond the immediate financial gains typically associated with venture capital. By prioritizing the creation of the future, he aims to position his company at the center of the artificial intelligence revolution. He believes that the current phase of development represents the most critical moment for the industry. More to follow.

Articles.Title: SoftBank's Son calls missing Anthropic investment one of his 'mistakes'

stories.Headline: AAIB probe report into AI 171 crash at ‘fag end’, Centre tells Supreme Court
stories.Summary:
The Centre told the Supreme Court on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, that the final Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau report on the Air India Flight 171 crash is at the fag end, and it asked for two or three weeks more for publication. The crash at Ahmedabad Airport killed 12 crew members and 229 passengers on June 12, 2025. On July 28, the court was told the report would be published anytime between the middle of September, with a buffer till the end of October. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Union government and the Directorate General of Civil Aviation, said the report was nearly complete.

Advocates Prashant Bhushan and Pranav Sachdeva, appearing for petitioner NGO Safety Matters Foundation, said the authorities have repeatedly sought adjournments in the case. Mehta denied any attempt to deliberately delay the report. In July, the apex court put on hold the petitioners' plea for a Court of Inquiry or a fair, transparent and technically sound investigation, in order to wait for the report. One petitioner is 91-year-old Pushkar Raj Sabharwal, father of Commander Sumeet Sabharwal, one of the pilots on the ill-fated aircraft.

The court had clarified that the trajectory of the litigation would depend on whether the AAIB report would be well-merited and accepted. The petitions, including one by a pilots' body, argued that an investigation of such magnitude ought to have gone to an independent agency under international protocols to which India is a signatory. The court opted to wait for the report, reasoning that the AAIB probe had substantially progressed. On Wednesday, Bhushan submitted that the probe had been on for a year and a half, and he had earlier alleged a conflict of interest, saying three of the five members of the investigation team were from the DGCA.

He said AAIB rules mandated a permanent body without DGCA members. Mehta had earlier explained that experts from the countries to which some of the passengers belonged were involved in the investigation. He said the investigation took time because each component of the aircraft had to be sent to the manufacturers, wherever they were located, for checking. The court is awaiting the report before deciding how the petitions proceed.

Articles.Title: AAIB probe report into AI 171 crash at ‘fag end’, Centre tells Supreme Court

stories.Headline: Rahul Matthan urges India to practice deploying AI models on its own infrastructure to serve intelligence at scale
stories.Summary:
Rahul Matthan wrote an opinion piece on November 17, 2026, regarding the global race for artificial intelligence. He argues that India must prepare to build and serve AI to its own people. The author believes India should not worry about being left behind in this race. He suggests that knowledge always moves from those who have it to those who do not. India must be ready to absorb this knowledge when frontier models arrive.

The US uses chokepoints like chip access and model availability to keep technical knowledge from geopolitical rivals. In 1999, the US put commercial satellites on the munitions list, which reduced their market share from 80 percent to 50 percent. These satellite export controls remained in place until the US government reversed them in 2014. In February, a US lab accused three Chinese firms of using 24,000 fake accounts for 16 million exchanges. OpenAI hid the raw chain of thought for its o1 model in 2024 to keep a competitive advantage.

Rahul Matthan, a partner at Trilegal, says India needs to practice deploying AI models on its own infrastructure. He wrote that India must learn to serve intelligence at a scale that a country of its size requires. Matthan believes that the process knowledge required to serve intelligence at scale is learned through trial and error. He argues that practicing on less capable open models will prepare India for more capable models. He suggests that having this investment will place India in the best position to take advantage.

Many countries worry that the world will be divided into AI haves and have-nots. Those who lack access to AI might find themselves out in the cold. US AI labs have been vehemently opposed to distillation, where one model is trained on another's answers. One Nvidia customer in Southeast Asia is under US investigation for allegedly moving billions of dollars of chips to China. Reports have linked one executive from that company to Chinese intelligence.

Britain banned textile machinery exports and skilled worker emigration by the end of the 18th century. Samuel Slater, an apprentice at Jedediah Strutt's mill in Derbyshire, memorized machinery designs and sailed to New York. Slater and Moses Brown opened a factory in Pawtucket in 1793 using a spinning frame. Britain lifted the emigration ban in 1824 and the machinery export ban in 1843. These historical examples show that technology controls are often subverted or eventually fail.

India must now build its own mill to be ready for frontier AI knowledge. The country should focus on the process of serving intelligence at scale. The author believes that AI is easy to reverse engineer by studying model responses. The articles do not state when India will begin these infrastructure projects. They leave open how India will acquire the necessary open models for its practice.

stories.Headline: ABBYY survey finds 57% of manufacturing leaders say AI adoption outpaces their governance
stories.Summary:
New research commissioned by ABBYY found that 57% of manufacturing leaders say AI is being adopted faster than they can govern it. The ABBYY Who Answers for AI: The Governance Gap report surveyed manufacturing leaders at businesses using AI. Marina Mayer reported the findings on November 19, 2026, in Supply & Demand Chain Executive. Only 17% of manufacturing bosses completely trust AI to operate without introducing unacceptable risks. Just over one-quarter, 26%, of manufacturing companies completely trust AI to produce accurate results.

The report found 33% of manufacturing leaders believe responsibility for harmful or false outputs should be shared between the organization and the vendor. Another 26% think the AI vendor should bear full responsibility, while 23% say it lies with the company using it. The rest said the end user or regulators should take the lead. Data governance requirements slow AI deployment, according to 67% of manufacturing leaders surveyed. Just 48% say their AI initiatives have exceeded expectations.

Roman Kilun, chief compliance officer at ABBYY, said businesses are embracing AI but many still struggle with key questions around accountability, governance and ROI. He said senior management needs to do a better job of communicating responsible AI policies companywide. He said it is often more junior staff who operate AI tools day to day and they should know which controls apply. He said AI requires organizations to know where data comes from, whether it can be trusted, how it can be used, and where it is stored and processed.

36% say ethical concerns such as bias and transparency slow down deployment of AI initiatives in manufacturing organizations. Nearly one-quarter, 24%, of manufacturing leaders cite data quality as their top challenge to achieving greater ROI from AI. Skills shortages is the next most significant barrier, followed by integration with existing systems at 13% and the cost of implementation at 12%. 94% of manufacturing leaders say senior leadership knows who is responsible for developing, implementing, and managing AI, but only 66% say the same for junior employees.

88% of manufacturing leaders surveyed have an AI governance framework in place, and of these 78% say it has made their AI initiatives more successful. They cite easier deployment at 57%, easier scaling at 56% and easier widespread adoption among employees at 54%. Less than half, 48%, of manufacturing companies have an AI incident reporting process in place, while only 32% have an AI kill switch and 36% have an AI roll back capability. 61% of manufacturing leaders say humans review all important AI decisions before action is taken, higher than the global average of 56%.

The most popular tools among manufacturing leaders are Generative AI at 82%, Agentic AI at 63% and Purpose-built AI at 59%. Manufacturing organizations are continuing to increase their investment in AI, with respondents expecting investment to increase by a further 19.1% next year, slightly above the global average of 18.8%. Only 17% of manufacturing bosses completely trust AI to operate without unacceptable risks, compared with an average of 22% globally. The articles do not say what action, if any, ABBYY or the surveyed manufacturers plan to take next.

Articles.Title: AI Governance Gap: Manufacturing Leaders Struggle to Keep Up

stories.Headline: OpenAI says its models cut chip area by up to 14% on AMD GPU IP and speed Jalapeño design
stories.Summary:
OpenAI said on November 18, 2026 that its models are quickly improving the chips that power AI, and in August it shared how OpenAI engineers used frontier models to accelerate development of its first custom inference chip, Jalapeño. OpenAI started using GPT-4o to help design Jalapeño in early 2025, and even that early model found ways to make nontrivial PPA improvements. The company evaluated successive model generations on two open-source processor designs, PicoRV32 and OpenTitan’s Ibex, to measure ability at end to end chip design tasks. OpenAI is working with Synopsys to integrate frontier intelligence with the electronic design automation tools engineers already use to design and verify chips. OpenAI partnered with AMD on PPA improvements and saw up to 14% improvement relative to heavily optimized baselines on the flagship GPU IP.

In the vector unit, which manages and executes parallel computing tasks, savings came from floating-point adders and multipliers, conversion functions, reduction logic, and the special-function unit. In the matrix unit, an arithmetic component, improvements accumulated across floating-point adders, multipliers, and low-precision dot-product circuits, and one multiplier redesign used about 15% less cell area in synthesis while reducing latency from two clock cycles to one. A separate adder redesign reduced cell area by about 15% while retaining its two-cycle latency. Across the broader Jalapeño design effort, the team estimates model-proposed changes reduced standard-cell area by about 13% in the vector unit and 10% in the matrix unit, and these optimizations were silicon proven during Jalapeño’s silicon bring-up. On AMD, the model identified further improvements by rewriting SystemVerilog RTL, representing roughly a year of progress achieved in less than 5 months.

OpenAI said AMD has already included some of these changes in a recent design it sent for manufacturing and added others to its production design files for use in future versions. OpenAI said it observed the model reason about RTL at the level of an expert microarchitect, and the model used Synopsys tools to verify that each rewrite preserved the block’s behavior and to evaluate trade-offs in power, performance, and area. AMD also verified single-digit percentage gains in PPA across key blocks of its upcoming next-generation flagship CPU using designs written by OpenAI’s model. OpenAI said it expects further PPA improvements on top of GPU and CPU relative to the most optimized baseline. OpenAI is partnering with Synopsys to train GPT-Synopsys, a new model, to use Synopsys EDA tools the way expert chip designers do.

PicoRV32 is a compact core designed for reprogrammable chips called FPGAs, and OpenTitan uses Ibex as the embedded processor in its security chip, each a complete processor core for embedded, microcontroller class workloads. OpenAI gave each model the original hardware description for each core and asked it to increase throughput, the number of instructions the core can execute per second. Designs scored zero if they failed a check or used more than 16 times the original core’s area, and for designs that passed OpenAI measured instructions per clock cycle on workloads hidden from the models, took the geometric mean across those workloads, and multiplied it by the maximum clock frequency estimated with Yosys. For each core OpenAI assigned the best throughput observed under the same constraints a score of 1.0, and the charts show the average score across runs, including those that scored zero. With a comparable budget of about 112,000 tokens per run, GPT-6.2 Astra had the highest average score on both cores, and GPT-6.1 Sol also outscored GPT-5.6 Sol on both.

On the existing PicoRV32 core, GPT-6.2 Astra has the highest mean score at the larger comparable budgets, and around 112,000 tokens its score is about twice GPT-6 Astra’s. On the existing Ibex core, GPT-6.2 Astra’s mean score continues to climb across the higher budgets it reaches, while GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol are closer together. For the second task OpenAI gave each model written requirements and templates from the open-source code showing how the core connects to the rest of the system, and the model chose how data would move through the core and how to divide the work into stages. For each core OpenAI kept the correctness checks, memory and cache settings, and throughput objectives the same as in the RTL optimization task, and at about 112,000 tokens per run all five models scored higher when they designed a core from written requirements than when they tried to improve the existing design, which held for both PicoRV32 and Ibex. GPT-6.2 Astra gained more on Ibex than on PicoRV32, and the full evaluation included 9,881 scored runs across both tasks, both cores, and all token budgets.

Starting from a PicoRV32 specification, GPT-6.2 Astra passes a mean score of 0.7 near 112,000 tokens and scores higher at the next two observed budgets. On Ibex, GPT-6.2 Astra averages about 0.75 near 112,000 tokens when designing from a specification, and its curve stays above the others at larger shared budgets. OpenAI said starting from written requirements gives the models room to omit features found in the original cores, such as performance counters and additional instructions, and those features may do little to improve throughput on the test workloads, which could explain part of the score advantage. OpenAI said requiring those features, setting a tighter limit on circuit area, and checking timing after physical synthesis would make the test more representative of production chip design. OpenAI said it has demonstrated that its models can explore new processor architectures in RISC-V evals and contributed net new improvements on top of sophisticated production designs such as Jalapeño and AMD’s next generation flagship GPU and CPU.

stories.Headline: Meta staff flag Muse AI privacy risks as researchers find exposed chats before US launch
stories.Summary:
Meta employees raised massive security concerns about the Muse AI agent before and after its release. These workers flagged serious doubts regarding privacy promises through internal channels during the launch week. Meta proceeded with the scheduled United States launch in September 2026 despite these warnings. Internal communications reviewed by Reuters showed employees feared the product was unreliable in real world conditions. The company launched the agent with claims that it was built for privacy and security.

The agent manages emails, calendars, and financial tasks through connected accounts and broad Android notification permissions. Meta began testing a human concierge phone feature with employees in August 2026 before public release. A vulnerability identified by Patrick Wardle put account tokens and dictated audio at risk for individual users. Claroc found that shared conversations were exposed through publicly searchable DNS records without requiring any login. These exposed records included financial reviews, business documents, and holiday schedules from entire companies and marketing firms.

Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts stated that the company prioritizes safety and follows strict internal rules. He described the examples provided by Reuters as isolated incidents and noted that Meta conducts extensive testing. Meta did not dispute that the internal posts from employees existed. The company temporarily disabled the sharing feature after being alerted to the DNS flaw. Meta subsequently restored the feature once a fix was in place to block the links.

Internal employees were described by Ars Technica as freaking out about the privacy implications of Muse. These workers observed behaviors that conflicted directly with how Meta marketed the product to the public. Users who shared conversations using the built in function were affected by the DNS discovery. Security researchers and IT experts now recommend that users treat broad device permissions with caution. Organizations are advised to establish clear policies about what information employees submit to AI assistants.

Meta is an American technology company headquartered in Menlo Park, California, founded by Mark Zuckerberg in 2004. The company rebranded from Facebook in 2021 to focus on the metaverse and Quest VR hardware. Muse operates in cloud virtual machines gated by a security process called Sentinel. Reuters tests showed Muse accessing private Signal messages and sending unsolicited bank balance figures to employees. The human concierge feature uses human contractors to handle calls when the AI cannot complete tasks.

Claroc confirmed that there was no evidence that anyone misused the exposed chats before the fix. Meta maintains that the AI agent is built with strong security foundations despite the reported failures. The articles leave open whether the pattern of issues suggests a systemic architectural failure. Experts suggest users monitor app permission settings to understand what data the agent can access. The reports do not state if Meta will change the broad permissions required by the app.

Articles.Title: Meta Employees Raise Muse AI Privacy Concerns, Exposing Security Flaws, Chat Leaks

stories.Headline: Letitia James launches ASSET unit to enforce New York AI safety law from January
stories.Summary:
New York Attorney General Letitia James launched a specialized unit on November 17, 2026, to enforce artificial intelligence regulations. This new office is designed to oversee compliance before a state law takes effect in January. The initiative focuses on the safety and transparency requirements that will soon apply to frontier model developers. This agency represents the first effort of its kind in the United States dedicated to AI laws. The new organization is called the AI Safety, Standards, Enforcement, and Transparency Unit, or ASSET for short.

It will require developers of frontier models to meet specific safety and transparency standards starting in January. These legal requirements aim to ensure that powerful artificial intelligence systems are developed and deployed responsibly. The unit will monitor these developers to ensure they follow the impending state safety laws. Letitia James is the official responsible for the creation and leadership of this novel regulatory unit.

Her office stated that this is the first unit in the country dedicated to enforcing AI laws. The Attorney General intends to use this group to hold technology developers accountable under the new state framework. By establishing ASSET now, the office aims to be ready for the upcoming regulatory changes. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Doubao Work reaches 2 billion yuan in annual recurring revenue within three months of launch
stories.Summary:
Doubao Work reached an annual recurring revenue of 2 billion yuan by November 18, 2026. The AI office application was launched only three months before hitting this financial milestone. Its daily active users have now exceeded 8 million people. Many enterprises integrated the tool into production line management and quality audits. These companies also used the AI for equipment operation and maintenance.

The system combines with Feishu collaboration to turn implicit knowledge into reusable organizational assets. In Changzhou, Ninebot uses the tool to automate 16 daily forms for attendance and overtime. This automation saves two clerks between 20 and 30 minutes of work every day. The tool also manages standard working hours and manpower data for different models. It now includes a memory function to reduce redundant data entry for line leaders.

He Yuchong, a production management specialist, used Doubao Work to polish functions based on site pain points. He described specific operation paths and expected effects to the AI to modify the system. He first troubleshot errors himself before telling the AI the phenomenon and repair logic. He then asked actual clerks and line leaders to test each updated version for convenience. He aimed to let AI take over repetitive tasks to free energy for high-value work.

Front-line engineers in Wuhan and Changzhou, and across a national supplier network, use these tools. Line leaders previously complained about redundant actions, such as selecting the same product model ten times daily. Managers formerly had to scroll through dozens of chat records or nested folders to find data. Now, managers use mobile terminals to check real-time output and efficiency while patrolling lines. Bosch China engineers also use the system to reduce time spent moving information.

TSMC faced high costs when building a wafer fab in Phoenix, Arizona, on December 6, 2022. The US plant cost 4 to 5 times more than plants in Taiwan, China. Compliance with 18,000 rules cost 35 million US dollars, and gross profit margins were only 8 percent. TSMC sent 500 engineers from Taiwan and trained 600 Arizona hires in Taiwan, China. These challenges delayed the 4-nanometer production line originally scheduled for mass production in 2024.

The AI tool now runs dashboards on large screens at the head of each production line. It automatically sends messages to responsible persons to remind them of stand-up meeting problems. The articles do not state the specific future revenue targets for Doubao Work. They leave open how other manufacturing sectors will integrate these specific AI organizational processes. The text does not detail the final results of the Bosch China implementation.

stories.Headline: Google Cloud launches object enrichments to extract AI metadata from stored objects
stories.Summary:
Google Cloud introduced object enrichments, a new Cloud Storage capability, on November 19, 2026, according to a blog post by Himanshu Kohli, Product Manager. The service uses AI models to automatically extract rich contextual metadata from Cloud Storage objects and saves it in place as object context. It gives customers access to AI models used by internal Google services such as Google Photos, offering image annotations like object detection and image labeling. The capability is available in preview as a fully managed service that also includes a high-quality PDF classification model. The post says the vast majority of enterprise information is unstructured, locked away in object storage as petabytes of images, PDFs, videos, and audio files.

Object enrichments offers image annotations at 75% cost savings compared to similar services from other cloud providers, and enriching 10 million images or PDFs costs just $700 according to published pricing. The five first-party Cloud Storage models for images and PDFs include object detection, face detection, image labeling, and explicit content detection, and the PDF classification model categorizes documents into standard business and industry categories like Finance, Games, News, and Health. Setting up an enrichment job takes three steps with no code required in the Google Cloud console or programmatically via the Cloud Storage API: define your scope by providing buckets and a processing location, choose your models, and grant IAM permissions. Object enrichments can scale to millions or billions of objects, orchestrates model inference, parses responses, and writes results to each object's object context with built-in retries and throttling. Object context is a specialized Cloud Storage metadata construct storing contextual information as structured key-value pairs alongside the object, sharing the object's durability and consistency, traveling with it during copy, move, and replication, and being removed when the object is deleted.

Antoine Castex, Principal Data & AI Architect at L'Oreal, said L'Oreal is the 4th largest advertiser in the world and that managing media assets at that scale is complex. He said object enrichments' high quality and cost-effective annotations enable L'Oreal to discover, understand, and govern content at scale, accelerating marketing and advertising operations while remaining compliant in all markets. He said object enrichments enables L'Oreal to label its extensive creative asset repository 100x faster at a fraction of the cost of existing pipelines and processes. Mayur Pillay, VP Partnerships at Hyperscience, said that even with a highly accurate baseline, Hyperscience leveraged object enrichments to drive a 50%+ lift in document classification accuracy while simultaneously reducing classification inference costs by 2-3x. Brandon Bunker, VP of Product AI at Vivint, said Cloud Storage object enrichments and BigQuery slash AI development from 6 months to 1 month while rapidly improving Vivint's models.

The post says agents need grounded knowledge, but reading every raw file at scale is cost- and performance-prohibitive, citing an operations agent pinpointing a doorstep package delivery or a roadway hazard by streaming thousands of smart-camera or vehicle frames on every user prompt. It names three historical challenges: cost, since running models over millions to billions of objects pushes organizations to process only a fraction of their data, creating blind spots; operational toil, since a self-managed pipeline means stitching together event triggers, queues, and custom infrastructure on Cloud Run or Google Kubernetes Engine with retry and error logic and job scheduling, and teams sometimes spend months on this plumbing; and fragmented metadata, which lands in a separate data store, requiring a second storage system, access policies across disconnected permission models, and cleanup jobs. Object context can flow natively into BigQuery via Storage Insights datasets, allowing SQL analytics, dashboards, and joins with structured enterprise tables without ETL code. Early customers use object enrichments for creative asset search and media archives, automated trust, safety, and content moderation, training data curation for frontier AI, and multimodal analytics.

The post describes use cases including finding a specific asset such as a red car driving at sunset or a vintage convertible in the desert during golden hour, scanning millions of daily user uploads and supplier catalogs for explicit content, and enriching hundreds of millions of raw camera and sensor files so ML engineers can pinpoint exact training cohorts in minutes rather than months. It says multimodal analytics can combine image and document insights with structured business data for personalization, fraud detection, and trend discovery, for example analyzing customer uploaded images alongside comments and recent sales data. For complex multimodal reasoning across text, PDFs, images, audio, and video, customers can leverage Gemini natively with object enrichments for summarization, entity extraction, transcription, and translation. Object enrichments is available in preview today in the Cloud Storage console and through the Cloud Storage API. The post directs readers to documentation, Storage Insights datasets in BigQuery, the Cloud Storage MCP server for IAM-scoped agent access, Cloud Storage pricing, and the console to enrich a first bucket in three clicks.

The post says teams can reach out at storage-ai@google.com to learn more and request access to the upcoming Gemini enrichments functionality. It says object enrichments handles the rest after setup, with no queues to manage, workers to scale, or glue code to maintain. It says administrators can use IAM to control who can read, add, update, or remove object context, and applications can filter object listings directly by object context key-value pairs or read context metadata alongside objects. It says object context shares the same durability and consistency properties as the underlying Cloud Storage object, so no cleanup jobs are needed. The post leaves open when Gemini enrichments will become available and what request access will involve.

stories.Headline: Nvidia commits 118 billion dollars in guarantees to help customers build AI facilities
stories.Summary:
Nvidia reported high data center revenue and disclosed financial guarantees on November 18, 2026. The company is committing 390 billion dollars to its various suppliers. It is also helping its customers finance powered facilities for AI deployments. These guarantees help customers secure the land, power, and facilities needed. This news follows the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang on November 12.

The total maximum gross exposure for these guarantees is 118 billion dollars. This includes 105 billion dollars for the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Ohio. That campus provides 4.25 GW across nine buildings under 20-year leases to OpenAI. Other guarantees include 9.5 billion dollars for power and 3.5 billion dollars for neocloud providers. The first guarantee exposure is expected to begin in fiscal 2029.

Interim CEO Colette Kress is leading the company while the board seeks a successor. Chairman Harvey Jones said directors unanimously accepted the resignation of Jensen Huang. He stated that the board does not intend to reinstate the former chief executive. Huang said he would be honored to return if the board decided it was best. The board will now consider both internal and external candidates for the role.

Elon Musk, Tim Sweeney, and Donald Trump supported the return of Jensen Huang. A public petition for his return drew more than 180,000 signatures, including many employees. Data center operators are affected because powered shells have become a major bottleneck. Stephen Sopko said Nvidia is acting as a credit enhancer to get facilities built. He cautioned against treating the full guarantee figure as neocloud financing exposure.

Jensen Huang resigned after reports of affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese agent. Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of 115.8 billion dollars, with data center revenue at 107.6 billion. Supply commitments rose to 390 billion dollars due to multiyear memory procurement and substrate deals. The company has manufacturing relationships with IBIDEN, King Yuan Electronics, and Unimicron Technology. Vera Rubin systems are now running at Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, and Oracle Cloud.

Nvidia expects fourth-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue to be 130 billion dollars, plus or minus 3 percent. This forecast assumes that no data center compute revenue will come from China. The company expects fourth-quarter gross margins to be between 71 and 72 percent. It will remain selective with guarantees as other capital sources mature over time. The articles leave open who the board will choose as the permanent CEO.

stories.Headline: BMO demonstrates quantum utility in machine learning feature selection using IBM quantum computers
stories.Summary:
BMO announced on November 19, 2026 that it had demonstrated quantum utility in a machine learning application using IBM quantum computers, with the work performed reliably at a scale beyond what exact traditional computing methods can practically reproduce. The announcement was made from Toronto, Chicago and San Francisco. The application was developed in collaboration with the Democritus University of Thrace (DUTH) and used IBM quantum computers, including the latest IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 processor. IBM's quantum research team reviewed the achievement. The work explores how quantum computing could help AI models identify which information matters most in complex datasets.

The application reimagines machine learning feature selection by adapting the Proxy Quantum Games framework, shifting it from a traditional classical statistical problem into a dynamic, quantum strategic game. Each feature of the dataset is a player, and a feature scores high when it moves together with the application's target, the model outcome variable, and low when it is uninformative or repeats other, unimportant features. The scores rank the features. The quantum game-based feature selection processes all of this on a quantum computer. The resulting method produces results with similar quality while only requiring one to two orders of magnitude fewer samples than traditional feature selection techniques.

Kristin Milchanowski, Chief AI and Quantum Officer and Director of the BMO Institute for Applied Artificial Intelligence & Quantum, said demonstrating quantum utility is an important milestone for BMO and an exciting step forward for the broader financial services industry. She said that while they remain in the early stages of application development, these projects show how quantum computing can help solve business problems in new ways. She said the work builds on years of research, collaboration and innovation focused on identifying practical applications that create value for clients, employees and shareholders. Scott Crowder, Vice President of IBM Quantum Adoption and Business Development, said he was excited to see BMO's progress toward real-world quantum use cases in the financial services industry using IBM's quantum computers to explore novel algorithmic approaches. Steve Tennyson, Chief Technology and Operations Officer at BMO, said innovation at BMO is about translating emerging technologies into meaningful business impact.

Tennyson said the milestone reflects years of investment in innovation, quantum computing, artificial intelligence and strategic partnerships, and demonstrates how BMO is turning emerging technologies into practical solutions that help clients improve decision-making and support long-term growth. The achievement positions BMO among a small group of global financial institutions exploring real-world quantum applications in the near term. Potential banking applications include more accurate client modeling, improved risk assessment and detection, and more personalized client experiences. BMO ranked ninth among financial institutions globally in the 2026 Quantum Index Finance ranking, an independent benchmark of enterprise quantum readiness, and is the highest-ranking Canadian commercial bank in the index, which measures institutions in the areas of quantum workforce, research and development, and adoption. BMO was recently recognized by Evident AI as one of the world's top 20 banks in AI and ranked #2 among 50 banks for AI use-case outcomes, the highest-ranking Canadian bank in the category, and achieved the top ranking in the Responsible AI Process indicator group.

BMO joined the IBM Quantum Network in February 2025 and continues to invest in quantum research, talent development and real-world applications. Through partnerships with the Chicago Quantum Exchange and Quantum Industry Canada, BMO is advancing practical applications of quantum computing across financial services. stories.Headline: Google reports threat groups use AI agent frameworks to automate attacks at machine speed
stories.Summary:
Google Threat Intelligence Group reported on November 17, 2026 that threat actors are using agentic workflows powered by AI-based offensive frameworks to automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation, which accelerates attacks to machine speed. The group said AI, first used experimentally, now sees large-scale adoption by both financially motivated and state-sponsored threat groups. GTIG highlighted the use of CAIRN, an open-source multi-agent penetration-testing framework, in an attack against the U.S. aerospace sector. Suspected North Korean hackers have also used Claude Code to deliver malware, according to the report.

Researchers estimate that unsophisticated, fully autonomous attacks requiring little human interaction will emerge within the next three months, and sophisticated fully autonomous agentic attacks are likely within six months. The FBI warned last week that multiple threat actors have weaponized the ARTEX AI pentesting framework since August, targeting financial, government, technology, defense and healthcare organizations. Google said attackers systematically abuse open-source pentesting suites including ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI and HexStrike AI, which facilitate adaptive attacks against internet-exposed endpoints vulnerable to low-complexity flaws. GTIG's AI Threat Tracker report cited a multi-agent system called exploit_agent that fully automated vulnerability finding and exploitation against French media, entertainment and education websites.

GTIG identified an exposed staging server hosting the exploit_agent framework, which integrates with multiple frontier and local LLMs, analyzes software updates on popular web apps to find flaws and automatically attempts to exploit them. Google said deploying such frameworks dramatically decreases the time defenders have to patch systems and also produces false leads, as seen with PHP2Shell, where hundreds of purported AI-generated proof-of-concept exploits appeared quickly. Google also observed UNC6836 using modified Claude Code to deliver the SOMBERMEME backdoor against cryptocurrency firms. AI is also routinely used in influence operations by state-backed groups, commercial vendors and political networks, and LLMjacking has become widespread, with attackers exploiting this new revenue stream at significant cost to affected organizations.

stories.Headline: HPE and AMD debut Lux AI cluster at No 14 on TOP500 with 220.79 petaflops
stories.Summary:
At SC26 in Chicago, HPE announced that Lux, an AI cluster built with AMD for Oak Ridge National Laboratory, debuted at No. 14 on the TOP500 with 220.79 petaflops of measured HPL performance. HPE said the system, purpose-built for AI training and inference, placed ahead of machines designed for traditional supercomputing workloads. Lux is the first dedicated AI system to come online for the U.S. Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission. HPE and AMD co-designed and co-constructed the cluster, which gives researchers across the U.S. multi-tenant, cloud-like access. The debut was announced on November 16, 2026, according to the articles.

Lux runs on direct liquid-cooled HPE ProLiant Compute XD685 systems with AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, AMD EPYC CPUs, and AMD Pensando DPUs. The network uses HPE Juniper Networking QFX switches running 800G Ethernet, with load balancing and congestion management that HPE says reduce bottlenecks and improve GPU utilization. HPE Networking Data Center Director handles intent-based deployment, management, and lifecycle automation. Half of Lux’s 3.5 million annual node-hours are dedicated to the Genesis Mission, and the other half are available for proprietary use, a total equivalent to about 400 nodes running around the clock for a year. HPE has made a $37 million in-kind investment in the program to support research projects.

Trish Damkroger, senior vice president and general manager of HPC and AI Infrastructure Solutions at HPE, said the company, with ORNL and AMD, had delivered breakthrough engineering innovation and was furthering what it can accomplish as a proven public-private partnership. She said HPE was proud of its continued collaboration and investment in the Genesis Mission to stand up one of its first AI systems. Georgia Tourassi, associate director of computing and computational sciences at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, said she was excited for the debut and the opportunities it creates to expand access to advanced computing resources. She said Lux will give researchers additional capacity and flexibility to advance innovative SI approaches in Earth system prediction, materials development, biology, and fusion energy. Thomas Zacharia, senior vice president of global public sector and strategic partnerships at AMD, said Lux shows what is possible when national laboratories, government and industry work together.

AMD said the cluster runs its ROCm software stack, and neither company has published a node or GPU count for the system. AMD said Lux is now open to scientific users. HPE describes Lux as the first deployment of HPE Networking products at a DOE national laboratory, bringing scalable, high-performance, open Ethernet to AI-driven science. The Genesis Mission is a DOE program that applies AI to energy research, scientific discovery, and national security on a platform combining AI, supercomputing, quantum systems, and scientific instruments. Zacharia tied Lux to an open, sovereign AI stack with tools that researchers across the country can use.

HPE announced Lux about a year ago as part of its broader collaboration with ORNL and AMD. The partnership also includes Discovery, a forthcoming next-generation supercomputer developed as the successor to Frontier, which first broke the exascale speed barrier. ORNL has said Discovery will pair AMD EPYC Venice CPUs with AMD Instinct MI430X GPUs on an HPE Cray Supercomputing platform, with delivery expected in 2028. Lux carries the integrated management and Silicon Root of Trust protection found across HPE ProLiant servers. The configuration equips Lux with the performance necessary for large model AI training and deep learning.

The articles do not say when Lux began operating beyond its debut at SC26. They leave open how many nodes or GPUs the system contains. They do not state which proprietary users will take the half of node-hours not dedicated to the Genesis Mission. They do not give a date for Discovery’s delivery beyond 2028. They do not say what the $37 million in-kind investment will fund specifically.

stories.Headline: Homeland Security Task Force launches Threat Disruption Center using TRM Labs AI under $95M no-bid deal
stories.Summary:
The Homeland Security Task Force launched the Threat Disruption Center to fight crypto fraud and cybercrime, Techmeme reported on November 18, 2026. The center uses TRM Labs' AI platform under a no-bid deal worth about $95 million, according to Bloomberg. Techmeme posted the item at 10:15 PM on November 18, 2026. The launch was reported alongside Anthropic's IPO pricing at $83 per share. Anthropic priced its upsized IPO above the $70 to $78 marketed range, raising $81.3 billion in the largest offering on record, topping SpaceX.

Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share on Wednesday, above the expected range, setting the stage for its Nasdaq listing under the ticker ANT. The filed range was $70 to $78, and Amendment No. 3, filed the day before, never raised it. The company sold 980 million shares, not the filed 825 million, for $81.3 billion gross, $79.4 billion to the company and $1.96 billion to selling holders, before the greenshoe. Anthropic raised about $3 billion from Japanese investors as part of the IPO, the lower end of its planned $3 billion to $3.5 billion range, according to a regulatory filing on Thursday. Anthropic now has $110 billion in cash alone, and its backers including Sequoia Capital, Lightspeed Venture Partners and Iconiq plan to buy billions of dollars' worth of shares.

Jason Matheny, founding director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology, said the AI community needs to put much more effort and money into systems protection to avoid costs of billions more later. Matheny said AI systems are not being developed with a healthy focus on evolving threats, despite increased funding by the Pentagon and the private sector. He said a lot of the techniques used today were built without intelligent adversaries in mind and were sort of innocent. Matheny leads the center, housed at Georgetown University's Walsh School of Foreign Service to provide policy and intelligence analysis to the government. He was previously assistant director of national intelligence and before that director of IARPA, and he currently sits on the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence.

Matheny spoke on September 4 during a panel at the 2019 Intelligence and National Security Summit. Masayoshi Son said passing on a 2023 opportunity to invest in Anthropic was a mistake, noting that by that point the firm had already decided to invest in OpenAI. SoftBank's founder sank $65 billion into OpenAI, and Anthropic lists this week at up to $1.4 trillion while OpenAI has pushed its IPO back and cut its raise by $10 billion. Rep. Jake Auchincloss said Anthropic should distribute $250 billion of its IPO shares into Invest America accounts, the universal capital accounts that exist for every American under 18 with a Social Security number. He said that if the $250 billion of shares went to 60 million American children, excluding the roughly 10 million with most wealth, that is ballpark $4,000 in equity each.

Anthropic's IPO attracted nearly $500 billion in investor orders, per CNBC, with institutional demand reaching about $400 billion while retail orders approached $100 billion. The company was considering expanding its IPO and pricing shares above $80, above the initial range of $70 to $78 per share, and also considering raising more than the initially planned $64.4 billion. Anthropic was expected to raise at least $68 billion through the IPO plus another $26 billion in a private placement, bringing the total offering to more than $94 billion and surpassing SpaceX's record $86.2 billion IPO in June. Amazon's $18 billion Anthropic bet is worth $159 billion at the IPO price. Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share, above its $70 to $78 range, putting the IPO volume $16.99 billion, or 26.4%, above the top end of the original range.

Trading was expected to begin on Nasdaq tomorrow under the ticker ANT, Anthropic said. Bloomberg reported Anthropic was said to be weighing an IPO price as high as $85 per share. Tim Carmody wrote that it is better for Anthropic and its investors to get the real IPO price than for people who buy it and flip it when it pops, and that if the stock fizzles at $80+, it is better for them to realize that loss too. Jeremiah Dillon wrote that nobody knows anything, asking whether Anthropic's token share is closer to 5% or 50%, and that on Ramp it tripled while on OpenRouter it fell 50% to 7%. The articles leave open how the Threat Disruption Center's no-bid deal proceeds and how Anthropic's shares trade after the Nasdaq debut.

stories.Summary:
U.S. banks halted loans for Asian AI data centers in November 2026. This action followed new rules from the U.S. Commerce Department. The administration moved to tighten rules after allegations that Nvidia chips were rerouted to China. Lenders withdrew from deals to avoid risks of violating these new government regulations. The suspension showed that Asia's financial industry was unprepared for this abrupt action.

The rules require licenses for chip shipments to Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand. They also restrict remote access to AI chips from Southeast Asia and other countries. Aolani Cloud, a Singapore partner of Nvidia, was denied a 480 million dollar loan. This loan would have funded graphics processing units for a data center in Malaysia. The hardware was intended for use by the Chinese technology company ByteDance.

The Commerce Department said it investigated Megaspeed's chip procurement since 2024. They coordinated with Singapore authorities to block Chinese companies from reaching technology remotely. Aolani Cloud stated it worked with regulators to ensure compliance without project disruption. The company spent considerable time with financing partners to anticipate regulatory risks. These efforts to secure the loan for the Malaysia project were unsuccessful.

Aolani Cloud and other data center operators are affected by these licensing requirements. Michelle Condie of the Center for Advanced Defense Studies said circumvention became easier. She noted that this allowed China to get around export controls regardless of legality. Lenders are now assessing billions of dollars in AI borrowings that are in progress. Some banks are also reviewing deals that were already closed.

The rules follow a scandal involving Alice Huang, the leader of Singapore company Megaspeed. Huang allegedly moved 7.5 billion dollars of Nvidia chips through Chinese companies since 2023. Last year, JPMorgan, Citigroup, Deutsche Bank, Mitsubishi UFJ, and Sumitomo Mitsui lent to Bridge Data Centres. Bridge Data Centres, backed by Bain Capital, sought 2.8 billion dollars for Thailand and Malaysia. Megaspeed was the counterparty for those loans, while ByteDance was the main tenant.

Bridge Data Centres replaced Megaspeed with Los Angeles based Zenlayer this year. A new loan from existing lenders was finalized in May. Malaysia is checking if Speedmatrix, a 2024 Megaspeed unit, re-exported chips to third countries. The articles leave open whether the banks that lent early last year did anything wrong.
