stories.Headline: TARSBOT and Aptiv partner to develop and scale industrial embodied AI robots for smart manufacturing
stories.Summary:
TARSBOT and Aptiv signed an agreement to deepen their strategic collaboration on embodied AI. This event took place on November 16, 2026, in the city of Shanghai. The signing occurred during the 9th China International Import Expo, which is known as the CIIE. Both companies agreed to work together to advance industrial robotic systems. This partnership focuses on the development and deployment of embodied AI technology.

Aptiv expects to deploy 100 TARSBOT A-Series industrial robots by the end of 2026. These robots cover 33 application scenarios and 8 manufacturing process categories, including flexible assembly. The parties plan to achieve mass production in 2026 using high-performance computing platforms. A larger fleet of 1,000 units is targeted with support from the Jiading District Government. The first batch of robots is already operating at an Aptiv smart factory.

The two companies are responsible for validating applications within real industrial environments. They stated that production insights will support the iterative development of the AI World Engine. This AWE system serves as the general-purpose foundation model for TARSBOT embodied AI. The partners aim to combine end-to-end AI capabilities with established engineering expertise. They believe this combination will support efficient and reliable deployment at a large scale.

Manufacturers worldwide are affected by a growing demand for intelligent automation and supply-chain efficiency. These companies see embodied AI as an important force for advancing next-generation productivity. The collaboration aims to demonstrate that scalable deployment can be validated in practical settings. Aptiv provides the intelligent power distribution solutions and computing platforms for the robots. These platforms support core functions like motion control, perception, and decision-making.

The companies have already been working closely to develop China's first industrial embodied AI robot fleet. The first phase of this project is currently being implemented at an Aptiv production site. This initial work focused on adapting robots to manufacturing requirements and real production processes. The signing at the CIIE marks a more systematic and scaled phase of their cooperation. This background establishes the foundation for their expanded strategic agreement in Shanghai.

TARSBOT and Aptiv will now use China's manufacturing environments to connect robotic systems with applications. They intend to provide a scalable industrial reference for expanding AI across additional scenarios. This effort aims to create broader opportunities for smart manufacturing on a worldwide scale. The articles leave open the specific timeline for the 1,000 unit fleet deployment. They also do not specify the exact date for the start of mass production.

stories.Headline: Asean members sign grid pact to share clean power and back regional AI growth
stories.Summary:
All eleven Asean member states signed an enhanced memorandum of understanding in Manila earlier this week. This pact entered into force on Sunday, November 15, 2026. The agreement establishes an integrated regional electricity network called the Asean Power Grid. This network aims to share clean power across borders in South-east Asia. The deal coincides with the COP31 conference taking place in Turkey.

The pact anchors cross-border interconnections, multilateral power trade, and financing for subsea cables and overland lines. Asean estimates it needs 764 billion US dollars for generation and transmission investment through 2045. The APG Financing Initiative involves the Asean bloc, the World Bank Group, and the Asian Development Bank. The Philippines, which just ended its 2026 Asean chairmanship, faces bottlenecks in its Mindanao, Visayas, and Luzon grids. These regional links provide a buffer when domestic generation is tight.

Energy Secretary Sharon Garin said the memorandum brings commitment to resilience, innovation, and partnership into practical focus. She stressed the importance of attracting multilateral and private capital for these projects. Robert Cooke of the Global Renewables Alliance said policymakers can use data centres as a force for renewables. He stated that hyperscalers have a commercial stake in funding grid upgrades to secure green electricity. These upgrades also shield server farms from extreme weather.

Rexor Amancio of the Global Renewables Alliance warned that data centres might displace green power from other users. He said this could drive up fossil gas and increase power prices for everyone. Over nine in ten Philippine business leaders say their country relies too much on fossil-fuel imports. This is the highest share among 18 economies surveyed by E3G, the Global Renewables Alliance, and the We Mean Business Coalition. Data centre operators are the primary group affected by these constraints.

South-east Asia wants to be an artificial intelligence hub, but grids rely on imported gas and coal. Global data centre electricity consumption rose 17 per cent in 2025, while AI-focused demand surged 50 per cent. Data centres accounted for roughly 40 per cent of global corporate renewable power-purchase agreements last year. The Philippines has a liberalised wholesale market, retail competition, and a green energy option programme. However, developers still face wheeling charges, permitting delays, and congested transmission lines.

The region must now turn digital infrastructure growth into investments for transmission, storage, and renewable generation. Regulators are under pressure to close accounting loopholes regarding 100 per cent renewable status claims. The International Renewable Energy Agency has a COP31 green data centre programme to prove electricity is locally sourced. Some builders are already installing onsite gas turbines to avoid multi-year connection queues. The articles leave open whether the sector will accelerate the green transition or lock in fossil-fuel demand.

stories.Headline: Chinese AI stocks fall as US administration plans to block data center equipment imports
stories.Summary:
Investors sold off Chinese artificial intelligence hardware exporters and hyperscalers on November 18, 2026, as signs of tougher United States technology curbs emerged. This market decline occurred ahead of a scheduled meeting between Chinese leader Xi Jinping and United States President Donald Trump. The downturn followed the removal of Jensen Huang as chief executive officer of Nvidia after Republicans lost the United States midterm election. These events pushed China's stock benchmark toward its lowest levels since mid-2025.

The Trump administration intends to block imports of Chinese data center equipment despite opposition from American technology firms. The Federal Communications Commission previously sought to ban new models of Chinese optical transceivers due to national security concerns. Nvidia now assumes it will have no data center chip sales to China, while Senator Tammy Baldwin introduced legislation to revoke the normal trade status of China. Consequently, the CSI300 and Shanghai Composite Index both fell roughly 0.4 per cent, and the Hang Seng Tech index dropped 1.5 per cent.

Louis-Vincent Gave of Gavekal Research stated that the downfall of Jensen Huang could have consequences extending far beyond the artificial intelligence sector. He noted that tighter financing might threaten the investment boom while political tensions reshape the relations between the two nations. Other affected companies included Alibaba, Tencent, and MiniMax, as well as optical parts makers Zhongji Innolight and Eoptolink. The latter two firms have seen their values drop more than 70 per cent from their peak levels.

President Trump met with leaders from Australia, Japan, and India in the Philippines on Tuesday before a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen. The Quad expressed grave concerns regarding economic coercion, although the group did not explicitly name China in its statement. While most tech stocks fell, the Star Chip Index rose 0.5 per cent on expectations that domestic chipmakers would benefit from restrictions. Gold stocks also tumbled nearly 5 per cent because of expectations that the United States would raise interest rates.

The raise comes a few months after OpenAI agents breached Hugging Face, according to the article. The round drew backing from people described as insiders at OpenAI and Meta, among other investors named in the piece. The story was reported exclusively by Sifted, which covers UK tech and European startups.

The funding is aimed at policing rogue AI agents, the governance problem the startup was built to address. The article ties the timing of the raise to the earlier breach involving OpenAI agents at Hugging Face. It names Gresham House Ventures as the lead investor in the $8m round. The piece describes Disseqt as building governance structures for AI agents rather than models themselves. The report does not give a valuation for the company.

The article paraphrases investors and others discussing why agent oversight matters, including the view that companies deploying agents need controls in place before incidents occur. It also refers to the Hugging Face breach as the kind of event that has pushed the issue up the agenda for AI labs and their partners. The named backers are presented as people with ties to OpenAI and Meta, alongside the lead investor. The article does not attribute a direct quote to any single named individual beyond short phrases.

The context given is the rapid spread of AI agents inside companies and the gap in rules for what those agents are allowed to do. The article says the raise follows the Hugging Face incident by a few months and frames Disseqt as one of the startups trying to fill that gap. It does not say what the new money will be spent on beyond the governance work, and it gives no timeline for a product or next funding step. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Nadia Shaw urges businesses to keep offline backups and manual procedures for AI outages
stories.Summary:
Nadia Shaw wrote an opinion piece on November 19, 2026, regarding the risks of relying solely on artificial intelligence. She argues that while these smart systems offer efficiency, they also create new vulnerabilities for both individuals and businesses. The author suggests that maintaining physical backups, such as paper notebooks, is a prudent strategy for the modern age. This approach ensures that essential tasks can continue even when digital services or networks fail completely.

The author explains that cybersecurity experts now warn that AI helps attackers find and exploit weaknesses at a greater scale. For businesses, this requires implementing security layers that restrict data access and limit what automated agents can do. Companies should require human approval for consequential transactions and ensure a specific person can revoke access immediately. Additionally, households are encouraged to keep small amounts of cash and physical copies of essential documents.

Nadia Shaw highlights the concept of cognitive debt, a term used by computer scientist Margaret-Anne Storey to describe a loss of shared understanding. This happens when teams move so quickly with AI that they can no longer explain how their systems work. Shaw suggests that the pressure to review AI work at high speeds leads to stress and fatigue for employees. She believes that people must continue practicing the skills needed to challenge and verify automated tools.

The article concludes that while digital payments and AI are useful, they cannot replace resilience during a total system failure. Businesses are advised to maintain tested offline backups and manual procedures that do not require an email login. The author emphasizes that a recovery plan is useless if it is trapped behind a failed digital account. Ultimately, the goal is to ensure that basic operations remain possible if the computer screens go dark.

These business leaders urged the governing body to significantly increase its financial investment in artificial intelligence and to remove various regulatory hurdles. They warned that the continent is currently at risk of falling further behind the technological progress made by China and the United States. The letter was signed by dozens of science and tech leaders who believe the region must act quickly to remain competitive.

The proposal requires the European Union to implement sweeping regulatory reforms and provide more funding for homegrown AI development. The authors specifically mentioned the need to address the 2024 AI Act, which they believe creates too many barriers for smaller companies. They argue that the current rules make it difficult for startups to compete with the massive resources of American giants like Microsoft and Google. The letter suggests that the EU should focus on creating a more supportive environment for innovation rather than focusing solely on restriction.

The CEOs of the three mentioned companies are responsible for the call to action and expressed deep concern over the current state of the industry. They stated that while the European Union has a strong foundation, it lacks a cohesive strategy to help its own companies grow. The leaders argued that the region cannot afford to be a mere consumer of foreign technology while its own innovators struggle. They believe that without immediate changes to policy and funding, Europe will lose its ability to influence the future of the field.

The context of this request involves a growing gap between European AI capabilities and those of the global leaders in the sector. The authors of the letter noted that the current regulatory environment often prioritizes safety and ethics over the speed of development. They believe that a more balanced approach would allow European firms to scale their operations more effectively. stories.Headline: SID AI releases SID-2 agentic search model and SID-2 Swarm multi-agent version
stories.Summary:
SID AI released SID-2, its second-generation agentic search model, on November 18, 2026, alongside a multi-agent version called SID-2 Swarm, according to MarkTechPost. SID-2 is a small search specialist rather than a general chat model, and it searches a user's data, reads the results, adapts and searches again instead of running a fixed rewrite, embed, search and rerank pipeline. Developers implement two search tools against their own backend, one for keyword search and one for vector search, and the model ends each episode by calling report_helpful_ids with a ranked list. No reindexing or data movement is required, because SID-2 only sees what the tools return. The context window is 262k tokens per the report and 256k on the sid.ai models page, and the model runs on a hosted API at platform.sid.ai plus Baseten and SageMaker reference paths.

SID-2 offers low, medium and high reasoning effort, each trained as a separate expert and then merged with multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and Metric Steering lets users target NDCG, F1 or Recall@k with k from 1 to 50. Training used two-stage reinforcement learning, where stage one optimizes retrieval quality only and stage two adds a multiplicative latency penalty that applies only to positive rewards, and a proposer-solver self-play loop generated hard queries against a frozen SID-1 solver. SID reports a 6x training-throughput gain over SLIME's default setup. On SID's 506-question validation set, SID-2 at high effort scores 0.14 to 0.22 higher per metric than the base model. All benchmark numbers are self-reported from Tables 2 to 4 of the report, measured on a 506-question benchmark across 19 corpora including HotpotQA, Enron emails, SEC filings, PubMed and BrowseComp-Plus.

SID-2 Medium scores 0.585 NDCG in 3.11 seconds, versus Claude Opus 5.5 at medium effort with 0.577 in 25.1 seconds, and SID-2 Swarm with 6 agents scores 0.701 NDCG in 17.7 seconds against GPT-6 Astra at max effort with 0.704 in 135 seconds. SID-2 Swarm with 12 agents scores 0.720 NDCG, the highest in the table, while SID-2 Low scores 0.556, which is 0.148 below GPT-6 Astra. BM25 scores 0.260 and vector search plus a reranker scores 0.287. Swarm leads on 11 of 19 corpora, and on WixQA a single high-effort agent matches Astra at about 232x lower cost, while at its lowest effort SID-2 beats 4 parallel SID-1 runs with 13x fewer FLOPs.

Astra still leads on California law, SEC filings and FiQA, and SID's latency figures assume 1 B200 GPU at 8 concurrent queries. SID argues that search gains more from reading more documents than from reasoning harder about each one, and in Swarm several agents message each other and fork their context into new agents so each explores a separate slice of the corpus. SID-2 is available through SID's API and on Baseten, with SDKs including a Python package called sid-sdk. The article notes that no model size, weights or independent evaluations have been disclosed yet.

stories.Headline: Chinese cement producers adopt AI and digital sensors to create smart green factories
stories.Summary:
Chinese cement producers are integrating artificial intelligence and digital sensors to transform energy intensive plants into smart, green factories as of November 18, 2026. Major companies like Anhui Conch Group Co., Ltd. in Wuhu, Anhui Province, are deploying driverless trucks and remotely operated excavators to automate the challenging raw material extraction process. These upgrades include the use of radar sensors that allow unmanned vehicles to navigate quarry roads safely even during periods of low visibility. The shift is part of a broader national effort to embed low carbon technologies and intelligent systems into traditional manufacturing sectors.

The transition requires the implementation of complex AI models, such as the one developed by Anhui Conch Group Co., Ltd. and Huawei, which utilizes computer vision and predictive analytics. This specific model identifies over 200 AI scenarios across 15 categories and has already deployed more than 40 applications for quality control and production optimization. One key tool is a clinker strength prediction model that allows operators to adjust kiln parameters in real time before laboratory results are finished. Additionally, a carbon capture project in Wuhu processes 50,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide annually to create industrial products and boost greenhouse tomato yields.

Company officials and industry experts are leading these changes, with Xu Yue of Conch Cement noting that AI allows for immediate adjustments to production parameters. Huang Yong of the same group explained that unmanned trucks now coordinate with excavators to improve the efficiency of hauling raw materials. Kong Xiangzhong, the former executive president of the China Cement Association, stated that nearly 70 companies have become smart manufacturing demonstration factories since 2021. Peng Shou from the Chinese Academy of Engineering added that market forces and policy are pushing the sector toward circular resource use and lower emissions.

This industry shift aligns with a wider government drive where the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology reports that over 30 percent of large manufacturing firms adopted AI by the first half of the year. Other leaders in the field include CR Cement, whose Tianyang plant in Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region became the first lighthouse factory in the sector. Meanwhile, BBMG Jidong Cement Group Co., Ltd. has established a zero employee production line at its Tongchuan plant with a daily capacity of 10,000 tonnes. These developments signal a strategic transition toward higher end products and a significant reduction in standard coal consumption.

stories.Headline: European Central Bank warns that AI valuations and sovereign debt threaten euro area financial stability
stories.Summary:
The European Central Bank published a Financial Stability Review on Wednesday, November 18, which highlighted several looming threats to the financial stability of the euro area. This comprehensive report warns that artificial intelligence valuations, sovereign debt levels, and geopolitical tensions are creating significant vulnerabilities across the region. The bank specifically noted that the non-bank financial sector is particularly exposed to these emerging risks in certain segments. These combined pressures could potentially test the overall resilience of an economy that grew by 0.4 percent during the third quarter of this year. The report explains that investors face direct exposure to AI valuation risks through euro-denominated debt issuances intended to fund expensive AI infrastructure.

High earnings expectations and extreme market concentration in United States technology firms increase the likelihood of an abrupt market repricing. Simultaneously, sovereign yields for longer-term maturities have climbed to their highest levels in twenty years and are expected to rise further. This environment of rising interest rates and inflation means that both banks and non-banks holding sovereign debt may suffer significant valuation losses. The European Central Bank stated that rising exposures to sovereign debt and artificial intelligence warrant close attention from financial regulators.

Officials warned that a sudden shift in the narrative surrounding AI could trigger market instability within a highly uncertain geopolitical environment. They also noted that the ongoing war in the Middle East could deteriorate macro-financial conditions and increase credit risks for various financial institutions. These authorities believe that the combination of prolonged headwinds and high valuations creates a precarious situation for the euro area. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Hugging Face releases a LoRA adapter that boosts Qwen3.8 coding success rates on SWE-bench Pro to 64.7%
stories.Summary:
The harness-hub team from Hugging Face released the Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted LoRA adapter on November 18, 2026. This specific adapter was trained using reinforcement learning to function within the pi coding agent toolkit. It allows developers to maintain an open base model while swapping in a small, harness-specific adapter for local coding agents. The team used two NVIDIA B200 GPUs for training, stopping at step 191 of a planned 1,000.

The adapter requires the Qwen3.8-27B base model, which is a dense hybrid with 262,144 native context. It features a LoRA rank of 32 and an alpha of 64, with a merged BF16 checkpoint weighing about 54 GB. This tool can run on vLLM with LoRA enabled or llama.cpp using a GGUF adapter on a Q8_0 base. It is released under the Apache-2.0 license and applies to several projections, including the q, k, v, o, gate, up, and down projections.

The developers reported that the adapter significantly improves coding success on specific benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro, the success rate rose from 39.2% to 64.7%, while Terminal-Bench 2.1 scores increased from 39.5% to 55.8%. They noted that the adapter achieves accuracy levels similar to the base model's thinking mode but uses about 4.5 times fewer tokens. Median turns on SWE-bench Pro dropped from 59 to 23, and Terminal-Bench 2.1 turns fell from 18 to 8.

The training process utilized the AsyncGRPO algorithm from TRL with eight rollouts per task at a temperature of 0.8. It involved 750 scale800 tasks and 300 TermGrade tasks, with rewards based on correctness and tool efficiency. To prevent reward hacking, the team used safeagents, a rule-based proxy that blocks calls to fetch benchmark answers. The adapter matches the base model's thinking-level accuracy without requiring long reasoning traces.

Articles.Title: New LoRA Adapter Lifts Qwen3.8 Coding Success From 39% to 65%

stories.Headline: China Securities Regulatory Commission denies requiring mutual funds to report AI exposure
stories.Summary:
The China Securities Regulatory Commission issued a formal denial on Wednesday regarding reports about new reporting rules. Online claims suggested that the agency had forced mutual fund companies to disclose their artificial intelligence exposure across all products. The regulator clarified that these specific rumors circulating on the internet were entirely untrue and lacked any factual basis. This official statement was published on the agency's official WeChat account to correct the misinformation.

The regulator emphasized that it has not required fund managers to submit any data regarding their AI investments. According to the agency, mutual fund managers are responsible for independently determining their own investment targets and portfolio weightings. These decisions must be made in accordance with their specific fund contracts and internal investment decision-making procedures. No new mandates have been implemented that would change how these companies report their holdings to the government.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission stated that the claims regarding mandatory AI exposure reporting were false. Separately, the China Association for Public Companies used its rumor-debunking platform to address another set of false claims. This platform noted that reports of a State Council executive meeting suggesting a lack of stock market support were fabricated. The association warned that such distorted information disrupts capital market expectations and has an extremely detrimental impact on investors.

The association urged internet users and investors to rationally assess information they find online and refrain from spreading rumors. They claimed that the false reports involved fabricated meeting content and a serious distortion of current government policies. The regulator continues to maintain that fund managers retain their autonomy over the assets they choose to hold. No further actions or policy changes were mentioned regarding the oversight of artificial intelligence investments in mutual funds.

Articles.Title: CSRC denies requiring funds to report AI exposure - China Daily Global Edition

stories.Headline: UNESCO, the EU and Jordan host a Paris event on AI and human rights for Human Rights Day 2026
stories.Summary:
UNESCO, the European Union, and the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan will host a high-level event on Wednesday, 25 November 2026. This gathering will take place from 3:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. in Room II at the UNESCO Headquarters in Paris. The organizers intend to mark Human Rights Day 2026 by examining how artificial intelligence affects human rights, inclusion, and information integrity.

This specific occasion occurs as the international community nears the 80th anniversary of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The program requires the screening of an AI-produced film called The Beginning by Jordanian filmmaker Ibraheem Diab. This movie uses the story of a child fleeing conflict to address themes like modern slavery, poverty, and children's rights. The event will also feature the publication titled Human Rights: Challenging 13 Common Misconceptions, which was created by UNESCO and the French National Consultative Commission on Human Rights. Furthermore, the session will highlight the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence as the first global standard-setting instrument.

Representatives from UNESCO, the OECD, and various Member States will lead a panel discussion alongside leading experts. These officials stated that while artificial intelligence offers opportunities for sustainable development, it also raises critical questions about equality and freedom of expression. They believe the technology must be designed and deployed in ways that remain ethical, human-centred, and based on fundamental rights. The speakers aim to show how AI can be used as a creative tool to promote peaceful societies and cultural diversity.

The broader context involves the rapid transformation of how people communicate, learn, and participate in public life through digital tools. Participants will explore the implications of these technologies for social cohesion and peacebuilding in an increasingly digital world. The event serves as a platform for dialogue on protecting human dignity against the challenges presented by artificial intelligence. Future efforts will focus on ensuring that innovation benefits all people while safeguarding the universal principles of freedom and equality.

stories.Headline: COP31 climate case studies feature AI-powered waste-to-energy project in Wuhan
stories.Summary:
A waste-to-energy project located in Wuhan, Hubei province, was featured in a collection of climate action case studies on November 9. This announcement occurred during the COP31 UN climate talks which were held in Antalya, Turkiye. The project was included in a bilingual publication that highlights various efforts to combat climate change. This specific collection was released to the public during a news conference on the opening day of the summit. The publication presents thirty different examples of climate action taken by Chinese companies and various industrial parks.

It was compiled by the publicity and education center of the Ministry of Ecology and Environment along with several partner organizations. The materials are designed to share practical and replicable approaches to achieving low-carbon development across different regions. These case studies aim to promote international exchanges regarding the most effective methods for climate action. Event organizers stated that the primary goal of the publication is to provide a roadmap for sustainable growth.

They believe that sharing these specific industrial examples will help other nations implement similar green technologies. The organizers emphasized the importance of cooperation and the exchange of knowledge to meet global environmental targets. By showcasing the Wuhan project, they hope to demonstrate the viability of AI-powered energy solutions. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Wuhan's AI-powered waste-to-energy project featured at COP31 - China Daily

stories.Headline: China's LineShine supercomputer remains the fastest system in the world
stories.Summary:
China's LineShine supercomputer maintained its position as the fastest system in the world during rankings released in Chicago on Monday. The machine, which is located at the National Supercomputing Center in Shenzhen, first claimed this top spot in June. It outperformed the American El Capitan system in both the TOP500 rankings and the High Performance Conjugate Gradients Benchmark. This achievement demonstrates the resilience of Chinese technological innovation despite various restrictions imposed by developed economies.

The system reached a sustained performance of 2.198 exaflops on the High Performance Linpack benchmark, placing it roughly 21 percent ahead of El Capitan. LineShine also led the HPCG Benchmark tests with 22 petaflops, while the American system reached 17.41 petaflops. It is the first supercomputer in TOP500 history to exceed 2 exaflops of sustained double-precision performance using only domestic central processing units. Meanwhile, the US Commerce Department issued an interim final rule requiring export licenses for advanced chips sent to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun stated that the United States is overstretching the concept of national security to target the high-tech industry of China. He argued that Washington views artificial intelligence competition as a zero-sum game and abuses export controls to interfere with normal trade. The Chinese government believes these discriminatory rules disrupt global supply chains and primarily serve to maintain American technological dominance. They maintain that China promotes inclusivity and open source models while the US coerces other nations into closed ecosystems.

The two nations previously agreed in September to create a communication channel for exchanging best practices and addressing unexpected AI incidents. Current APEC meetings in Shenzhen provide an opportunity to put this consensus into practice through active cooperation. Both countries share a responsibility to ensure that artificial intelligence remains under human control and advances general human progress. China warns that a fragmented AI landscape could leave developing economies lagging behind during the next technological revolution.

Articles.Title: Make AI a field for cooperation, not rivalry: China Daily editorial - China Daily Global Edition

stories.Headline: APEC member economies coordinate policies to share artificial intelligence benefits across the region
stories.Summary:
Nicolas Miailhe, a board member and AI lead of the France-Pacific Territories Economic Cooperation Committee of the Pacific Economic Cooperation Council, recently discussed regional cooperation. He spoke about these issues ahead of the APEC Shenzhen 2026 meeting to address global prosperity. The discussions focused on the leadership of President Xi Jinping and his call for deeper collaboration. This effort aims to ensure that the benefits of artificial intelligence are shared widely.

The initiative requires economies to work together to distribute the advantages of AI to citizens and consumers. Without this collective effort, individual nations will likely struggle to spread prosperity across their populations. The goal is to forge a shared global prosperity during the current age of artificial intelligence. This process involves coordinating policies across the various member economies of the Asia-Pacific region.

Nicolas Miailhe described the leadership and the call for deeper regional cooperation as very encouraging. He emphasized that cooperation is essential because economies cannot successfully share AI benefits in isolation. The focus remains on creating a system where technological advancements lead to widespread economic growth. He believes that working together is the only way to ensure that AI serves everyone.

Articles.Title: APEC cooperation advances shared prosperity in the AI age - China Daily

stories.Headline: China approves agreement to establish the World AI Cooperation Organization
stories.Summary:
On November 10, 2026, China's National People's Congress Standing Committee approved the agreement establishing the World AI Cooperation Organization, making China the first of its 38 founding members to do so. The decision was taken at the 25th session of the committee's 14th term. China proposed the organization, which it hosts, and its president unveiled it at a July event held alongside the 2026 World Artificial Intelligence Conference. Thirty-eight countries joined as founding members, and the organization's stated aim is to help countries share in the opportunities AI brings. Preparations are still underway before full operations begin, and more countries are invited to join.

The articles say Beijing has named cooperation and support for developing AI capabilities in the Global South as priorities. According to the reporting, the organization should encourage consultation and shared contributions among members, support AI for the public good, and promote a governance framework that is fair and reasonable. The report on China's approval sits alongside an editorial from China Daily dated November 11, 2026, which argues for Sino-US AI cooperation. That editorial urges both countries to prioritize cooperation while keeping competition within reasonable limits. It also calls for multilateral platforms such as APEC to help bridge gaps on AI governance.

The editorial describes remarks by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent at the National Committee on US-China Relations in New York on Tuesday. Bessent called for a constructive relationship based on balance and reciprocity and hoped the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen this month would advance a new bilateral AI dialogue. He said the dialogue aims to guard against shared risks and prevent misunderstandings between the two systems. According to the editorial, Bessent said both sides expect to exchange best practices for testing advanced models before release and have agreed to set up a direct channel for alerting each other to serious incidents.

The China Daily editorial also criticizes Washington's current restrictions on Chinese technology. It says Microsoft and other companies and trade groups have reportedly urged the administration to reconsider a planned ban on imports of a crucial component used in AI data centers, arguing the ban would hurt US competitiveness. It further notes that Washington has been weighing bans on new Chinese optical transceivers over claims of data theft or malware risk that the editorial says have never been substantiated. The editorial concludes that AI risks cross borders and that Washington would benefit from moving beyond zero-sum thinking and heeding the business sector.

Articles.Title: Sino-US AI cooperation necessary for the common good of humanity: China Daily editorial - China Daily Global Edition

stories.Headline: Hong Kong police deploy AI surveillance network to prevent crime and protect national security
stories.Summary:
The Hong Kong Police Force announced on Wednesday that the city's AI-powered surveillance camera network serves to prevent crime and safeguard national security. This system, known as SmartView, activated its facial recognition technology on Monday to help maintain public order and protect lives. Officers intend to use these advanced tools to locate missing children in large crowds and investigate criminal activities more efficiently. The network was originally launched in 2024 as a regional government initiative to expand surveillance across the city.

The police have already deployed more than 10,000 cameras on government buildings, police vehicles, and both ordinary and smart lampposts. Authorities plan to increase the total number of cameras to 60,000 by 2028 and will connect the network to shopping mall systems this year. To protect privacy, surveillance footage is kept for no more than 31 days, while facial recognition data is stored for a maximum of 180 days. The police force stated that personal data will be held only as long as necessary and for no more than six months.

The police force told the Global Times that facial recognition features are restricted to a small number of trained officers who need supervisory approval. They explained that the AI functions as an investigative tool to help officers analyze footage, but all flagged information requires human review. Every operation is logged and reviewed for compliance to ensure that officers follow existing procedures and privacy laws. The force emphasized that they still rely on other investigative methods before deciding on any further action.

Articles.Title: Hong Kong’s AI-powered surveillance camera network also safeguards national security, personal data protected, police force tells GT - Global Times

stories.Headline: Turing security centre publishes UK AI sovereignty roadmap urging a shared open-weight model by late 2027
stories.Summary:
The security research centre at the Alan Turing Institute, known as CETaS, published a sovereignty roadmap for British artificial intelligence on 18 November 2026. This strategic document argues that the United Kingdom should pool its data, money, expertise, and compute to create a medium-sized open-weight model. The plan targets a first build of this sovereign model by late 2027 to ensure essential services remain functional during crises. This approach focuses on resilience through optionality rather than total self-sufficiency, providing a foundation for sensitive work in security, defence, and critical infrastructure.

The roadmap requires the AI Minister to take charge of sovereignty by early 2027 through a new Cabinet sub-committee. It proposes a Strategic AI Capability label for critical firms that commit to investing in British jobs and infrastructure in exchange for faster visas and funding. For public-sector buyers, the plan suggests maintaining two separate model options from different countries to mitigate disruption risks. The government would coordinate this effort through the Prime Minister's office and the AI Taskforce, while the Turing Institute could provide central technical leadership.

Report author Sam Stockwell stated that the choices made over the next 12 to 18 months will decide if the country keeps meaningful control over these technologies. He believes these tools are fundamental to the operation of public services and the broader national economy. The proposal follows a sovereignty vision released in September and arrives as a Commons committee seeks statutory safety rules for frontier AI. While the dual-supplier recommendation is seen as an easy procurement change, the shared sovereign model remains the most ambitious goal requiring government backing.

Articles.Title: Turing's CETaS sets out a UK AI sovereignty roadmap to 2030 - Resultsense

stories.headline_source: Turing's CETaS sets out a UK AI sovereignty roadmap to 2030

stories.Headline: DeepSeek limits user access to its AI services due to insufficient computing capacity
stories.Summary:
DeepSeek restricted conversations and document reading on its website and app due to insufficient computing capacity. These restrictions began on November 15 for individual users of the service. The company limited the processing of long conversations that were inactive for 72 hours. Document reading was also capped at 10,000 tokens or the first 20 pages. These changes expose constraints pushing Chinese AI developers to seek growth beyond large models.

DeepSeek charges only via API and lacks a paid consumer tier for its users. On November 13, it announced application APIs for online search, file input, and model safety. Text and image search fees are 5 yuan per 1,000 calls, while text recognition costs 1.5 yuan. Z.AI shares closed at HK$335 on November 17, down 32.9 percent over four trading days. MiniMax shares closed at HK$116 on November 17, falling 35.6 percent over four trading days.

Yao Shuqiao of Haitong International said DeepSeek must allocate limited resources to paying customers. He expects computing power to remain tight and demand to grow exponentially by 2027. Yao also noted a broader cutoff risk tied to developments regarding Nvidia Corp. AI expert Xiao Rui compared the model to a horse and the harness to equipment. Xiao characterized harness development as an engineering challenge rather than a computing capacity challenge.

Users on Xiaohongshu complained about restrictions and offered to pay for a subscription service. Moonshot AI suspended new Kimi K3 subscriptions in July and apologized for rate limits. Enterprise customers now generate more than 70 percent of revenue for Moonshot AI's Kimi. A Menlo Ventures report says Chinese models account for 89 percent of U.S. enterprise spending. Z.AI announced a cooperation agreement with China Mobile for token technology and industry solutions.

Chinese labs are slowing foundational model advances to emphasize agents, software tools, and partnerships. DeepSeek released V4.1-Flash on September 10 but has not released a Pro version. MiniMax has not yet released its Pro model which has roughly 3 trillion parameters. Moonshot AI launched Kimi Hosted Agents on November 5 for running agents in the cloud. DeepSeek introduced its MIT-licensed DeepSeek Harness on August 13 to lower participation barriers.

DeepSeek launched a desktop version on September 29 that reached 1.5 million daily users. Daily token consumption for this version reached around 92 trillion by November 4. Harness-optimized smaller models can deliver 90 percent of larger model capabilities at 4 percent cost. Developers are now competing on ecosystem completeness as differences among the models continue narrowing. The articles leave open how developers will manage the risk of Nvidia-related chip cutoffs.

Articles.Title: In Depth: DeepSeek’s Computing Crunch Pushes China’s AI Developers Beyond Models - Caixin Global

stories.headline_source: In Depth: DeepSeek’s Computing Crunch Pushes China’s AI Developers Beyond Models

stories.Headline: Commentary: Despite AI Boom, China’s Chipmakers Have Yet to Catch Up to Nvidia
stories.Summary:
Chinese semiconductor shares recently experienced a rally, but this financial trend does not indicate a technical breakthrough in computing power. Domestic AI chip companies are expanding their reach because restrictions on American technology provide strong incentives for local buyers. However, engineers still require significant time to build reliable alternatives to the hardware produced by Nvidia Corp. The primary challenge is whether these domestic chips can run leading AI models reliably and economically at scale. Industry estimates for 2025 place the combined accelerator revenue of seven public Chinese suppliers at approximately 17.7 billion yuan, or 2.7 billion dollars. Including smaller independent vendors brings that total to roughly 3 billion dollars, while Huawei is estimated to contribute another 10 to 11 billion dollars.

Total domestic market revenue for 2025 is expected to reach between 13 and 14 billion dollars. Projections for 2026 suggest the listed group will earn 5 to 5.5 billion dollars, while Huawei Ascend could reach 15.5 to 18 billion dollars. The author of the commentary argues that a captive market should not be confused with a competitive product. They state that Chinese developers still prefer Nvidia because of the mature CUDA software platform and superior cluster reliability. The author suggests that China must compete at the system level, using strategies like the Huawei supernode to overcome manufacturing limits.

They believe vendors must provide transparent benchmarks and compatibility with frameworks like PyTorch and vLLM to reduce switching costs. The domestic industry currently faces obstacles regarding advanced fabrication capacity and high-bandwidth memory, which limit the delivery of competitive accelerators. Reliance on regulatory loopholes to obtain foreign hardware is described as a vulnerability rather than a sound industrial policy. To succeed, the author claims that China must direct more engineering toward domestic systems and demand measurable results. Future progress depends on whether these companies can move beyond demonstration projects to create repeat deployments that actually work.

Articles.Title: Commentary: Despite AI Boom, China’s Chipmakers Have Yet to Catch Up to Nvidia - Caixin Global

stories.Headline: Tarek Ziadé runs a 180 billion parameter model on 32GB of RAM using optimized SSD streaming
stories.Summary:
Tarek Ziadé developed a method to run large Mixture of Experts models on limited hardware on November 18, 2026. He utilized a MacBook M5 with 32 GB of unified memory to execute the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model, which contains 180 billion parameters. This specific model features 48 layers of 512 experts with 10 active experts, totaling 121 GB in FP8 format. The process involves streaming only the necessary experts from the SSD to the memory while keeping dense weights and n-gram tables resident.

The implementation requires installing a specific pull request from the Hugging Face Transformers GitHub repository to enable optimized offloading. To fit the model within the 32 GB limit, Ziadé used 3-bit quantization for the experts and a separate cache pool for different expert sizes. He implemented a system that reads the next layer's experts while the current layer is being computed to increase speed. These changes allowed the system to reach a peak memory usage of 25.4 GiB, requiring other applications like web browsers to be closed.

Ziadé explained that he wanted to rely less on online models and run larger ones locally on his hardware. He noted that previous methods like the Accelerate path were too slow, and he aimed to fix offloading directly within the Transformers library. By optimizing the KV cache and using bigger chunks for prefill, he increased prefill speeds from 68 to approximately 228 tokens per second. He stated that streaming experts directly from the SSD now performs within 6 percent of the Strata framework regarding token generation.

Articles.Title: 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

stories.Headline: Strike Graph launches Integration AI to collect compliance evidence from any API
stories.Summary:
Strike Graph announced the launch of Integration AI on November 18, 2026, in Seattle. This new agentic AI solution allows the company to automatically collect compliance evidence from any software that possesses an API. The system uses two separate AI agents to read public vendor documentation and build the necessary backend and user interface connections. This process removes the need for customers to install software agents or manual tools within their own infrastructure. The new tool connects API to API and applies collected evidence to more than 30 different frameworks.

This includes major standards such as SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, and CMMC, which eliminates the need for duplicate work. To maintain security, the integrations are restricted to read-only operations and utilize an endpoint allowlist. All credentials are kept in a secure secrets vault and remain completely separate from the AI build process. Justin Beals, the founder and CEO of Strike Graph, stated that quick and continuous access to evidence is essential for successful compliance. He explained that Integration AI overcomes previous roadblocks by allowing the platform to collect evidence from any system with an API.

Beals noted that the graph-based evidence model ensures that a single piece of data counts toward every framework a customer pursues. The company treats vendor documentation as data rather than instructions to prevent prompt-injection attacks. Human engineers must review the research plan and the final code before any integration is deployed to production. Each script runs in an isolated sandbox environment to ensure that a flaw in one connection cannot spread to others. Integration AI is available to all Strike Graph customers starting today.

Articles.Title: Strike Graph Launches Integration AI to Automate Continuous Compliance Evidence Using Any Existing Tool - Dark Reading

stories.headline_source: Strike Graph Launches Integration AI to Automate Continuous Compliance Evidence Using Any Existing Tool

stories.Headline: NTT DATA's Tulloch says AI threats push clients from annual audits to live risk scores
stories.Summary:
Ben Tulloch, executive managing director of advisory services for Asia Pacific at NTT DATA, said AI-driven threats are pushing companies from annual security audits to live risk scores that update whenever a company changes its software. He spoke to CRN Asia at the NTT R&D Forum 2026 in Tokyo and at a media roundtable there. He said each new feature or AI agent a company releases can open a fresh weakness or link systems in ways no one has checked. He said companies are producing software faster than ever, and a new agent built in one part of a business could expose a vulnerability elsewhere that the company did not know about. He said the traditional model, in which an outside firm spends several weeks reviewing a company and issues a grade for the year, had fundamentally changed in three months.

Tulloch said the traditional motion was to bring in someone to audit you, do a six-week assessment, get the stamp and come back next year. He described a live risk score, which tracks a company’s exposure as it changes, as a concept that was not around three or four months ago. He said a company could say its teams deployed more code today and that this increased exposures for reasons A, B and C, and therefore it needed to do something. He said NTT DATA had not found fewer than 100 vulnerabilities at any enterprise client in Asia Pacific, though the number varies with a client’s size, industry and exposure to the outside world. He said a medium-sized client would typically have hundreds, while one large client in Australia had more than 4,000 vulnerabilities.

Tulloch attributed the vulnerability counts to companies not assessing their software libraries, the ready-made blocks of code that developers borrow rather than write themselves, and said it is quite staggering. He said NTT DATA had been rethinking its approach to cybersecurity with clients since Anthropic announced its Claude Mythos Preview model in April. He cited a technical assessment published on 7 April in which Anthropic said the model could identify and exploit previously unknown vulnerabilities in every major operating system and web browser when directed to do so. He told reporters that AI can test every possible route into a system, so a collection of medium-risk weaknesses can now be exploited in ways that were not practical before. He said the first problem for many organisations is simply knowing where they stand, and that no one really knows whether you are being attacked or not until you are being attacked.

Tulloch said that once you understand your vulnerability, you cannot unsee that, and you are compelled to act. His roundtable presentation, citing CrowdStrike’s 2026 Global Threat Report, put the average breakout time, meaning how long an attacker takes to move from a first foothold to other systems, at 29 minutes. He said the fastest was 27 seconds, and in one case data was taken out of a network within four minutes. He said this made the long-standing 1-10-60 benchmark, which gives security teams one minute to detect an attack, 10 minutes to investigate it and an hour to contain it, no longer workable. NTT DATA’s alternative is a machine-first response in which software takes the first containment step, such as cutting off a user session or stopping a compromised AI agent, and then passes the case to a person.

Tulloch said at the roundtable that this does not mean taking humans out of the loop, but that a machine has to be the first response to an AI threat. Asked who decides which actions a machine may take without approval, he said such decisions were moving beyond the chief information security officer to the CEO and the board. He said that if the CISO’s only metric was containment, that may be a great risk to revenue, so the CEO will be thinking about customer impact, revenue impact, people impact, as well as security. He did not say whether automated containment had ever shut down legitimate systems at a client, saying he was not sure he could answer that question. He said the attack surface, meaning the range of entry points open to attackers, had also grown as more staff across the business build their own AI agents, sometimes with low-code tools that require little programming.

Tulloch pointed to newer technologies such as MCP servers, which let AI agents connect to company applications and data, as changing what agents can reach. He said at the roundtable that this shift moves part of the problem out of the security team’s hands, because engineering flaws out is a software development problem and that is a different group of people. He noted that NTT DATA had formed partnerships with Google and cloud security company Wiz in recent months, and that Wiz’s code-scanning tool is used to flag weaknesses while software is still being written. He said that in regulated sectors such as banking and insurance, AI agents need to be highly accurate, and that you cannot be 30% wrong, you have got to be aiming for 98, 99%, and then bring the human in the loop for that. He said NTT DATA AIVista, the group’s AI firm in Silicon Valley, was working on neuro-symbolic AI, which pairs machine learning with rule-based logic, with the aim of keeping agents within defined limits and with insurance and banking as its main focus.

Tulloch said many of the agent-focused startups he saw at an event in Jakarta the previous week talked about productivity rather than quality. He said that in any regulated process it comes down to quality, that you have to be able to trust it, and that if you do not trust it, you will not deploy it, not at scale. He said clients are also asking for help managing the agents they already run, covering token costs, the usage charges for running AI models, access to data and the ability to show auditors what the agents have done. He said it is a sign of clients being serious about AI when they say they have these agents now and ask for help managing them, and that many software-as-a-service options for this are expensive, so clients are looking for lower-cost ways to do it. He said the last of the four areas in NTT DATA’s approach is preparing for post-quantum cryptography, encryption designed to withstand future quantum computers.

Tulloch told the roundtable that Singapore expects critical infrastructure operators to have migration plans by March 2027. He said that, as far as he was aware, no one can yet break current encryption with a quantum computer. He said the immediate risk is that attackers can steal encrypted data now and decrypt it once quantum computers are capable enough, a tactic known as harvest now, decrypt later. Asked about Malaysia, he said he was not personally aware of its plans, and he expected banks operating across both markets to follow Singapore’s timeline. He said most of the banks in Malaysia and Singapore are across borders, so they are probably more likely going to fall to the Singapore timelines, unless Malaysia is more stringent.

Articles.Title: AI pushes cybersecurity from annual audits to live risk scores, says NTT DATA - CRN Asia

stories.Headline: Civil servants submit AI and data ideas to a 2026-27 challenge run by NTT DATA with government
stories.Summary:
Civil servants across government were invited to submit ideas for using artificial intelligence and data to improve public services when the 2026-27 Civil Service AI & Data Challenge opened for applications, in a competition run by NTT DATA with the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport and the Cabinet Office. The competition is open to civil servants in all departments, roles and grades, and it asks them to identify problems they encounter in their day-to-day work that could be addressed through better use of AI and data. The strongest proposals will be developed through a Dragons' Den-style competition, and the winning project will receive £50,000 of support to help bring the idea to life. Applications are open until 10 December 2026, and civil servants can submit an idea, volunteer to join a project team, or do both through the Challenge website. The latest competition follows last year's programme, which has seen at least seven AI and data projects taken forward by government departments and agencies.

Among them is an initiative proposed by last year's winner, Marlon Woodley, a verification assurance officer at the Department for Work and Pensions, whose idea focuses on improving the tools available to benefits caseworkers to reduce errors and accelerate decision-making. Previous Challenges have also generated proposals to support peatland restoration and to improve information-sharing between the NHS and the DWP following a death. For the 2026-27 programme, eight teams of civil service volunteers will be established to develop the most promising proposals, supported by a government-wide network of data leaders, and the competition will culminate in July 2027, when a panel of senior Civil Service digital leaders will select the winning project. Minister for digital government Stephanie Peacock said civil servants across the country see first-hand where technology could make a real difference to people's lives, whether that is speeding up decisions, reducing avoidable admin or making public services easier to use, and that the Challenge gives them the opportunity to turn that experience into action. Government chief data officer Aimee Smith said she saw last year how the Challenge enables civil servants in every role, department and grade to help improve public services, and that it is also a brilliant way for them to improve their skills and experience in digital technologies.

David Filmer, head of public sector at NTT DATA UK&I, said AI and data have enormous potential to transform public services and make a tangible difference to people's lives, and that it is a privilege for the company to support civil servants in turning their ideas into reality. The Challenge is also supported by government Chief AI officer Kalbir Sohi and DCMS permanent secretary Susannah Storey. Woodley said that winning has been a life-changing experience and that he is now involved in a project to see his idea through to implementation, improving the tools used by benefits caseworkers to reduce errors and speed up decisions. The programme is also intended to develop digital skills across the Civil Service by giving participants experience of working on technology projects alongside colleagues from other departments and disciplines.

Articles.Title: Civil servants challenged to turn AI ideas into better public services - THINK Digital Partners

stories.headline_source: Civil servants challenged to turn AI ideas into better public services

stories.Headline: Giovanni Carraro says open-weight AI models give enterprises more control over cost and customization
stories.Summary:
Open-weight AI models are creating new possibilities for how organizations deploy, customize and manage artificial intelligence, according to a Kyndryl article published on 18 November 2026. Unlike proprietary models, which are typically accessed through a provider, open-weight models give enterprises the option to run AI within their own infrastructure. The article says open-weight AI is expanding enterprise choice and changing how leaders evaluate cost, control and risk. Giovanni Carraro, Senior Vice President, Global Strategic Alliances at Kyndryl, discusses the trade-offs between open and closed models as more firms move from experimentation to enterprise-wide AI adoption. The article asks why open-weight AI models are gaining attention among enterprise leaders.

Carraro says organizations are moving beyond experimentation and thinking more seriously about how AI fits into their operations, infrastructure and long-term business strategies. He says cost, control and customization are driving much of the interest, and some organizations are finding that open-weight models can be a part of their enterprise tools. Open-weight models allow organizations to access, download and customize trained AI models to meet specific business needs, giving them greater control over where AI runs, how data is managed and the cost model under which it operates. He says that flexibility may become increasingly valuable as enterprises balance growing demands with operational and financial considerations. The article says the flexibility raises important questions about cost, sovereignty, security and long-term strategy.

Carraro says the choice between open-weight and closed, proprietary AI models should not be an either-or decision. He says both have advantages, and the right choice depends on an organization's needs and how it plans to use AI. He says it is helpful to think about surfaces and engines, where surfaces are where you access the tool and engines are the AI model the surface directs to. He says proprietary models are typically accessed through web, desktop and mobile applications, through APIs either directly from the developer or via managed cloud platforms, through command-line tools and IDE extensions, and increasingly through integrations embedded in enterprise software.

He says the AI provider manages much of the underlying infrastructure in these instances, which can simplify deployment and ongoing maintenance for the end user. Carraro says proprietary models can still offer choices of hosting location and capacity, and in some cases can offer fine-tuning within the model provider's available options. He says open-weight models can offer greater flexibility over where and how AI operates, and organizations can host them in private cloud or on-premises environments, or even on individual devices. He says organizations can customize certain models for specialized tasks, and some open providers offer models through cloud services, which means they would manage the infrastructure and maintenance.

The article says the conversation should not be about whether open-weight or proprietary AI models are better, but about understanding which model can deliver the greatest value to an organization, including meeting its security requirements. The article says organizations may also turn to specialized models, whether open or closed, to achieve their goals. The article says Kyndryl can help customers navigate their AI partner choices. It says the conversation about enterprise AI is evolving as organizations move beyond experimentation.

The article carries a read time of 1 minute and is dated 18-Nov-2026. It says open-weight AI is expanding enterprise choice and changing how leaders evaluate cost, control and risk. The article says it is also important to distinguish open-weight models from other kinds of models. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Open-weight AI promises more control. What’s the catch? - Kyndryl

stories.Headline: Kyndryl CEO Martin Schroeter says companies must control AI agents and build governance into their design
stories.Summary:
Kyndryl Chairman and CEO Martin Schroeter gave adapted remarks during a fireside chat with cybersecurity expert Nuno Mateus-Coelho at the Web Summit in Lisbon on November 12, 2026. The article was published on kyndryl.com on November 18, 2026, with a read time of one minute. Schroeter said cybersecurity remains top of mind for Kyndryl's customers. He said the world now has two things to deal with: bad actors and agents that are misguided, incorrectly built or uncontrolled. He said bad actors are going to use AI to try to break into systems and that Kyndryl sees it every day.

Schroeter said the second concern is about agents, which he called the new world. He said there are examples of agents moving outside their sandbox or doing things they were not intended to do. He said Kyndryl is building agents for its customers, that they are all controlled, and that Kyndryl has visibility into them. He said Kyndryl knows what the agents are doing, what they are allowed to do and what they cannot do. He said the agents are controlled through what Kyndryl calls Kyndryl Bridge.

Schroeter said you have to create agents, control them and set their permissions the right way, as is done with many other things in infrastructure. He said that at the end of the day agents are software code, but they are relentless, goal-seeking pieces of software. He said agents need to be controlled. He said that across industries, the companies getting this right and thinking ahead have, first and foremost, a complete view of their inventory. He said Kyndryl helps its customers do this.

Schroeter said those companies have a complete view of the hardware, software, operating systems and everything in their inventory. He said they also know what patches have been applied. He said that allows Kyndryl's customers to prioritize what they need to protect specifically, because not everything is equally important. He said the first thing is to know what you have. He said the governance of agents is a top concern.

Schroeter said these companies do not build agents and then try to figure out how to govern them. He said they use tools like what Kyndryl calls policy as code. He said Kyndryl can ingest their business rules, their infrastructure and the business logic they are trying to follow. He said you can then apply the policy you already have in place to the new piece of code you are introducing into your infrastructure. He said governance cannot be an afterthought and has to be part of the design.

Schroeter said you need to be able to shut agents down or control them and make sure you have a resilient system. He said that if you know what you have, build policy governance into the design, and have a way to keep your systems resilient if something goes wrong, you are among the companies at the forefront of this in every industry. The article ends mid-sentence, asking what role industry should play in shielding customers from geopolitical risks and helpi. The article gives no further remarks, no other speakers and no additional dates or figures. More to follow.

stories.Headline: OpenAI builds Codex sandbox to limit filesystem and network access for agent commands
stories.Summary:
The articles are a single OpenAI engineering post dated November 18, 2026, titled Inside the Codex sandbox, which says OpenAI built the Codex sandbox so Codex can run commands on a user's computer within filesystem and network limits the user controls. OpenAI says it takes a defense in depth approach to safeguarding agents, with training and alignment plus features in its agentic harness, Codex. The post says running commands on your computer is one of the most common and potentially risky things Codex does. It describes a sandbox as limiting what a program can access while it runs. It gives a photo-organizing example where commands could read and modify files in ~/Pictures while network access is blocked to prevent uploads.

Users configure the sandbox through permission profiles, which define the filesystem and network restrictions for a Codex session, and the post covers defaults, design, configuration, enforcement on macOS, Linux and Windows, and reuse in other tools. With a Git repository as the workspace root, the built-in :workspace profile allows writes within the workspace while keeping directories such as .git and .codex read-only, so Codex can edit source code without seeking permission for every change while preventing direct changes to .codex/config.toml or Git hooks under .git/hooks. It allows broad filesystem reads subject to the user's existing OS permissions, because compilers, runtimes and build tools depend on SDKs, libraries and configuration outside the repository, and restricting reads to the workspace would break many ordinary workflows, with the tradeoff that sensitive files elsewhere, such as config files containing API keys, may remain readable. It disables network access, blocking direct uploads to external services including attempts to exfiltrate data the command can read, and also preventing legitimate operations such as downloading dependencies. The post says these restrictions prevent a large class of bad behavior but harmful actions are still possible, for example the agent could inject malicious code into a locally installed package such as node_modules/prettier, a change that might not appear in git status because node_modules is often ignored by Git, and if the user's editor runs that copy of Prettier on save, simply saving a file could execute the malicious code outside the Codex sandbox.

The post says OpenAI prefers to invest heavily in OS-specific sandboxing rather than virtual machines or containers, so Codex constrains commands running in the user's existing environment instead of moving computation to a separate environment. It says a laptop often serves as a bespoke dev environment that developers can change on a whim, reproducing it in a Docker container can take work, and some workflows still depend on tools that run on the host. It gives the example of developing an iOS app on a Mac, where Codex inside Docker could not run the iOS build toolchain of native Mac executables or launch the iPhone simulator, and a Docker-based workflow could delegate builds and simulator operations to the Mac host but those operations would execute outside the container's sandbox and would need their own restrictions. The harness exposes the OS-specific mechanisms through a common API across macOS, Windows and Linux that takes a command and a permission profile, and if the profile allows limited network access the caller must supply a network proxy to enforce those limits. The post shows a simplified spawn_command_under_sandbox function taking program_and_args, cwd, env, permission_profile and network_proxy and returning a Child handle, and says each child process inherits its parent's sandbox constraints, so restrictions apply throughout the process tree initiated by the command, even to descendants that outlive the original process.

The post says the Codex harness executes tool calls generated by the model, and for coding tasks the most commonly used tool is a shell tool that runs commands much as a user would in an interactive shell such as Bash. It examines the one-shot exec_command shell tool, showing a simplified ExecCommandToolCall class with cmd, workdir, shell, login defaulting to True and timeout_ms of 10_000, and a perform_exec_command function that builds program_and_args from the shell or the SHELL environment variable or /bin/sh with -lc or -c and the command, calls subprocess.Popen with cwd defaulting to the turn's cwd, pipes stdout and merges stderr into stdout, and collects output and exit code. To sandbox the command, the harness replaces subprocess.Popen() with spawn_command_under_sandbox(), supplying the permission profile and, when needed, the network proxy, as shown in perform_exec_command_with_sandboxing. The exec_command tool lets the model request different permissions for an individual command, with sandbox_permissions set to use_default, with_additional_permissions or require_escalated, a justification string only for require_escalated, and additional_permissions only for with_additional_permissions.

The post says the harness decides whether to grant the request, using the default sandbox config for the turn under use_default, expanded access within the sandbox under with_additional_permissions, and execution outside it under require_escalated, evaluating the request based on the user's preferences, for example prompting the user directly or routing the request to auto-review, and if execution is authorized Codex passes the appropriate permission_profile and network_proxy with the original command arguments. The post says the shell tool is the primary consumer of spawn_command_under_sandbox(), and the harness also reuses its sandboxing infrastructure for operations such as reading and modifying local files, and the codex sandbox command lets you incorporate sandboxed command execution into your own tools. A named permission profile lets you reuse the same filesystem and network restrictions across projects, defined under [permissions] in config.toml, and the post gives a profile named dev that extends the built-in :workspace profile with the description "Development with extra read-only protections." The dev profile adds write access to ~/build-cache and places additional restrictions on files in the workspace, with filesystem entries granting read-only access (read), read and write access (write) or blocking access entirely (deny), and the :workspace_roots table lets you define rules for paths relative to a project's workspace roots.

The post says profiles starting with ":" are provided by Codex, and the description is displayed when /permissions is run in the Codex CLI. The post says the Codex CLI by default uses its working directory as its workspace root. The post says the articles leave open how the remaining sections on network permissions, layering configuration and enforcing limits, the codex sandbox command example sandboxing an MCP server, the network proxy, and building on the Codex sandbox for Linux and Windows continue beyond the text provided. It refers readers to the Codex security cookbook for guidance on tailoring sandbox permissions and combining them with other protections in an enterprise environment.

It refers to Unrolling the Codex Agent Loop for how the Codex harness executes tool calls generated by the model. It says the code shown is a simplified version of the actual API and of how the exec_command tool call would be honored without sandboxing. It says the diagram showing how the pieces fit together from configuration to running a sandboxed command is explained in the sections that follow. More to follow.
