stories.Headline: Malka launches YuviLab and Israel's education ministry picks its Spark platform for English learning
stories.Summary:
Moti Malka was away on reserve duty when his wife struggled to help their 10-year-old son study for an English test while schools were shut and screens had become the fallback. Malka, a father of four and an AI architect at a high-tech firm, used AI to build a game in which his son had to form English sentences correctly to advance in a race. He told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency it took him two minutes to build and his son was captivated by the game and how it was made. That experiment turned into YuviLab, an educational AI platform Malka launched in March to encourage children toward building, experimenting and thinking creatively. Earlier this month, YuviLab announced that the Education Ministry had selected Spark, its AI-powered personalized learning platform, for the English-language component of Project 720, a government-led initiative to bring personalized learning into Israeli schools.

Malka worked on the first version during downtime as a commander in a Home Front Command search-and-rescue unit focused on evacuating people from missile impact sites, and while sheltering with his own family and their newborn. A 2022 Israel Internet Association survey found that about a quarter of Israeli youth spent six to eight hours a day on screens, while 11% spent more than eight hours. A study by Israel's National Institute for Health Policy Research found that nearly half of parents reported an increase in young children's screen time, with families of reservists and evacuees reporting bigger increases, and nearly a quarter said ordinary screen-use rules were infeasible under wartime conditions. A study by Sharon Cayzer-Haller, a Hebrew University researcher, followed 318 Israeli adolescents during the first months after the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack and found that 46 percent belonged to a balanced-user group that reported the highest levels of well-being. Yuvi was developed with support from Microsoft and is hosted on Microsoft Azure, where AI-generated content is filtered and personally identifiable information is not stored, and Microsoft's 2025 education report said 86% of global education organizations now use generative AI.

Malka said his initial goal was to move children from consuming content to creating it, and that children quickly learn to work with the platform by describing what they want, testing the result and refining the prompt. He admitted he has not written a single line of code in nearly two years. He said the feature displaying generated code in real time was encouraged by Microsoft education specialists, who argued that children are naturally curious about how things work and should be able to look under the hood. He described Yuvi as a way for kids to enter STEM, shorthand for science, technology, engineering and math, fields where Israel has been struggling. He said he agrees with part of the critique of AI in schools, that schools should focus on the principles behind AI rather than tools that are constantly evolving, and that some children treated the process as magic, giving vague instructions and accepting outputs that looked complete even when they did not match what they had asked for.

Cayzer-Haller told JTA that not all screen time is the same and that the key question is not how many hours adolescents spend online but how they use digital media. At an education conference in Jerusalem last week, Arab Israeli content creator Nuseir Yassin, known as Nas Daily, mused that if he ran the Education Ministry he would teach only English during the first two years of school, and predicted that within five years classrooms of 40 students could have five AI agents providing personalized instruction. A survey presented at the same conference found that 87% of Israeli teenagers felt schools were failing to prepare them for the future, nearly 80% expected AI to replace much of teachers' work, while only 50% of teachers agreed. A report by the Brookings Institution released earlier this year, drawing on more than 400 studies and consultations across 50 countries, concluded that the risks of generative AI in children's education currently outweigh its benefits, particularly because of its potential to undermine foundational learning.

Lea Shahar, who left her job as a programmer in high tech as generative AI took off and now teaches coding to high-school students, said the tools are changing too quickly to build a curriculum around them and that schools would do better to spend more time on skills children are less likely to develop alone on a screen, including interpersonal communication and languages. Spark is already in use in Israeli schools through Project 720's mathematics and science pilot, with Yuvi working across dozens of local authorities, including Jerusalem, Rishon LeZion and Netanya. The expansion into English follows an announcement by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Education Minister Yoav Kisch of plans to expand AI-assisted English instruction, after just 22% of Israeli ninth-graders met national English curriculum requirements last year. The latest results from PISA, an international assessment of 15-year-olds released in September, showed Israeli students scoring well below the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development average in mathematics, science and reading, with scores in all three subjects falling to an all-time low.

Last year, the Education Ministry announced a national plan to bring AI into classrooms from fourth through 12th grade, with teacher training, new curricula and tools developed with major technology companies including Google, Microsoft, Apple and Nvidia. In its education report, Microsoft said AI training has not kept pace with adoption, with 45% of educators globally and 52% of US students saying they had received no AI training, and an Israeli survey of more than 27,000 teachers, published in November by the Education Ministry, found that while 76% had received AI training, only about half felt equipped to help students use it. Spark is a paid platform for schools, while Yuvi's student-facing platform is free and lets children build games, apps and learning projects, with tools for parents and teachers to connect that work to school material and track progress. Available in Hebrew, English, Russian and Arabic, the game-building platform lets a child choose whether to create a game, a lesson or another project, and one student asked Yuvi to build an escape room for learning English in which the player can leave the room only by solving language questions.

Another student modeled his game on the Iron Dome air defense system, with the player intercepting incoming missiles by answering arithmetic questions correctly, and others have built projects inspired by Minecraft or Roblox. Yuvi has since expanded beyond its original focus on gamifying learning, with the company now concentrating on personalized learning in schools, and its platforms reach tens of thousands of children and are used by thousands of teachers, according to Malka. It uses several AI models rather than a single chatbot, so a coding request, a math explanation and a creative prompt are not all handled the same way, and the platform routes each task to the model designers have determined is best suited for it while adapting to the child's language and level. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Cantwell and Rounds urge Jay Clayton to draft a national strategy against AI-assisted cyber threats
stories.Summary:
On November 18, 2026, two members of the United States Senate sent a bipartisan letter to the White House regarding recent cyber outages. Senators Maria Cantwell of Washington and Mike Rounds of South Dakota urged the administration to better protect national infrastructure from threats aided by artificial intelligence. The lawmakers expressed concern that current American defenses are not keeping pace with the ability of AI to exploit software weaknesses. They specifically highlighted how autonomous AI agents could introduce new security risks and bypass traditional cyber defenses.

The senators requested that AI czar Jay Clayton develop a new national strategy to address these evolving cyber threats. This plan would require a task force to bring together federal agencies and AI companies to secure digital infrastructure. The proposal also calls for the creation of security standards for autonomous AI agents to prevent unauthorized bank transactions. Clayton, who was appointed to his role in early October, is already leading a government task force to produce an AI policy by the end of January.

Senator Cantwell and Senator Rounds argued that AI can quickly find software vulnerabilities while repair patches often take weeks or months to install. They cited recent AI-boosted cyberattacks in Japan that caused large-scale data breaches at various companies and financial institutions. Jay Clayton, who also serves as the Director of National Intelligence, is expected to face questions about these issues during his testimony before the House Committee on Homeland Security on Wednesday morning. The White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Tuesday.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently spoke to reporters in the Philippines to reassure the public about the stability of American systems. He stated that there is zero evidence that outages affecting the Federal Aviation Administration, United Airlines, and Microsoft Outlook were connected. Rubio claimed there is no reason to believe these isolated instances were caused by criminals, nefarious actors, or other nation states. It remains unclear if artificial intelligence played any specific role in the recent outages impacting travelers and consumers.

stories.Headline: Canonical lets Ubuntu Pro users install AI-written Surge security patches before human review
stories.Summary:
Canonical has begun letting Ubuntu Pro customers install security patches written by AI agents before its own engineers finish reviewing and testing them, the company said on November 18, 2026. The patches come from a system called Surge, which Canonical built to fix known vulnerabilities in Ubuntu's userspace software, meaning everything outside the operating system's kernel. They ship through a new opt-in channel called the Edge archive. If you leave Edge switched off, nothing changes in how your updates are checked, because Ubuntu's regular security updates still get human validation before release. Switch it on and you get fixes sooner, but you also take on a job Ubuntu's own testing normally handles, which is deciding whether a patch is safe to run in production.

Ubuntu's security teams have already shipped twice as many fixes as they did last year, and the company says AI agents are behind a wave of vulnerability reports and attacks across open source. Human review and soak testing, where a fix runs for an extended stretch to catch problems before release, take longer than some customers are willing to sit exposed, and Canonical's answer is that "we need to fight AI with AI." Surge passes the work down a line of AI agents, each with one job. The first reads vulnerability feeds, matches each report to Ubuntu packages, and drops anything that does not affect Ubuntu.

The next grabs the upstream fix and the code around it, then several competing models each write their own backport, which means adapting a fix made for the current version of a program to the older version a stable Ubuntu release ships. A panel of separate judge models looks over the candidates and has to reach a consensus. If the judges deadlock, are not confident, or run into an unusual case, the patch goes to a human on the Ubuntu security team. Anything that makes it through gets built and run through the same deterministic tests as any other Ubuntu package, and the company says this setup protects against regressions and against supply-chain attacks, where someone slips malicious code into software through its build or update path.

Kernel fixes stay out of Surge's hands, because the kernel needs a different backporting setup and just shipping the newest version would be a big stability risk for enterprise systems. So kernels now run on a two-week Stable Release Update cycle, with the cycles overlapping so a new proposed kernel lands every week. Surge is aimed at the backlog of vulnerabilities that are already known, while new flaws, including the ones Canonical's automated research turns up, still go through coordinated disclosure, with the company reporting them privately and working with upstream maintainers under embargo before anything goes public. "We strongly disagree with those who have abandoned coordinated disclosure practices," the company wrote.

stories.Headline: EigenOrbit publishes a quantum-inspired adapter method that keeps certified robustness in medical image classifiers
stories.Summary:
EigenOrbit, working with dermatologists at the Hospital Maggiore of Trieste and researchers from the University of Trieste, has published a method for adapting medical image classifiers to new tasks while keeping a mathematical guarantee that small image changes cannot alter their predictions. The paper, titled Quantum-inspired orthogonal adapters for certifiably robust medical image classification, is available on arXiv under the identifier 2611.18775, and the code has been released as open source. The method uses orthogonal adapters built from reconfigurable beam splitter circuits, a structure taken from quantum computing, which reduces the number of trainable parameters while preserving the original network's Lipschitz bound. The work was reported on November 18, 2026. Certified robustness computes, for every image, a radius within which no perturbation can change a prediction, and the article notes that the EU AI Act in Article 15 and the U.S. FDA's draft guidance on AI-enabled devices both address the robustness of such systems.

The difficulty the team addressed is that certified networks are trained on general image collections, while medical datasets are too small to train them from scratch, and standard fine-tuning methods including LoRA change the network's Lipschitz bound so the guarantee weakens. Because the beam splitter circuits are orthogonal for any choice of parameters, the adapted network keeps exactly the Lipschitz bound of the original, and a 2048-wide layer needs 11,264 trainable angles instead of about 4.2 million weights. All computations run on classical hardware, and the circuits map directly to shallow quantum circuits. The team adapted a certified ImageNet network called BRONet to trichoscopic images from 143 patients for alopecia diagnosis and to images from 57 patients for alopecia areata activity. In the diagnosis tests, 63.8% of test images were classified correctly and certified at a perturbation radius of 36/255, compared with 31.6% for LoRA and 35.6% for full fine-tuning.

At a larger radius of 108/255, the butterfly adapter still certified 20.4% of images while LoRA and full fine-tuning certified none, and the butterfly adapter's classification accuracy of 80.4% stayed close to full fine-tuning at 82.5% and above LoRA at 71.5%. The adapter trains about 100,000 parameters, over 300 times fewer than full fine-tuning, and adversarial attacks using PGD and APGD-T confirmed the certificates, with none succeeding within a certified radius. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first study of certified robustness in trichoscopic image classification. The stated next steps include patient-level validation on larger datasets and certified backbones built entirely from quantum-inspired orthogonal layers.

Articles.Title: EigenOrbit Develops Quantum-Inspired Method for Robust Medical Image AI

stories.Headline: Naren Gangavarapu sets out the CLEAR standard for checking agentic AI results
stories.Summary:
Naren Gangavarapu completed an 18-month deployment of 25 production agents across a large travel and cruise group, and wrote in a CIO article published on 18 November 2026 that the results cannot be checked. He read 50 published accounts of agentic AI in production and found escalations down, handling times down, conversion up and onboarding compressed from weeks to days. The window is rarely stated, the denominator almost never, and concurrent initiatives that could have produced the same movement go unnamed. He wrote that this usually is not dishonesty, because nobody has told practitioners what a defensible result looks like. He said the cost lands on CIOs weighing a major agentic investment, who cannot tell a result achieved at peak trading volume from one achieved in a quiet quarter.

He set out the CLEAR standard, five tests for a reportable agentic AI result, sitting beneath the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001, which tell you to measure but not what a reportable number looks like. C is concurrent changes registered, asking what else changed in the same window and could independently produce the result. L is a locked window, fixed before the result was known and including the hardest trading conditions. E is evidentiary custody, asking which system produced the count, who defines the category and who reviewed the figure. A is an attributable baseline, separating gain from re-engineering the process from gain from clearing accumulated slack, and R is reference volume, asking whether the underlying volume held steady and whether that is stated.

He wrote that four tests ask for disclosure, which is cheap, while the locked window asks for pre-commitment, which is costly because it forecloses discovering later that a different period tells a better story. In his experience the locked window does most of the work. He wrote that CLEAR is not a validity standard, because a result that passes all five is still a single-organization observation, and that it gives you an account a skeptic can attack. He said medicine and machine learning research already have reporting standards such as CONSORT-AI and REFORMS, while agentic deployments do not. He wrote that the most important control in the deployment cost nothing to build.

Any line-of-business manager, from the wholesale desk to the cruise operations floor, could stop an agent within ninety seconds, with no ticket and no approval. If the manager was wrong, the agent was restarted and the matter discussed at the next recalibration session, because being wrong cost an hour of throughput while being slow could cost a customer. He wrote that a manager using that control is the system working as designed, and that the failure is the override that is not logged. The record that would have shown a tolerance band was miscalibrated never exists, and the agent's statistics are computed over a population from which a conscientious human has removed the hard cases. Every downstream metric then improves, escalation rates fall because escalations were intercepted first, and confidence scores look strong because low-confidence decisions were pulled out by hand.

He wrote that this echoes Lisanne Bainbridge's 1983 "ironies of automation", in which the human handles what the designer could not automate with no way to feed that judgment back into the design. He said no care at write-up time recovers a record that was never captured, and that measurement in agentic systems is a daily operating discipline, not a reporting exercise. The team treated agents as high-volume junior team members, fast, tireless and capable of significant harm if poorly supervised, and every manager with agents adopted six habits. The habits were a five-minute morning review of overnight agent activity treated as a floor walk, a weekly scorecard written for operations covering completion, escalation rate and decision confidence, and an exception-first culture asking what the agent flagged as uncertain. They also included explicit human-agent teaming norms on when a human overrides, when they defer and how it is logged, scenario playbooks for the ten likeliest failure modes owned by operations, and a monthly recalibration session reviewing tolerance limits against incident data.

He wrote that the fourth habit carries the most weight and gets the least attention, and that the sixth is how the organization learns, by asking what fired that should not have and what did not fire that should have, both answerable only if the override record is complete. One design decision supported all six: autonomy was allocated by reversibility, not risk appetite, which non-technologists can classify at design time and which maps straight to a control, so the less reversible the action the earlier a human must stand in the loop. Of the 25 agents, seven could act without confirmation, and thirteen either required it or were barred from autonomous external communication. He wrote that three outcomes were used internally to justify further investment and two came out weaker under CLEAR.

The escalation result largely survived, because the six-month window was fixed to include peak season, contact volume was flat year over year and counts came from the system of record reviewed by finance rather than the agent team, but Tier 1 is the organization's own classification, so the absolute figure cannot be compared across organizations. The onboarding baseline was not attributable, because the 23 days included time in a standing backlog and part of the gain came from clearing that queue rather than shortening the process. The third result was the weakest, because a marketplace rebuild and opt-in dynamic pricing ran in the same window as the AI-native search capability credited with most of the uplift. He wrote that two of three carrying material qualifications is probably typical, and that a result which survives disclosure of its weaknesses is worth more than one never tested.

He advised checking whether human overrides of agent decisions are logged and inspecting the log rather than asking whether one exists. He advised locking the measurement window before the next reporting cycle and writing down the period, the denominator and everything else changing in the same interval, which costs nothing in advance and is impossible afterward. He wrote that if you ship agent changes weekly there is no stable intervention to lock a window around, so report rolling comparisons and say so, and that if the agent does work nobody did before, name the tests that do not apply instead of quietly dropping them. He wrote that disclosure has commercial cost, that the team withheld volumes but disclosed the comparison basis, and that disciplined reporters will look weaker than those who are not, a coordination problem no one practitioner can solve.

Articles.Title: Your agentic AI results can’t be checked. Here’s how to fix that

stories.Headline: Beni Beeri Issembert argues that corporate decisions shape how AI models explain Israel
stories.Summary:
Beni Beeri Issembert wrote an article on November 18, 2026, about how corporate decisions shape AI explanations of Israel. He argues that large language models reflect the choices of the people who build them. These companies decide which training data to use and which languages to cover. Product teams also write rules about how to treat specific subjects. Tuning processes reward some answers while penalizing others.

The author cites a January 2025 WIRED report on the DeepSeek R1 model and its different filters in various apps. He mentions a July 2025 Associated Press report about Grok 4 and Elon Musk's xAI company. The ADL reported anti-Israel bias in GPT, Claude, Gemini, and Llama in March 2025. Ynet reported in October 2025 that Israel's Foreign Ministry hired a firm for GPT framing results. Two December 2025 studies in Science and Nature examined how chatbots change political views.

Beni Beeri Issembert says that the companies building these systems are responsible for the choices inside them. He believes that a chatbot that never commits to a position is of no use to users. He suggests that important claims should link to sources that actually support the information provided. He argues that readers need a way to challenge answers and get corrections. He states that independent researchers should test systems in Hebrew, Arabic, and English.

The ADL noted that questions about Israel and the war had the highest refusal rates in their study. Christoph Steinert and Daniel Kazenwadel found that GPT-3.5 gave higher casualty estimates in Arabic than in Hebrew. Their study used data from earlier wars, such as 2014, and was summarized by the University of Zurich. The Science study involved almost 77,000 British participants who discussed topics with chatbots. These participants were sometimes more persuaded by inaccurate models that used factual claims.

The author references Walter Lippmann's 1922 writing on the manufacture of consent and the role of supplied pictures. He also cites Hannah Arendt's 1967 essay on truth and politics regarding factual information and opinion. He mentions the biblical book of Genesis and the concept of being created in a divine image. He notes that the murder of families in Kibbutz Beeri can be treated as one perspective. He explains that chatbots provide private pictures without bylines or opinion pages.

The author wants a system where dates are visible and contested positions are attributed to specific people. He calls for a product that explicitly tells the reader when it restricts a certain subject. He believes users must ask whose image they see when a machine speaks to them. The articles do not say if the Foreign Ministry's public diplomacy campaign actually worked. They leave open whether chatbots are currently moving public opinion about Israel today.

stories.Headline: BBVA researchers train transformer models on app navigation data to personalize banking
stories.Summary:
BBVA's AI researchers developed a model that interprets how customers interact with the bank's mobile app, providing a deeper understanding of their needs and paving the way for more personalized and proactive banking. The research was presented at ICAIF, a leading conference on AI applied to finance. The paper was presented on November 15 in Milan at the ACM International Conference on AI in Finance. Asier González-Rodríguez is one of the paper's authors. The paper was presented at a pioneering event held as part of the conference, dedicated to research into foundation and multimodal models for the banking sector.

The research analyzed approximately 1.6 billion navigation sessions from eight million customers, covering one year of activity, using anonymized data. Of these, 90 million sessions were selected to train the new models. BBVA began exploring the use of embeddings in 2018. In 2023, this research focused on navigation data from the bank's app, transforming sequences of screens visited by customers into anonymized vector representations. The approach used until now was based on Word2Vec.

Researchers explored the use of Transformers, a deep learning architecture that makes it possible to analyze sequences and identify relationships between their elements, and which underpins large language models. Each screen visited in the app is treated as a token, the basic unit of data that AI models read and generate, while the sequence of screens viewed during a session functions much like a sentence. Through self-supervised learning, the model learns to recognize navigation patterns directly from activity logs, without the need to manually label each sequence. Researchers developed a hierarchical tokenization system that groups related screens and makes it possible to interpret new features based on existing categories, avoiding the need to rebuild the system whenever the app changes. A decoder architecture was ultimately selected, which learns to predict the next screens in a sequence and combines contextual information from the entire navigation journey to generate a compact, reusable representation.

The AUC metric increased by 2.7% in relative terms compared with the baseline model, also outperforming the result achieved with Word2Vec. The solution is integrated into a process that serves approximately eight million active users and processes four million sessions per day. BBVA is already taking the first steps towards developing a multi-source foundation model capable of integrating different dimensions and providing a foundation for building multiple AI applications. The models developed so far focus on one specific dimension of customer behavior: digital navigation. Much of a person's relationship with their bank is also reflected in other sources of information, ranging from transactions and account activity to interactions with relationship managers, phone calls and branch visits.

Physicist Nathaniel Craig, a visiting scientist at OpenAI, worked with GPT-6 Astra on a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model. Craig leads the particle theory group at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and is a permanent member of its Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics. In an October preprint prepared with the aid of GPT-6 Astra, Craig proposed a candidate definition on a lattice, a grid representing spacetime. Astra helped turn Craig's strategy into a construction and took the lead in developing the detailed proof. The Standard Model describes the known elementary particles and three of the four fundamental forces, the strong force, the weak force, and electromagnetism.

The success of the theory rests on outstanding agreement between theoretical calculations and experiments across eighteen orders of magnitude, from the low energies of hydrogen's 21-centimeter radio emission to the high energies of collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. For the full Standard Model in continuous spacetime, we don't have a nonperturbative definition, or even an understanding of whether the interacting theory is mathematically well defined. Lattice field theory has led to remarkable progress in our understanding of the strong force over the last few decades, including a quantitative understanding of the mass of the proton from first principles. The weak force treats left- and right-handed fermions differently, and so does not look the same under mirror reflections that exchange left and right. If we try to put a left-handed fermion on the lattice, the most natural rules give you a right-handed partner you never asked for.

The research presented at ICAIF represents another step towards realizing BBVA's ambition of a multi-source foundation model. The goal is to move towards an intelligent, comprehensive and unified understanding of customers, providing a foundation for deploying AI models and agents across different use cases. BBVA is building a foundation for a new generation of AI models that can contribute to a deeper understanding of customers' needs and expectations. Craig's October preprint proposed a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model. The articles leave open what comes next for both the foundation model and the lattice definition.

stories.Headline: Nick Hodges says AI agents will soon write code humans cannot understand
stories.Summary:
Nick Hodges wrote in InfoWorld on November 18, 2026, that he lost a five-year-old bet with his daughter that non-fungible tokens would be a major part of gaming by that week, and she told him he knows nothing about the gaming community. She did concede he was right that agentic coding would become the norm, though she had been skeptical about using AI to write code until she read about a company that used AI to solve a gaming problem a Unity engineer had called unsolvable. Hodges says he is less interested in the gaming community's controversy over AI's harm than in the fact that AI solved a problem considered not solvable, and that everyone will need to get used to this. He notes AI has been doing such things for a while, citing that in May an OpenAI internal model disproved a central conjecture in discrete geometry, the Erdős unit distance problem, a result that was not a complete answer but opened a door humans quickly walked through. Fábio Caversan, the CTO of the Stefanini Group, told Hodges recently that people should get used to whatever they code today being outdated in six months.

Hodges writes that AI is not only better at coding than humans but will soon be orders of magnitude better, doing things we have not thought of yet, and that if Caversan is right, AI code generation will soon be overtaken by something even more functional that produces things we have not imagined. He says a lot of effort now goes into reviewing AI-written code to make sure it is up to snuff, but we may need to prepare for a world where the code agents write is so different that we cannot understand what they are doing. He suggests we are probably not far from the code not mattering, not because agents write such good code but because they write code we have not seen before and cannot currently conceive of. Hodges asks how we trust code that becomes something humans cannot or do not need to understand, and says the job of software developer seems to change almost to that of a QA engineer, validating instead of producing.

If an agent produces something that runs and does exactly what we ask in a manner we do not care about, he writes, the job becomes proving that what it does is correct and what we want. As with the Erdős problem, he says, we probably should not take the agent's word for everything but simply walk through that open door. He concludes that when we say something cannot be done, what we really mean is that no human has done it yet. The article is an opinion piece and does not say what happens next beyond Hodges's argument that developers should prepare to validate rather than produce code.

Articles.Title: AI agents will soon surpass us

stories.headline_source: AI agents will soon surpass us

stories.Headline: FBI reissues advisory warning that criminals use ARTEX to automate business intrusions
stories.Summary:
The FBI reissued its FLASH advisory from the previous week about cybercriminals using ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration testing framework, to target businesses globally, according to a Benzinga report published on November 18, 2026. The bureau said attackers can use ARTEX to automate intrusions and potentially move from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours. According to the advisory, the framework was used during the October ConnectWise supply-chain compromise, which exposed Microsoft 365 customer environments. The FBI directed companies and other organizations to monitor suspicious automated activity and to report potential compromises through the Internet Crime Complaint Center.

Cryptocurrency bettors doubt that artificial intelligence caused the recent Federal Aviation Administration outage, even as the FBI repeated its warning about AI tools automating cyberattacks on businesses. Polygon-based Polymarket currently assigns only a 3% chance that the federal government officially attributes last week's nationwide flight ground stop to AI. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the problem appears tied to a router installation by an FAA contractor, with investigators still trying to pin down whether the failure was human error, a bad device or something else. Multiple outages over the last week have businesses and the administration on edge, including a Microsoft outage that disrupted access to Outlook and Teams.

Thousands of JPMorgan Chase customers reported problems accessing their accounts on Monday, and NSANet, the internal classified communications network for the National Security Agency, also went offline on Tuesday. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said authorities found zero evidence of a coordinated cyberattack behind outages at Microsoft, JPMorgan, airlines and government agencies. Microsoft shares were sliding Tuesday as software stocks faced pressure from outage concerns, AI disruption fears and cybersecurity worries. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the FBI's call for monitoring and reporting through the Internet Crime Complaint Center.

Articles.Title: FBI Reissues Warning About AI-Powered Cyberattacks on Businesses as Crypto Bettors Dismiss AI Link to FAA Outage

stories.headline_source: FBI Reissues Warning About AI-Powered Cyberattacks on Businesses as Crypto Bettors Dismiss AI Link to FAA Outage

stories.Headline: Israel can turn AI infrastructure constraints into opportunity through energy planning, article says
stories.Summary:
A sweeping Democratic victory in the US midterm elections has raised investor concern that data center projects will face more local opposition and tighter restrictions, according to an opinion article by Lior Prosor published by The Jerusalem Post on November 18, 2026. The article says the market routing last Thursday showed that AI trade investors now worry about delays in electricity supply and computing capacity. It argues the market may be overstating the impact of these delays and that the period could be a buying opportunity. For Israel, the article says, the situation should also be a wake-up call.

The article says opposition to data centers stems from residents wanting to know who will pay to expand the grid and what communities will receive, such as tax revenues and local jobs. It points to BAAJA, a bipartisan permitting reform package whose sponsors released an updated version on November 7, which aims to streamline approvals and expand the transmission grid while requiring data centers to cover the costs they add. The package has not passed and would not eliminate local authorities' powers. The article also says a delay in a US project does not necessarily mean lost sales for suppliers, because another customer elsewhere may take the equipment, and it cites SpaceX building capacity outside the US, including a large project in Saudi Arabia, and renting compute through short-term contracts at market prices. It says SpaceX has reported that at current prices new deployments pay back their investment in less than a year.

The article says Israel can become a significant player without matching US investment levels, but the government and the national AI directorate need to connect computing ambitions to an energy plan they can execute. It lists immediate priorities as electricity generation, storage, transmission and grid connections, and calls for a multiyear plan with funding, clear accountability and delivery targets. It says microgrids and regional partnerships in energy and infrastructure should be added alongside expansion of the national grid. The article names Phinergy, which develops long-duration aluminum-air backup power as an alternative to diesel, Turbogen, which offers microturbines for local electricity generation including for smaller data centers, and Bezeq, which could see greater demand for connectivity between distributed computing sites.

The article says not every use of AI requires a giant data center, because inference can often take place in smaller facilities and local systems close to users and electricity sources. It says the difficulty of building AI infrastructure increases the value of those who can deliver it, and that investors may find opportunities in companies the market is punishing too severely. For Israel, it says, this opens a path to build domestic capabilities and sell the world solutions to a shortage everyone is facing. The article notes that its forecasts can prove wrong and computing prices can fall.

Articles.Title: Israel could turn the AI infrastructure crunch into an opportunity

stories.headline_source: Israel could turn the AI infrastructure crunch into an opportunity

stories.Headline: Protesters rally outside Nasdaq as Anthropic opens at $83 and police make arrests
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026, Anthropic executives gathered at Nasdaq in New York City's Times Square for the opening bell as the company's initial public offering priced shares at $83, with initial demand appearing strong before the stock started trading at midday. Outside Nasdaq, demonstrators affiliated with groups including Stop Funding Billionaires, Climate Defiance, Sunrise NYC, Act Up NYC, NYC-DSA, JVP-NYC, Climate Defenders, Planet Over Profit and New York Communities for Change held signs reading "Stop Tech Oligarchs" and "Freeze AI" as the stock ticker raced by on screens behind them. Representatives of the group used a small, hot-pink megaphone to address the media and onlookers, and between speeches they chanted slogans such as "Hey, hey. Ho-ho. This IPO has got to go!" and "Anthropic, get off it, put people over profit!" Their concerns ranged from the potential economic impact if the AI bubble bursts to AI's effects on the environment, healthcare, surveillance, and jobs. There were arrests, and one demonstrator in a Greenpeace T-shirt was led away by police after seating themselves with a sign at the entrance to Nasdaq.

James Inniss, an organizer with New York Communities for Change, said the group was there because Anthropic poses a threat, not in a Terminator-Skynet style, but in a pension fund style, because AI is a bubble that he called worse than 2008 with the real estate crisis. He said that if pension funds are the ones stripped in five or 10 years when this bubble bursts, then the people affected have to be out there to fight and tell everybody that is not acceptable and not okay. Bryce Rogers, an organizer with a group called Resisting Automated Disempowerment (RAD), said he was there to protest the fact that the IPO was moving ahead despite a lack of information about the risks the company's technology poses, and that reading the auditing firm METR's recent report on Anthropic left him with more questions than answers. Rogers praised New York's Responsible AI Safety and Education (RAISE) Act and called for more organizing to demand greater regulation and transparency, saying people can reclaim authorship of their future. Brandon Cuicchi of ACT UP New York said he was concerned about AI's impact on healthcare, saying hospitals are cutting staff and trying to replace it with AI, medical offices are trying to pre-screen people with AI instead of a live professional, and AI is deciding medical outcomes and treatments in this country. Kenny Moll, an activist affiliated with a campaign called QuitGPT and the Sunrise Movement, said he was concerned about the environmental impact of AI but also about the relationship between AI firms, surveillance, and the government, saying these companies are working hand in hand with fascist governments and that cannot be allowed.

Aber Kawas, a Palestinian-American democratic socialist recently elected as a New York State Senator, said AI companies are among the biggest enemies of the progressive movement. She said people across the nation are trying to turn the tide to create a country where their state and city invest in communities during an affordability crisis and not in war and destruction, and that the biggest enemies to that are AI companies and corporate interests which drive the government to invest in things like AI companies that are destroying the climate and destroying people's lives. In a statement following the demonstration, organizers attributed a quote to one of the demonstrators who was arrested, saying their demand is clear: freeze reckless AI development and don't bail out Big Tech when their bubble inevitably pops.

Articles.Title: No Bailout for the AI Bubble, Anthropic IPO Protesters Say

stories.headline_source: No Bailout for the AI Bubble, Anthropic IPO Protesters Say

stories.Headline: Denmark and Ukraine sign declaration for Danish forces to train military AI on Ukrainian battlefield data
stories.Summary:
Denmark’s Ministry of Defense announced on Tuesday that Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus and his Ukrainian counterpart, Yevhenii Khmara, signed a declaration agreeing to cooperate on the development of artificial intelligence, according to a Kyiv Post report dated November 18, 2026. Under the agreement, the Danish armed forces will receive large quantities of battlefield data and images from Ukraine, which they will use to train their own warfighting AI models. The deal gives Denmark direct access to Ukraine’s advanced Avengers Labs, which has built an extensive database drawn from millions of battlefield images and other information. Avengers Labs was initiated by Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense and uses the DELTA target detection system, which has created an annotated dataset obtained from more than 100,000 drone video streams each month. Denmark joins what the Danish ministry described as an exclusive club, since the United Kingdom was the first international partner to gain access to the platform.

The agreement requires Danish experts to work with their Ukrainian counterparts on the extensive dataset so they can train their own AI models and applications. That work is meant to accelerate the integration of artificial intelligence into military operations in support of the defense capabilities of both countries. Denmark’s armed forces are also establishing their own AI Center, which will be the focus for implementing the new agreement. The center will coordinate cooperation with companies and research institutions that will enhance the country’s defense technology contribution. The Danish ministry said the cooperation would help develop the combat power of the Danish defense forces through knowledge of artificial intelligence and new technologies.

Bruus said technology on the battlefield is constantly developing and that Ukraine is at the forefront in this area. He said it is therefore very valuable that Denmark can learn from Ukraine through cooperation, though he acknowledged it rests on a sad basis. Bruus also said Denmark continues its unwavering support for Ukraine while strengthening the capabilities of its own armed forces through the sharing of AI and emerging military technologies. The Kyiv Post report describes the Danish ministry’s announcement as the source for the details of the declaration and the access it grants.

The report places the agreement in the wider context of Denmark’s support for Ukraine and its effort to build up its own military technology. It says the Danish armed forces are setting up an AI Center that will serve as the hub for the new cooperation and for coordination with companies and research institutions. The Kyiv Post, which describes itself as Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995, carried the announcement. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the establishment of the AI Center and the planned work with Ukrainian counterparts.

Articles.Title: Ukrainian Combat Data to Help Shape Denmark’s Next Generation of Military AI

stories.headline_source: Ukrainian Combat Data to Help Shape Denmark’s Next Generation of Military AI

stories.Headline: Jennifer Wood says auditors must validate AI output and challenge it with professional skepticism
stories.Summary:
Jennifer Wood, a partner and the assurance service line leader at the Bonadio Group, wrote in a Bloomberg Tax article published on November 18, 2026, that artificial intelligence must test rather than replace auditors’ professional skepticism. She said the AICPA’s new guidance on using AI in financial reporting and auditing, published on October 13, 2026, arrived at the perfect time and is nonauthoritative but increasingly relevant to audit quality and peer-review readiness. She said the practice aid lacks guidance on how firms should consistently validate and document AI-assisted procedures, particularly when AI is used to identify exceptions or support audit conclusions, along with practical examples. She said the biggest challenge for audit firms is determining when auditors can trust AI output, how to validate it, and when their own professional skepticism requires them to challenge it.

Wood said AI does not change auditors’ responsibility to secure sufficiently appropriate audit evidence but changes how they fulfill that responsibility. She said the biggest misconception is that AI is simply a faster way to perform existing tasks, when it is actually an opportunity to rethink how audits are performed. She said an AI output can be accurate without being complete, and she prefers the expression “validate before relying.” She said her firm has used AI for financial statement tie-outs and document analysis, and that a tie-out involving more than 100 pages historically consumed nearly two days of staff time, which AI can accelerate while identifying inconsistencies a human reviewer might overlook, though the auditor must still confirm the results. She said that in a hypothetical example of using AI to review 1,000 revenue contracts and identify unusual recognition provisions, the tool flags 25 contracts and all 25 are legitimate exceptions, but it might have overlooked another 10 contracts containing problematic provisions, so every exception identified was accurate yet the analysis was incomplete.

Wood said professional skepticism has historically focused on challenging management’s assertions, estimates, and representations, but now auditors must also challenge the technology that helps them evaluate those assertions. She said AI-generated work can look remarkably polished and authoritative, which can create a false sense of confidence, and auditors should instinctively ask what evidence supports a conclusion, what assumptions were made, and what might have been missed. She said AI creates additional responsibilities for engagement partners and reviewers, who need to understand how AI is being used on their engagements and whether appropriate validation has occurred, without needing to understand every technical aspect of the underlying model. She said firms need clear policies defining approved AI tools, permissible uses, confidentiality requirements, and expectations for validation and documentation, and that documentation for AI-assisted audit procedures should identify the tool used, the purpose of the procedure, the relevant inputs and outputs, how results were validated, and how the work influenced audit conclusions.

Wood said firms should distinguish between AI used for administrative efficiency and AI used to support audit evidence, which warrant different levels of oversight, and should incorporate AI governance into their existing system of quality management rather than treat it as a separate technology initiative. She said AI can improve audit quality and reduce the risk of human fatigue associated with repetitive procedures, citing financial statement tie-outs and document analysis as examples, and that AI can quickly summarize key provisions in a lengthy lease agreement or debt agreement so the auditor can focus on evaluating the accounting implications. She said the goal should be better audits, not just faster ones, and the greatest opportunity is reinvesting time saved in higher-value audit activities including risk assessment, investigating exceptions, and challenging management’s assumptions. She said that over the next three to five years, the firms that succeed will be those that integrate AI into their methodologies, invest in quality management, and fundamentally rethink how they develop their people, and that the firms that differentiate themselves won’t necessarily be using AI the most but will be demonstrating that AI is making their audits better.

Articles.Title: AI Must Test, Not Replace, Auditors’ Professional Skepticism

stories.headline_source: AI Must Test, Not Replace, Auditors’ Professional Skepticism

stories.Headline: Seoul researchers develop deep learning model that raises pathologists accuracy in detecting rare kidney cancer
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Asan Medical Center in Seoul developed a deep learning model to identify a rare and aggressive kidney cancer called fumarate hydratase-deficient renal cell carcinoma. This study, published in npj Digital Medicine, tested the tool using 335 digitized pathology slides to see if it could help doctors distinguish this specific cancer from other renal types. Twenty-one pathologists, including seven residents and fourteen specialists, examined 30 challenging cases both independently and with the assistance of the AI. The results showed that AI assistance increased overall diagnostic accuracy from 60% to 73.3% and improved precision from 66.7% to 77.8%.

The AI model, built on the ResNeXt101 architecture, flags suspected cases and generates color-coded maps to highlight suspicious tissue regions for the doctors. It is designed to help pathologists identify patients who may require additional genetic analysis or immunohistochemistry testing for a final diagnosis. The study found that receptive doctors improved their accuracy but had a median overreliance rate of 80%, meaning they often accepted incorrect AI advice. Resistant doctors were less influenced by AI errors, but they showed no statistically significant improvement in their diagnostic accuracy during the tests.

Professor Yong Mee Cho stated that AI could help clinicians recognize rare cancers they might otherwise overlook to ensure patients receive confirmatory testing. Professor Namkug Kim noted that effective AI use requires skills independent of traditional diagnostic expertise, which suggests a need for tailored human-AI collaboration strategies. The researchers questioned whether conventional clinical training adequately prepares doctors to critically assess AI recommendations to avoid overreliance. Future studies in routine pathology settings will determine if specialized training can help doctors benefit from AI while reducing the risk of errors.

Articles.Title: AI can detect rare cancer, but can doctors use it?

stories.headline_source: AI can detect rare cancer, but can doctors use it?

stories.Headline: BusPatrol runs AI school bus cameras in Montgomery County that generate tickets but show little decline in violations
stories.Summary:
BusPatrol, a company that operates artificial-intelligence-powered cameras on roughly 35,000 school buses in 24 states and more than 350 school districts, began operating in Montgomery County in 2017, and by the 2019, 20 school year all Montgomery County Public Schools buses had been equipped with cameras, according to an investigation by Bloomberg Businessweek in partnership with Type Investigations. The investigation found that school bus cameras in the county have generated more than 375,000 tickets and $92 million in fines, but that violations have remained relatively consistent, with little evidence that collisions near stopped school buses have declined. The number of citations per active camera barely changed over five years, averaging 36 per active camera in 2020 and falling only to 34 by 2025. The investigation also identified at least three children who were struck by drivers while getting on or off stopped school buses in Montgomery County since 2017, based on a review of local news reports and school bus camera footage. There has been some more recent improvement in the numbers, with Montgomery County police reporting 40,854 citations for illegally passing stopped school buses during the 2025, 26 school year, a 19.1% decrease from the previous school year, though thousands of drivers continue to pass stopped school buses while their red lights are flashing and stop arms are extended.

The BusPatrol cameras use artificial intelligence to identify vehicles that appear to illegally pass a stopped school bus with its stop arm extended, capturing video and images of the vehicle including its license plate and sending that footage to local law enforcement for review, and police determine whether a violation occurred, so the technology does not automatically issue a ticket. The county's Vision Zero program has defended the cameras as a tool for accountability and education, as well as a way to collect information about dangerous driving around school buses. The investigation raises a broader question about whether more citations are translating into fewer dangerous encounters for children. Other communities across the Washington region also use school bus stop-arm enforcement cameras, although those programs were not included in the national investigation.

In Falls Church, Virginia, the city issued 1,193 school bus camera citations in 2025, more than twice the 546 citations issued when the program began in 2015, while Fairfax County launched its own school bus camera enforcement program in 2025 and recorded more than 6,300 citations or warnings between April 2024 and Dec. 17, 2025. Washington, D.C., also installed stop-arm safety cameras on 25 school buses in 2024, and the District's program is separate from the BusPatrol system examined in the investigation. The debate over school bus camera enforcement comes as Montgomery County continues to track pedestrian safety concerns, recording 336 pedestrian-involved crashes countywide during the first nine months of 2026, including 17 fatal crashes, figures that include pedestrian crashes throughout the county and are not limited to school buses or school zones. The central question remains whether automated school bus enforcement is doing enough to prevent children from being struck by drivers, or whether additional safety measures are needed beyond issuing citations.

Articles.Title: Do Montgomery County AI-powered school bus cameras make children safer?

stories.headline_source: Do Montgomery County AI-powered school bus cameras make children safer?

stories.Headline: Researchers map AI uses across construction lifecycle and find mitigation outweighs adaptation
stories.Summary:
An international team of researchers from Australia, Finland, Morocco and Thailand systematically reviewed a decade of published research on how artificial intelligence can support climate adaptation and mitigation at every stage of a construction project, from material production through demolition. The review, published in the KeAi journal Risk Sciences, followed PRISMA guidelines and combined bibliometric and content analyses to map where AI is being applied, how mature those applications are and what barriers stand in the way of adoption. The authors propose a lifecycle-based framework linking AI applications to climate outcomes, technological maturity and adoption barriers. Buildings and construction consume vast quantities of concrete, steel and aluminum and account for a substantial share of global energy use and energy-related carbon emissions, and the sector faces growing pressure both to cut its climate impact and to become more resilient as extreme weather events intensify.

The review found that AI can contribute across the whole construction lifecycle, including lower-carbon and more resilient materials, greener procurement and supply chains, energy-efficient and climate-resilient design, optimized equipment and scheduling on site, smarter building operation and maintenance, and better recycling and waste recovery at end of life. The team distilled these contributions into a conceptual framework identifying three principal pathways: cleaner and more resource-efficient energy use, decarbonization of the built environment, and responsible production and consumption of resources. The evidence is unevenly distributed, with most studies focused on mitigation such as cutting emissions and energy use and far fewer exploring adaptation such as climate-resilient infrastructure or extreme-weather preparedness. Applications such as predictive maintenance, building energy optimization and computer-vision monitoring are relatively mature, whereas generative climate-resilient design and fully integrated digital twins remain largely at the pilot stage.

Corresponding author Fahim Ullah of Victoria University in Australia said AI should not be treated as an isolated technological application but as a lifecycle-wide enabling technology that works best when integrated with complementary tools such as building information modeling, digital twins and the Internet of Things. He said the presence of AI capability does not automatically produce a net-positive climate outcome, because training and operating the models requires computational resources and electricity, and the climate benefits of AI must be evaluated against its own environmental footprint. Ullah added that AI can make a major contribution to a low-carbon, climate-resilient construction industry but is neither a standalone solution nor inherently sustainable. The authors also identify key barriers including poor data quality, interoperability problems, high implementation costs, organizational readiness, regulatory uncertainty and cybersecurity concerns, and they stress that AI is not environmentally neutral.

Articles.Title: A Lifecycle Framework for Artificial Intelligence in Sustainable Construction Research

stories.headline_source: A Lifecycle Framework for Artificial Intelligence in Sustainable Construction Research

stories.Headline: Ejaaz Ahamadeen examines Anthropic's AI models ahead of its IPO and the race to self-improvement
stories.Summary:
In a Yahoo Finance video published on November 19, 2026, In the Loop host Ejaaz Ahamadeen examined Anthropic's evolving AI models ahead of the company's highly anticipated initial public offering and the accelerating race toward more advanced artificial intelligence. Ahamadeen broke down the latest predictions for recursive self-improvement, the point at which an AI system could autonomously improve its own capabilities. He described recursive self-improvement as an AI model so smart that it can design, build and research the next version of itself, an AI smarter than the smartest AI researcher. He said the researchers paid hundreds of millions of dollars to work at these AI labs are, in effect, building their own replacement. He added that the part exciting investors is not the self-improving part but what it means, because such a model could theoretically be pointed at any profession, any vertical or any hard task.

Ahamadeen referred to an AI 2027 report whose authors made predictions back in 2025 or perhaps 2024, and he said they had one of the most accurate predictions so far. One of their cases covered when self-improving technology would arrive and when white-collar work would be replaced by AI. He said they have now moved up their dates, having been about 10 months late, and they predict this to happen as early as the end of next year, 2027. He described a world where an AI model can automate 99% of white-collar work, which makes up trillions of dollars worth of value in the economy. He then posed the question of what one would value the company that created such a model, if the leading model that does that is an Anthropic Claude model.

Ahamadeen acknowledged that listeners might hear him and say he is just selling propaganda for Anthropic, but he said he has looked into the research and the data. He said it is not just Anthropic proving it, but also OpenAI and Google, and that all three companies have made public statements saying they are very close to achieving recursive self-improvement. He said OpenAI has solved a bunch of really complex hard math and physics problems, and Google is solving a lot of complex science problems and advancing its own scientific experiments internally. He said Anthropic is focused on biology and medicine and cancer specifically. He noted that all of this assumes Anthropic is able to overcome a number of challenges that still lay ahead of it.

The video ran alongside coverage of Anthropic's Nasdaq debut, with a live blog inviting readers to follow the big listing, and the stock was quoted at 94.62, up 11.62 or 14.00%, in one snapshot and at 95.40, up 12.40 or 14.94%, in another. The broader market was lower on the day, with the S&P 500 down 106.49 or 1.45% at 7,217.14, the Dow 30 down 882.42 or 1.76% at 49,315.75 and the Nasdaq Composite down 363.75 or 1.49% at 24,066.13. The video's description said Ahamadeen examines Anthropic's models ahead of the IPO and explores the accelerating race toward more advanced artificial intelligence. The page listed no further news stories on the subject.

Articles.Title: The timeline for AI to take over white-collar jobs is shrinking

stories.headline_source: The timeline for AI to take over white-collar jobs is shrinking

stories.Headline: An innovation professor argues that the most valuable AI may sometimes choose to do nothing
stories.Summary:
A professor of innovation who writes about technology and management argued in a Fast Company piece published on November 18, 2026, that the most valuable artificial intelligence may sometimes be the one that chooses to do nothing at all. He described how the human brain works as an efficient optimizer that quickly adopts any effortless shortcut, noting that people once memorized many phone numbers but now barely recall their own because the numbers sit a few clicks away. He said he never uses chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini to write his articles, because writing is how he makes concepts stick in his mind for teaching and discussion, and he compared an unused skill to a muscle that atrophies. He added that he does use AI to translate passages, find supporting articles and check whether his explanations come across clearly, but he keeps writing itself as a skill he wants to protect.

The article asked whether an AI can learn when its intervention would make things worse, using a hypothetical sales agent that spots a customer nearing renewal and instantly reviews the account, writes a personalized email, offers a discount and schedules a follow-up. If the customer would have renewed anyway, the piece said, the company has wasted an interaction, risked alienating the customer and given up margin for nothing, so even perfectly executed tasks can rest on a perfectly wrong decision. It cited a Microsoft study titled "When to show a suggestion? Integrating human feedback in AI-assisted programming," which used data from 535 programmers to evaluate a system that withheld suggestions likely to be rejected, and found that optimizing for suggestion acceptance could produce lower-quality suggestions. The author argued that experienced employees develop judgment over many iterations about when to follow up, when to escalate and when too many interventions look messy, and that this judgment is something companies pay for, while AI evaluations tend to reward visible activity the way a hyperactive employee might be rewarded.

The author said managers buying or deploying AI should find out what outcome the system is trying to improve and design ways to learn whether its actions actually helped, warning that a renewal following an email does not prove the email caused the renewal and that useful comparisons may require carefully designed experiments. He stressed that human oversight, the now-famous human-in-the-loop, must remain, with people defining the obligations and limits within which the system can learn, because a missed warning or an unanswered complaint can be costly. He said he has not seen an AI system that reviews an account, checks the evidence in corporate ERP or CRM systems and decides that contacting the customer would probably make things worse, and he argued that the accumulated learning behind such a decision should stay under the company's control even if the model or vendor is replaced. Such a system might make a disappointing demo, he concluded, but it could be excellent business.

Articles.Title: The smartest AI might be the one that leaves us alone

stories.headline_source: The smartest AI might be the one that leaves us alone

stories.Headline: Ravi Mhatre says frontier AI firms must be public
stories.Summary:
Early Anthropic investor and Lightspeed Partner Ravi Mhatre said in a CNBC interview on November 19, 2026, that it is extremely important for frontier artificial intelligence companies to be public. The interview, which appeared on the Halftime Report, covered the company's record IPO and frontier artificial intelligence models, among other topics. The segment ran three minutes and nineteen seconds and was posted about forty-two minutes before the page was captured. CNBC also posted a separate interview with early Anthropic investor Matt Murphy, who said the firm is extremely bullish about the future of the company. A clip of Bryn Talkington said Anthropic's raise solidifies the capital spending, and another clip said Anthropic is enjoying working with SpaceX, according to CEO Dario Amodei.

The coverage places the comments alongside Anthropic's record IPO, which the Mhatre interview description names without giving a figure, a date or an exchange. The page gives no size for the raise, no valuation and no share price, and it does not say when the listing took place. The only timing on the page is the November 19, 2026 date of the Mhatre interview and the posting times of the related videos. The related segments also tie the company to capital spending, through Talkington's remark that the raise solidifies the capex spend, and to a working relationship with SpaceX, which Amodei is said to describe as enjoyable. The articles do not say what the capital spending covers or what the SpaceX work involves.

Mhatre is identified as an early investor in Anthropic and a partner at Lightspeed, and he made the public company comment in the Halftime Report interview. Murphy, also described as an early Anthropic investor, said in his own CNBC interview that the firm is extremely bullish about the future of the company. Amodei, the CEO, is cited in a video description as saying Anthropic is enjoying working with SpaceX. Talkington's comment that the raise solidifies the capex spend is carried as a video clip. The page attributes these remarks through its video descriptions and does not provide fuller quotes from any of the speakers.

The page offers no further context on why public status matters for frontier artificial intelligence companies, and it does not say whether Anthropic has commented on the point. It also gives no details on the IPO itself beyond calling it a record, so the size, timing and terms of the listing remain unstated. What happens next is not described in the articles, which consist of the interview page and its related video listings. The only forward-looking note comes from Murphy, whose bullish view concerns the future of the company rather than any specific plan or event.

Articles.Title: Early Anthropic investor Ravi Mhatre: 'Extremely important' that frontier AI companies are public

stories.headline_source: Early Anthropic investor Ravi Mhatre: 'Extremely important' that frontier AI companies are public

stories.Headline: Apollo CEO Marc Rowan says the AI buildout may need about $8 trillion in capital
stories.Summary:
Apollo Global Management CEO Marc Rowan warned that the AI buildout could require about US$8 trillion of capital, Yahoo Finance reported on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. Bailey Pemberton wrote the article, which was published at 3:11 AM CST and runs about three minutes. Rowan argued that this AI funding need may push more borrowing into private credit and away from traditional U.S. bond markets. He flagged that financing large scale AI infrastructure could influence borrowing costs and funding access for companies outside the tech sector. Apollo Global Management trades on the NYSE under the ticker APO.

Apollo is a US based diversified financial group with a US$70.8b market cap that focuses on credit, private equity, infrastructure, secondaries and real estate. The Victory Capital partnership and the planned Victory Apollo Private Markets Fund aim to distribute Apollo's private credit and real asset strategies to a wider base of wealth and retirement investors. Apollo made a US$2.5b commitment to Focus Financial Partners and issued US$600m of junior subordinated notes. The TD Cowen Financials & Fintech Conference on 18 November 2026 may give extra detail on how management plans to capture any AI driven financing flows. stories.Headline: Partly releases Interpreter 3, an AI model trained on vehicle repair that beats general models on parts and planning
stories.Summary:
Partly released Interpreter 3, an AI reasoning model trained specifically on vehicle repair, on 18 November 2026, alongside benchmark results showing it outperformed general-purpose models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google at identifying vehicles, sourcing parts and planning repairs. The Austin-based company says the model named the exact vehicle variant for 19 of every 20 cars, against four in 20 for the best general model tested. Interpreter 3 never named the wrong variant, handing uncertain cases to a person, while expert human reviewers misidentified 18 of 250 vehicles on their first attempt. In parts lookup, it returned the correct OEM part first 75% of the time, ahead of Google's Gemini 4 Argon at 63%, OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra at 62% and Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 at 50%.

For repair planning, 37% of its suggestions matched work the shop later added, more than double the 17% achieved by Gemini 4 Argon, with fewer than half as many incorrect suggestions. Partly ran the tests this month against six general models with web search, using 250 vehicles, 257 parts and 100 repair jobs from a US shop whose data had not been used to train Interpreter. The benchmarks were run by Partly itself, and Interpreter 3 drew on licensed OEM catalogue data from more than 50 brands that the general models did not have. That is also the point of the comparison: in repair, exact OEM data is an advantage general models cannot easily replicate from the open web.

Levi Fawcett, co-founder and Chief Executive of Partly, said every decision in repair depends on the exact car in front of you, which is what makes it so hard for general models. The company launched its PartlyRepair AI assistant for body shops in the US earlier this month and is piloting it with some of the largest US multi-site operators. Interpreter already powers its products in Europe and Australasia, according to the company. The articles do not say what happens next beyond those launches and pilots.

stories.Headline: Jesse Rome tells CX Today that AI makes selling harder and salespeople must become industry experts and trusted partners
stories.Summary:
Jesse Rome of Aslan Sales Training spoke to CX Today's Sean Nolan in an interview published on 18 November 2026 about how sales teams can use AI without losing the human side of selling. Rome said selling has become harder since he and Nolan did it, and that AI is a big reason. He said buyers have more information than ever before and ask why they need a sales rep if they can learn things on AI. He said the shift to virtual has created more decision makers in the room, with leaders from APAC and EMEA able to join a video call together. He said buyers now look for a solution partner who can make sense of different tools, tariffs and socioeconomic factors.

Rome said Aslan surveyed a thousand people in the B2B space and asked what is the number one thing they look for. He said buyers no longer need somebody who is an expert on products but people who are an expert on the industry. He said 90% of them named understanding their industry and having a unique solution as the number one decision-making factor. He said selling is harder, AI has given more information than ever, and socioeconomic factors are crazy. He said salespeople need to be more of a solution consultant and a trusted partner, not just a product expert.

Rome said Aslan has been around for about 30 years as a global sales training consulting firm partnering with large, medium and small organizations worldwide. He said it helps implement sales methodologies, organizational change and the conversion of product experts into trusted partners through enablement and certification. He said the foundation is being other centered, putting the needs of everybody you interact with before your own. He said people forget 90% of what they learn within a week, so Aslan Plus reinforces it through certifications, knowledge checks and AI-powered exercises. He said the future of AI is that it will start to replicate close to 80% of our productivity at 20% of the cost.

Rome said Aslan Plus is an AI-powered enablement platform built to help sellers sell, managers coach and organizations train and scale their go-to-market more efficiently. He said it works across four functions: comprehend, apply, master and integrate. He said application is the meat of the platform, with AI role plays as the flagship product and the right content at the right moment. He said mastery covers product, coaching and training certification, tracking compliance and development, because too many people are quiet quitting and the top 10% are not being invested in.

He said Aslan used to be just a methodology company and is now a full enablement partner, so the platform must sit in the flow of work in the CRM, communication tools, CMS and SSO. Rome said he probably fits into the bucket of salespeople hesitant about AI and thinks of himself as maybe a little smooth talking. He said you need humility, and you are either getting better or getting worse, with no staying the same. He said change is imminent and it is about whether you are ahead of the curve or behind it.

He said AI is helping with workflows and messaging now, and that if you are not growing the bottom line in an organization of 200 reps, they will look at how to optimize your role. He said the human side of selling will never be replaced, the world of account managers and solution partners is where a lot of the growth is going, and AI will duplicate and scale exactly who you are. Rome said every person is motivated by purpose or profit, either wanting to make more money or help more people. He said those motivated by money should learn a tool that duplicates their efforts and makes them more efficient if it stays in their voice and the right process.

He said those who care about customers should implement AI because it will make sure you do not forget Cheryl's birthday. He said it will make sure you know about a merger and acquisition two weeks ago in their industry that will affect the global economics of those warehouses before it gets to you. He said if you truly care about your customers you will implement this because it gives more insights on the industry. He said whether you are motivated by purpose or profit, this can help you either way.
